<P><B>Deion Luywnn Sanders Sr.</B> (<SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</SPAN><SPAN title="'d' in 'dye'">d</SPAN><SPAN title="/iː/: 'ee' in 'fleece'">iː</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɒ/: 'o' in 'body'">ɒ</SPAN><SPAN title="'n' in 'nigh'">n</SPAN></SPAN>/</A></SPAN></SPAN>; born August 9, 1967), nicknamed <B>Primetime</B>, is a former <A href="/wiki/American_football" title="American football">American football</A> and <A href="/wiki/Baseball" title="Baseball">baseball</A> player who works as an analyst for <A href="/wiki/The_NFL_Today" title="The NFL Today">CBS Sports</A> and the <A href="/wiki/NFL_Network" title="NFL Network">NFL Network</A>. He was inducted into the <A href="/wiki/Pro_Football_Hall_of_Fame" title="Pro Football Hall of Fame">Pro Football Hall of Fame</A> in 2011.</P>
<P>Sanders played football primarily at <A href="/wiki/Cornerback" title="Cornerback">cornerback</A>, but also as a kick returner, punt returner and occasionally wide receiver. He played in the <A href="/wiki/National_Football_League" title="National Football League">National Football League</A> (NFL) for the <A href="/wiki/Atlanta_Falcons" title="Atlanta Falcons">Atlanta Falcons</A>, the <A href="/wiki/San_Francisco_49ers" title="San Francisco 49ers">San Francisco 49ers</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys" title="Dallas Cowboys">Dallas Cowboys</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Washington_Redskins" title="Washington Redskins">Washington Redskins</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Baltimore_Ravens" title="Baltimore Ravens">Baltimore Ravens</A>, winning the <A href="/wiki/Super_Bowl" title="Super Bowl">Super Bowl</A> with both the 49ers and the Cowboys. An <A href="/wiki/Outfielder" title="Outfielder">outfielder</A> in baseball, he played professionally for the <A href="/wiki/New_York_Yankees" title="New York Yankees">New York Yankees</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Atlanta_Braves" title="Atlanta Braves">Atlanta Braves</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds" title="Cincinnati Reds">Cincinnati Reds</A> and the <A href="/wiki/San_Francisco_Giants" title="San Francisco Giants">San Francisco Giants</A>, and participated in the <A href="/wiki/1992_World_Series" title="1992 World Series">1992 World Series</A> with the Braves. He attended <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_University" title="Florida State University">Florida State University</A>, where he was recognized as a two-time <A href="/wiki/College_Football_All-America_Team" title="College Football All-America Team">All-American</A> in <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_Seminoles_football" title="Florida State Seminoles football">football</A>, and also played <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_Seminoles_baseball" title="Florida State Seminoles baseball">baseball</A> and ran <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_Seminoles_track_and_field" title="Florida State Seminoles track and field">track</A>.</P>
<P>Sanders founded the <A href="/wiki/Prime_Prep_Academy" title="Prime Prep Academy">Prime Prep Academy</A> <A href="/wiki/Charter_school" title="Charter school">charter school</A> in 2012 and has coached at the school. The school was closed January 30, 2015, due to financial insolvency.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> In 2014, he debuted his new show, the <I>Deion Family Playbook</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_life">Early life</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=1&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Early life">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="High_school">High school</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=2&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: High school">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Sanders was born in <A href="/wiki/Fort_Myers,_Florida" title="Fort Myers, Florida">Fort Myers, Florida</A>. He attended <A href="/wiki/North_Fort_Myers_High_School" title="North Fort Myers High School">North Fort Myers High School</A> in <A href="/wiki/North_Fort_Myers,_Florida" title="North Fort Myers, Florida">North Fort Myers</A>, and was a <A href="/wiki/Letterman_(sports)" title="Letterman (sports)">letterman</A> and All-State honoree in football, basketball and baseball. In 1985, Sanders was named to the <A href="/wiki/FHSAA%27s_All-Century_Team" class="mw-redirect" title="FHSAA's All-Century Team">Florida High School Association All-Century Team</A> which selected the top 33 players in the 100-year history of high school football in the state.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Kansas_City_Royals" title="Kansas City Royals">Kansas City Royals</A> selected Sanders out of North Fort Myers High School in the sixth round of the <A href="/wiki/1985_Major_League_Baseball_draft" title="1985 Major League Baseball draft">1985 Major League Baseball draft</A>. He did not sign with the Royals.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>

<P>Sanders enrolled at <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_University" title="Florida State University">Florida State University</A> and played three sports for the <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_Seminoles" title="Florida State Seminoles">Florida State Seminoles</A>: <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_Seminoles_football" title="Florida State Seminoles football">football</A>, <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_Seminoles_baseball" title="Florida State Seminoles baseball">baseball</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Florida_State_Seminoles_track_and_field" title="Florida State Seminoles track and field">track</A>. Beginning his freshman year, he started in the Seminoles' secondary, played <A href="/wiki/Outfield" title="Outfield">outfield</A> for the baseball team that finished fifth in the nation, and helped lead the track and field team to a conference championship.</P>
<P>Under <A href="/wiki/Head_coach" title="Head coach">head coach</A> <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Bowden" title="Bobby Bowden">Bobby Bowden</A>, Sanders was a two-time consensus <A href="/wiki/All-American" class="mw-redirect" title="All-American">All-American</A> cornerback in 1987 and 1988, and a third team All-American in 1986, <A href="/wiki/Interception" title="Interception">intercepting</A> 14 passes in his career, including three in <A href="/wiki/Bowl_game" title="Bowl game">bowl games</A>, and managed to return one interception 100 yards for a <A href="/wiki/Touchdown" title="Touchdown">touchdown</A> breaking <A href="/wiki/Fred_Biletnikoff" title="Fred Biletnikoff">Fred Biletnikoff</A>'s interception return record by one yard. He won the <A href="/wiki/Jim_Thorpe_Award" title="Jim Thorpe Award">Jim Thorpe Award</A> in 1988. He was also a standout <A href="/wiki/Punt_returner" class="mw-redirect" title="Punt returner">punt returner</A> for Florida State, leading the nation in 1988 with his <A href="/wiki/Punt_return" class="mw-redirect" title="Punt return">punt return</A> average, and breaking the school's record for career punt return yards. Sanders made an interception with 5 seconds left to seal Florida State's 13-7 win over Auburn in the <A href="/wiki/1989_Sugar_Bowl" title="1989 Sugar Bowl">1989 Sugar Bowl</A>, during the 1988 postseason. Based on those accolades, his jersey at Florida State, #2, was retired in 1995. He finished his career with 126 punt returns for 1,429 yards.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<P>While playing baseball under head coach <A href="/wiki/Mike_Martin_(baseball_coach)" title="Mike Martin (baseball coach)">Mike Martin</A> at Florida State, Sanders <A href="/wiki/Batting_average" title="Batting average">hit</A> .331 in 1986; he was known more for <A href="/wiki/Stolen_base" title="Stolen base">base stealing</A>, compiling 27 stolen bases in 1987.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2015)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>Sanders once played the first game of a baseball <A href="/wiki/Doubleheader_(baseball)" title="Doubleheader (baseball)">doubleheader</A>, ran a leg of a <A href="/wiki/4_%C3%97_100_metres_relay" title="4 × 100 metres relay">4 × 100 relay</A>, then returned to play another baseball game.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>

<P>Sanders played a nine-year, part-time baseball career, playing left and center field in 641 games with 4 teams. He was originally drafted by the <A href="/wiki/Kansas_City_Royals" title="Kansas City Royals">Kansas City Royals</A> in the 6th round of the <A href="/wiki/1985_Major_League_Baseball_draft" title="1985 Major League Baseball draft">1985 draft</A>, but did not sign with them. The <A href="/wiki/New_York_Yankees" title="New York Yankees">New York Yankees</A> selected Sanders in the 30th round of the <A href="/wiki/1988_Major_League_Baseball_draft" title="1988 Major League Baseball draft">1988 Major League Baseball draft</A>, and he signed with the team on June 22.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2015)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> He opened the 1989 season with the <A href="/wiki/Albany-Colonie_Yankees" class="mw-redirect" title="Albany-Colonie Yankees">Albany-Colonie Yankees</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Class_AA" class="mw-redirect" title="Class AA">Class AA</A> <A href="/wiki/Eastern_League_(baseball)" title="Eastern League (baseball)">Eastern League</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> Though he planned to leave the Yankees in July to attend NFL <A href="/wiki/Training_camp" title="Training camp">training camp</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> he became embroiled in a contract dispute with the Falcons, and used the Yankees as leverage. He received a promotion to the major leagues, and spent the summer with the <A href="/wiki/Columbus_Clippers" title="Columbus Clippers">Columbus Clippers</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Class_AAA" class="mw-redirect" title="Class AAA">Class AAA</A> <A href="/wiki/International_League" title="International League">International League</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> He made his <A href="/wiki/Major_league_baseball" class="mw-redirect" title="Major league baseball">major league baseball</A> debut on May 31, 1989.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Sanders made the Yankees' <A href="/wiki/Opening_Day" title="Opening Day">Opening Day</A> roster for the 1990 season.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> On May 22, 1990, Sanders became involved in a dispute with <A href="/wiki/Chicago_White_Sox" title="Chicago White Sox">Chicago White Sox</A>' <A href="/wiki/Catcher" title="Catcher">catcher</A> <A href="/wiki/Carlton_Fisk" title="Carlton Fisk">Carlton Fisk</A>. Sanders started by stepping up to the plate with one out and a runner on third, drawing a dollar sign in the dirt before the pitch and then failed to run to first base after hitting a routine pop fly to shortstop, trotting back to the dugout instead. The Yankee fans booed, and Fisk told Sanders to "run the fucking ball out" and called Sanders a "piece of shit." Later in the game, Sanders told Fisk that "the days of slavery are over." Fisk was furious. "He comes up and wants to make it a racial issue, there's no racial issue involved. There is a right way and a wrong way to play this game."<SUP id="cite_ref-fisktribune_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-fisktribune-11">[11]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-fiskNewsday_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-fiskNewsday-12">[12]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-forumchannel_13-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-forumchannel-13">[13]</A></SUP></P>
<P>By mid-July, Sanders expressed that he was unsure if he would remain with the Yankees or report to NFL training camp for the upcoming NFL season.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP> He requested a $1 million salary for the 1991 season, and the Yankees ended negotiations on a contract extension with Sanders. He left the team, finishing the 1990 season with a .158 batting average and three home runs in 57 games.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> In September 1990, the Yankees placed Sanders on <A href="/wiki/Waivers_(baseball)" class="mw-redirect" title="Waivers (baseball)">waivers</A> with the intention of giving him his release, as Yankees' <A href="/wiki/General_manager_(baseball)" title="General manager (baseball)">general manager</A> <A href="/wiki/Gene_Michael" title="Gene Michael">Gene Michael</A> said that Sanders' football career was stunting his baseball development.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Sanders later signed with the <A href="/wiki/Atlanta_Braves" title="Atlanta Braves">Atlanta Braves</A> for the <A href="/wiki/1991_Major_League_Baseball_season" title="1991 Major League Baseball season">1991 MLB season</A>. On July 31, Sanders hit a key three-run homer to spark a comeback win against the <A href="/wiki/1991_Pittsburgh_Pirates_season" title="1991 Pittsburgh Pirates season">Pittsburgh Pirates</A> during the Braves' run to the <A href="/wiki/National_League_West_Division" class="mw-redirect" title="National League West Division">National League West Division</A> title. However, he had to leave the Braves the very next day to report to the <A href="/wiki/1991_Atlanta_Falcons_season" title="1991 Atlanta Falcons season">Atlanta Falcons</A> because of a clause in his NFL contract and missed the postseason. Before the <A href="/wiki/1992_NFL_season" title="1992 NFL season">1992 season</A>, Sanders reworked his NFL deal whereby he still reported to the Falcons for training camp in August, but was allowed to rejoin the Braves for the postseason.</P>
<P>During his most productive year in the majors, the <A href="/wiki/1992_MLB_season" class="mw-redirect" title="1992 MLB season">1992 season</A>, he hit <A href="/wiki/Batting_average" title="Batting average">.304</A> for the team, stole 26 bases, and led the <A href="/wiki/National_League" title="National League">NL</A> with 14 <A href="/wiki/Triple_(baseball)" title="Triple (baseball)">triples</A> in 97 games. During the <A href="/wiki/1989_MLB_season" class="mw-redirect" title="1989 MLB season">1989 season</A>, he hit a major league <A href="/wiki/Home_run" title="Home run">home run</A> and scored a touchdown in the NFL in the same week, the only player ever to do so. Sanders is also the only man to play in both a <A href="/wiki/Super_Bowl" title="Super Bowl">Super Bowl</A> and a <A href="/wiki/World_Series" title="World Series">World Series</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-autogenerated1_17-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-autogenerated1-17">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:272px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Deion_Sanders_Braves_1993.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Deion_Sanders_Braves_1993.jpg/270px-Deion_Sanders_Braves_1993.jpg" width="270" height="193" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Deion_Sanders_Braves_1993.jpg/405px-Deion_Sanders_Braves_1993.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Deion_Sanders_Braves_1993.jpg/540px-Deion_Sanders_Braves_1993.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1302" data-file-height="931" /></A>

Sanders batting for the Braves in 1993.</DIV>

<P>In four games of the <A href="/wiki/1992_World_Series" title="1992 World Series">1992 World Series</A>, Sanders batted .533 with 4 <A href="/wiki/Run_(baseball)" title="Run (baseball)">runs</A>, 8 <A href="/wiki/Hit_(baseball)" title="Hit (baseball)">hits</A>, 2 <A href="/wiki/Double_(baseball)" title="Double (baseball)">doubles</A>, and 1 <A href="/wiki/Run_batted_in" title="Run batted in">RBI</A> while playing with a broken bone in his foot. Despite Sanders's performance, the Braves ultimately lost to the <A href="/wiki/1992_Toronto_Blue_Jays_season" title="1992 Toronto Blue Jays season">Toronto Blue Jays</A> in six games. In Game 3, he narrowly avoided being a victim of what would have been only the second triple play in World Series history (following <A href="/wiki/Bill_Wambsganss" title="Bill Wambsganss">Bill Wambsganss</A>'s unassisted triple play in <A href="/wiki/1920_World_Series" title="1920 World Series">1920</A>). With Sanders on second base and <A href="/wiki/Terry_Pendleton" title="Terry Pendleton">Terry Pendleton</A> on first, <A href="/wiki/David_Justice" title="David Justice">David Justice</A> hit a deep fly ball to center field that Blue Jays center fielder <A href="/wiki/Devon_White_(baseball)" title="Devon White (baseball)">Devon White</A> unexpectedly caught with a leaping effort. Pendleton passed Sanders on the bases for the second out, but umpire <A href="/wiki/Bob_Davidson_(umpire)" title="Bob Davidson (umpire)">Bob Davidson</A> called Sanders safe after he scampered back to second base. Replays showed that Toronto third baseman <A href="/wiki/Kelly_Gruber" title="Kelly Gruber">Kelly Gruber</A> tagged him on the heel before he returned to second.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 1997, Sanders finished 2nd in the NL with 56 stolen bases in 115 games while with the <A href="/wiki/1997_Cincinnati_Reds_season" title="1997 Cincinnati Reds season">Cincinnati Reds</A> before leaving baseball for three years.</P>
<P>Sanders returned to the <A href="/wiki/2001_Cincinnati_Reds_season" title="2001 Cincinnati Reds season">Reds</A> in 2001, but was released after playing in only 29 games and batting just .173. Following his release from the Reds he signed a minor league contract with the <A href="/wiki/Toronto_Blue_Jays" title="Toronto Blue Jays">Toronto Blue Jays</A> triple-A affiliate, <A href="/wiki/Syracuse_Chiefs" title="Syracuse Chiefs">Syracuse Chiefs</A>. Sanders was hitting .252 for Syracuse before the Washington Redskins found a loophole in his contract which compelled him to return to the Redskins. His football contract had been negotiated to allow for Sanders to play both baseball and football, but the terms of the contract stated that Sanders could miss NFL training camp and the first few games of the season only if he were playing Major League Baseball. Since he was not then on an MLB roster, Sanders had to leave Syracuse and return to the Redskins so he would not violate his NFL contract. But before arriving at training camp, Sanders informed Redskins personnel he was retiring from professional baseball. In his final professional baseball game, Sanders hit a solo home run and an RBI single in Syracuse's 12-6 win over the <A href="/wiki/Toledo_Mud_Hens" title="Toledo Mud Hens">Toledo Mud Hens</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP> As those in MLB and the NFL urged Sanders to concentrate on only one sport, he would often explain, "football is my wife and baseball is my mistress."<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Draft_and_Atlanta_Falcons">Draft and Atlanta Falcons</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=6&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Draft and Atlanta Falcons">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>At the 1989 <A href="/wiki/NFL_Scouting_Combine" title="NFL Scouting Combine">NFL Scouting Combine</A>, Sanders ran a 4.27<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP> second <A href="/wiki/40-yard_dash" title="40-yard dash">40-yard dash</A>. <SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP> He was the fifth pick overall in the <A href="/wiki/1989_NFL_Draft" title="1989 NFL Draft">1989 NFL Draft</A> by the <A href="/wiki/Atlanta_Falcons" title="Atlanta Falcons">Atlanta Falcons</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> where he played until <A href="/wiki/1993_NFL_season" title="1993 NFL season">1993</A>. Despite fumbling (and recovering) his first NFL punt (which was re-kicked on a penalty), Sanders ran for a touchdown on his second attempt of his first game. During his time in Atlanta, he intercepted 24 passes (including a career-high 7 in 1993), three of which he returned for touchdowns. In <A href="/wiki/1992_NFL_season" title="1992 NFL season">1992</A>, he also led the league in kickoff return yards (1,067), yards per return (26.7) and return touchdowns (2). On October 11, 1992, Sanders played in a Falcons game at Miami and then flew to Pittsburgh, hoping to play in the Braves' League Championship Series game against the Pirates that evening and become the first athlete to play in two professional leagues in the same day.<SUP id="cite_ref-autogenerated1_17-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-autogenerated1-17">[17]</A></SUP> Sanders ultimately did not, however, appear in the baseball game that night.<SUP id="cite_ref-autogenerated1_17-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-autogenerated1-17">[17]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP> Over his five years with the Falcons, Sanders scored ten touchdowns (three defensive, three kick returns, two punt returns, and two receptions).</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="San_Francisco_49ers">San Francisco 49ers</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=7&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: San Francisco 49ers">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>After five seasons Sanders signed on to play <A href="/wiki/1994_San_Francisco_49ers_season" title="1994 San Francisco 49ers season">the 1994 season</A> with the <A href="/wiki/San_Francisco_49ers" title="San Francisco 49ers">San Francisco 49ers</A>, where he had arguably his best season as a professional football player, recording six interceptions and returning them for an NFL best and a then-NFL record 303 yards and three touchdowns. Two of his interceptions were returned for a gain of at least 90 yards, making him the first player to do this in NFL history. On October 16, 1994, Sanders made his dramatic return to the <A href="/wiki/Georgia_Dome" title="Georgia Dome">Georgia Dome</A> in a 49er uniform. After getting into a scuffle with his former Falcon teammate <A href="/wiki/Andre_Rison" title="Andre Rison">Andre Rison</A>, Sanders intercepted a pass from quarterback <A href="/wiki/Jeff_George" title="Jeff George">Jeff George</A> and returned it 93 yards while mockingly staring down the entire Falcons sideline before high-stepping into the end zone. Sanders was later voted the <A href="/wiki/1994_NFL_season" title="1994 NFL season">1994</A> <A href="/wiki/National_Football_League_Defensive_Player_of_the_Year_Award" title="National Football League Defensive Player of the Year Award">NFL Defensive Player of the Year</A> and recorded an interception in the 49ers 49–26 victory over the <A href="/wiki/1994_San_Diego_Chargers_season" title="1994 San Diego Chargers season">San Diego Chargers</A> in <A href="/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXIX" title="Super Bowl XXIX">Super Bowl XXIX</A>, earning him his first championship ring.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Dallas_Cowboys">Dallas Cowboys</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=8&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Dallas Cowboys">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Following his successful season with the 49ers, Sanders, along with his agent <A href="/wiki/Eugene_E._Parker" class="mw-redirect" title="Eugene E. Parker">Eugene Parker</A>, courted numerous teams in need of a cornerback. The several teams in the "Deion Sweepstakes", as it was called by the media, were the <A href="/wiki/Philadelphia_Eagles" title="Philadelphia Eagles">Philadelphia Eagles</A>, <A href="/wiki/Oakland_Raiders" title="Oakland Raiders">Oakland Raiders</A>, <A href="/wiki/Miami_Dolphins" title="Miami Dolphins">Miami Dolphins</A>, <A href="/wiki/New_Orleans_Saints" title="New Orleans Saints">New Orleans Saints</A>, San Francisco 49ers and the Dallas Cowboys, who had lost their starting cornerback <A href="/wiki/Kevin_Smith_(cornerback)" title="Kevin Smith (cornerback)">Kevin Smith</A> to injury for the rest of the season.</P>
<P>On September 9, 1995 (which fell in Week 2 of that NFL season), Sanders signed a lucrative contract with the Dallas Cowboys (seven years, $35 million with a $12.999 million signing bonus, because owner <A href="/wiki/Jerry_Jones" title="Jerry Jones">Jerry Jones</A> was superstitious of the number 13),<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP> essentially making him, at the time, the highest-paid defensive player in the NFL. Sanders later stated in his book <I>Power, Money & Sex: How Success Almost Ruined My Life</I> that the Oakland Raiders offered him more money than any other team, but he chose to play in Dallas for more time on the offensive side of the ball, a chance to win back-to-back Super Bowls, and because of his friendship with Cowboys wide receiver <A href="/wiki/Michael_Irvin" title="Michael Irvin">Michael Irvin</A>. <A href="/wiki/Arthroscopy" title="Arthroscopy">Arthroscopic surgery</A> kept him sidelined until his debut in Week 9, which was once again in Atlanta against the Falcons; the Cowboys won, 28-13. He went on to help the <A href="/wiki/1995_Dallas_Cowboys_season" title="1995 Dallas Cowboys season">Cowboys</A> win their third title in four years in <A href="/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXX" title="Super Bowl XXX">Super Bowl XXX</A> against the Pittsburgh Steelers, where he returned a punt for 11 yards and caught a 47-yard reception on offense, setting up Dallas' first touchdown of the game and a 27–17 victory. Sanders played four more seasons with Dallas, earning <A href="/wiki/Pro_Bowl" title="Pro Bowl">Pro Bowl</A> selection in all of them. On June 2, 2000, he was released in a salary cap move.<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Washington_Redskins">Washington Redskins</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=9&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Washington Redskins">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Soon after being released by the Cowboys, the <A href="/wiki/Washington_Redskins" title="Washington Redskins">Washington Redskins</A> and <A href="/wiki/Daniel_Snyder" title="Daniel Snyder">Daniel Snyder</A> signed Sanders to a hefty $56 million, 7-year contract.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP> At the end of the <A href="/wiki/2000_NFL_season" title="2000 NFL season">2000</A> season and an above-average statistical year, Sanders abruptly retired after only playing one year with the Redskins.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Baltimore_Ravens">Baltimore Ravens</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=10&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Baltimore Ravens">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/2004_NFL_season" title="2004 NFL season">2004</A>, Sanders announced that he was going to end his retirement, after being lured back to football by Ravens cornerback <A href="/wiki/Corey_Fuller" title="Corey Fuller">Corey Fuller</A>, linebacker <A href="/wiki/Ray_Lewis_(American_football)" class="mw-redirect" title="Ray Lewis (American football)">Ray Lewis</A> and best friend <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.deionsanders21.com/career/">Joe Zorovich</A>. A major reason for doing so was to play with Ray Lewis. He signed a 1-year deal with the <A href="/wiki/Baltimore_Ravens" title="Baltimore Ravens">Baltimore Ravens</A> to be a <A href="/wiki/Nickelback_(American_football)" class="mw-redirect" title="Nickelback (American football)">nickelback</A>. Sanders chose to wear the number 37, which matched his age at the time, to preemptively let people know that he was well aware of his relative senior status as an NFL player (additionally, the number 21, used by Sanders throughout his career, was already being worn by Ravens Pro Bowl cornerback <A href="/wiki/Chris_McAlister" title="Chris McAlister">Chris McAlister</A>). Against the Buffalo Bills in Week 7 of 2004, Sanders scored his ninth career interception return touchdown, moving him into a tie for second place with <A href="/wiki/Ken_Houston" title="Ken Houston">Ken Houston</A> and <A href="/wiki/Aeneas_Williams" title="Aeneas Williams">Aeneas Williams</A>, and behind <A href="/wiki/Rod_Woodson" title="Rod Woodson">Rod Woodson</A> (with 12) for all-time in the statistical category.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:172px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Deion_Sanders.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Deion_Sanders.jpg/170px-Deion_Sanders.jpg" width="170" height="218" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Deion_Sanders.jpg/255px-Deion_Sanders.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Deion_Sanders.jpg/340px-Deion_Sanders.jpg 2x" data-file-width="932" data-file-height="1194" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Deion_Sanders.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Sanders in 2008.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>In January 2006, after playing two seasons as a corner and safety for Baltimore in which the Ravens did not qualify for the postseason, Sanders once again retired from the NFL and became an analyst for the <A href="/wiki/NFL_Network" title="NFL Network">NFL Network</A>.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Legacy">Legacy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=11&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Legacy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>During his 14-year NFL career, Sanders was a perennial All-Pro and one of the strongest pass defenders ever. He was known for being a relatively poor tackler and he was not much of a factor in run support.</P>
<P>Sanders also occasionally lined up with his team's offense. During the <A href="/wiki/1996_NFL_season" title="1996 NFL season">1996 season</A>, Sanders skipped the <A href="/wiki/1996_Major_League_Baseball_season" title="1996 Major League Baseball season">baseball season</A>, concentrating on football, and attended the first <A href="/wiki/National_Football_League_Training_Camp" class="mw-redirect" title="National Football League Training Camp">NFL training camp</A> of his career to better familiarize himself with the nuances of the wide receiver position. He became only the second two-way starter (after the Cardinals' <A href="/wiki/Roy_Green" title="Roy Green">Roy Green</A>) in the NFL since <A href="/wiki/Chuck_Bednarik" title="Chuck Bednarik">Chuck Bednarik</A> for the first half of the season due.</P>
<P>Sanders is the only man to play in both a Super Bowl and a World Series,<SUP id="cite_ref-autogenerated1_17-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-autogenerated1-17">[17]</A></SUP> to hit an MLB home run and score an NFL touchdown in the same week, and to have both a reception and an interception in the Super Bowl. He is one of two players to score an NFL touchdown six different ways.<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP></P>
<P>During his career, Sanders intercepted 53 passes for 1,331 yards (a 25.1 yards per return average), recovered four fumbles for 15 yards, returned 155 kickoffs for 3,523 yards, gained 2,199 yards on 212 punt returns, and caught 60 passes for 784 yards. Sanders amassed 7,838 all-purpose yards and scored 22 touchdowns: nine interception returns, six punt returns, three kickoff returns, three receiving, and one fumble recovery. His 19 defensive and return touchdowns was an NFL record (now held by <A href="/wiki/Devin_Hester" title="Devin Hester">Devin Hester</A>). In the postseason, Sanders added 5 more interceptions, as well as 3 receptions for 95 yards, 4 carries for 39 yards, and two touchdowns (one rushing and one receiving). He was selected to eight Pro Bowls and won the <A href="/wiki/NFL_Defensive_Player_of_the_Year_Award" class="mw-redirect" title="NFL Defensive Player of the Year Award">NFL Defensive Player of the Year Award</A> in <A href="/wiki/1994_NFL_season" title="1994 NFL season">1994</A>.</P>
<UL>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/College_Football_News" title="College Football News">College Football News</A></I> named Sanders #8 in its list of 100 Greatest College Football Players of All-Time.</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/The_Sporting_News" class="mw-redirect" title="The Sporting News">The Sporting News</A></I> named Sanders #37 in their <A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Sporting_News_%E2%80%93_Football%27s_100_Greatest_Players&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="The Sporting News – Football's 100 Greatest Players (page does not exist)">Top 100 Football Players of the Century</A> released in 1999.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/ESPN" title="ESPN">ESPN</A> named Sanders #74 in its list of the 100 Great Athletes of the Century released in 1999.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/NFL.com" class="mw-redirect" title="NFL.com">NFL.com</A> named Sanders #34 on NFL's Top 100 list released in late 2010</LI>
<LI>On November 11, 2010, Sanders was inducted into the Atlanta Falcons' Ring of Honor.</LI>
<LI>On February 5, 2011, Sanders was announced as a <A href="/wiki/Pro_Football_Hall_of_Fame" title="Pro Football Hall of Fame">Pro Football Hall of Fame</A> inductee in his first year of eligibility.</LI>
<LI>On May 17, 2011, Sanders was announced as a <A href="/wiki/College_Football_Hall_of_Fame" title="College Football Hall of Fame">College Football Hall of Fame</A> inductee.</LI>
<LI>On August 6, 2011, Sanders was inducted into the <A href="/wiki/Pro_Football_Hall_of_Fame" title="Pro Football Hall of Fame">Pro Football Hall of Fame</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP></LI>
</UL>
<P>Sanders also had a rushing TD in the playoffs (against the Philadelphia Eagles in January 1996). This makes him (including post season) one of only two players in NFL history (<A href="/wiki/Bill_Dudley" title="Bill Dudley">Bill Dudley</A> being the other) to score a touchdown six different ways (interception return, punt return, kickoff return, receiving, rushing, and a fumble recovery).</P>
<P>On February 6, 2011, at <A href="/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLV" title="Super Bowl XLV">Super Bowl XLV</A> in Arlington, Texas, Sanders performed the pre-game coin toss.</P>
<P>Sanders did not attend classes or take final exams during the fall semester of his senior year at Florida State, yet played in the <A href="/wiki/Sugar_Bowl" title="Sugar Bowl">Sugar Bowl</A> against Auburn. This caused the Florida State Legislature to create the 'Deion Sanders rule', whereby a football athlete at any state university could not play in a bowl game if he failed to successfully complete the previous semester.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 1995, he signed with the Dallas Cowboys for a minimum yearly base salary and a nearly $13 million signing bonus in an attempt to circumvent the NFL's salary cap. This caused the NFL to institute its own 'Deion Sanders rule' whereby a prorated portion of a player's signing bonus counted against the salary cap.<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Media_appearances_and_pop_culture_fame">Media appearances and pop culture fame</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=12&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Media appearances and pop culture fame">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Leon_Sandcastle" title="Leon Sandcastle">Leon Sandcastle</A></DIV>
<P>Sanders became known for sporting a "<A href="/wiki/Do-rag" title="Do-rag">do-rag</A>" or <A href="/wiki/Bandana" class="mw-redirect" title="Bandana">bandana</A> and for his high-stepping into the end zone followed by his <A href="/wiki/Touchdown_celebration" title="Touchdown celebration">touchdown dance celebrations</A>. At the end of his Hall of Fame speech, he put a bandana on his bust.<SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP></P>
<P>His "Prime Time" nickname was given to him by a friend and high-school teammate, <A href="/wiki/Florida_Gators_football" title="Florida Gators football">Florida Gators</A> defensive back Richard Fain. The two played pickup basketball games together during the <A href="/wiki/Prime_time" title="Prime time">prime time</A> television hour, and Sanders' athletic display during those games earned him the nickname. His other nickname is "Neon Deion".<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[33]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Following his first Super Bowl victory with the <A href="/wiki/San_Francisco_49ers" title="San Francisco 49ers">San Francisco 49ers</A>, Sanders hosted <I><A href="/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live" title="Saturday Night Live">Saturday Night Live</A></I>, broadcast on February 18, 1995.</P>
<P>In January 1995, Sanders became the official spokesman of the <A href="/wiki/Sega_Sports" class="mw-redirect" title="Sega Sports">Sega Sports</A> line of <A href="/wiki/Video_game" title="Video game">video games</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP> Sanders has also appeared in television commercials for such companies as <A href="/wiki/Nike,_Inc." title="Nike, Inc.">Nike</A>, <A href="/wiki/Pepsi" title="Pepsi">Pepsi</A>, <A href="/wiki/Burger_King" title="Burger King">Burger King</A>, <A href="/wiki/Pizza_Hut" title="Pizza Hut">Pizza Hut</A>, and <A href="/wiki/American_Express" title="American Express">American Express</A>. These included a <A href="/wiki/Wile_E._Coyote_and_Road_Runner" class="mw-redirect" title="Wile E. Coyote and Road Runner">Road Runner</A> Pepsi ad, with Sanders as <A href="/wiki/Wile_E._Coyote" class="mw-redirect" title="Wile E. Coyote">Wile E. Coyote</A>, and a <A href="/wiki/Pizza_Hut" title="Pizza Hut">Pizza Hut</A> commercial in which he appeared with Dallas Cowboys owner <A href="/wiki/Jerry_Jones" title="Jerry Jones">Jerry Jones</A>. He also makes a <A href="/wiki/Cameo_appearance" title="Cameo appearance">cameo</A> as himself in the film <I><A href="/wiki/Celtic_Pride" title="Celtic Pride">Celtic Pride</A></I>.</P>
<P>Sanders, known for his custom-made showy suits and flashy jewelry, frequently capitalized on his image. On December 26, 1994, Sanders released <I><A href="/wiki/Prime_Time_(Deion_Sanders_album)" title="Prime Time (Deion Sanders album)">Prime Time</A></I>, a rap album on Bust It Records (<A href="/wiki/MC_Hammer" title="MC Hammer">MC Hammer</A>'s label, of whom Sanders is a friend) that featured the singles "Must Be the Money" and "Prime Time Keeps on Tickin'". The album was universally panned by critics, and despite Sanders' fame, neither the album nor its singles charted in the Top 40.</P>
<P>Sanders also appeared in Hammer's "<A href="/wiki/Too_Legit_to_Quit_(song)#Music_video" class="mw-redirect" title="Too Legit to Quit (song)">Too Legit to Quit</A>" music video, and his alter-ego "Prime Time" showed up in Hammer's "<A href="/wiki/Pumps_and_a_Bump_(video)" class="mw-redirect" title="Pumps and a Bump (video)">Pumps and a Bump</A>" video. Hammer, a big sports fan, had launched a new enterprise during his career called Roll Wit It Entertainment & Sports Management and boasted such clients as <A href="/wiki/Evander_Holyfield" title="Evander Holyfield">Evander Holyfield</A>, Deion Sanders and <A href="/wiki/Reggie_Brooks" title="Reggie Brooks">Reggie Brooks</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[35]</A></SUP> In 1995, Hammer released "Straight to My Feet" (with Deion Sanders) from the <I><A href="/wiki/Street_Fighter_(1994_film)" title="Street Fighter (1994 film)">Street Fighter</A></I> <A href="/wiki/Street_Fighter_(soundtrack)" title="Street Fighter (soundtrack)">soundtrack</A> (released in December 1994). The song charted #57 in the UK.</P>
<P>After retiring from the NFL, Sanders worked as a pre-game commentator for <A href="/wiki/CBS_Sports" title="CBS Sports">CBS</A>' <I><A href="/wiki/The_NFL_Today" title="The NFL Today">The NFL Today</A></I> until <A href="/wiki/2004_NFL_season" title="2004 NFL season">2004</A>, when contract negotiations failed. Sanders turned down a 30% salary increase demanding to be paid $2.5 million, the highest of any NFL TV analyst. He was replaced by <A href="/wiki/Shannon_Sharpe" title="Shannon Sharpe">Shannon Sharpe</A>. During Sanders' run, he participated in several sketches. The first was "Primetime and 21st", a mock street corner where Sanders (not yet a regular panelist) would give his opinions. Another was his "Sanders Claus" persona, one of numerous sketches that involved young kids in football jerseys, representing NFL players, receiving a sarcastic gift from Sanders. Deion actually debuted as "Sanders Claus" in a set of Nike commercials. Sanders still takes presents at Christmas time to local children's hospitals in his area dressed as "Sanders Claus".<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (December 2012)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:247px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Deion_Sanders_2008.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Deion_Sanders_2008.jpg/245px-Deion_Sanders_2008.jpg" width="245" height="184" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Deion_Sanders_2008.jpg/368px-Deion_Sanders_2008.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Deion_Sanders_2008.jpg/490px-Deion_Sanders_2008.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1200" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Deion_Sanders_2008.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Sanders as an NFL Network analyst in 2008.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Sanders frequently made guest appearances on <A href="/wiki/ESPN" title="ESPN">ESPN</A>, especially on the <A href="/wiki/ESPN_Radio" title="ESPN Radio">ESPN Radio</A> <A href="/wiki/Dallas" title="Dallas">Dallas</A> affiliate, and briefly hosted a show called <I>The New American Sportsman</I>. He also hosted the <A href="/wiki/Miss_USA_2002" title="Miss USA 2002">2002 Miss USA</A> pageant.</P>
<P>Sanders also was co-host of the 2004 <A href="/wiki/GMA_Music_Awards" class="mw-redirect" title="GMA Music Awards">GMA Music Awards</A> broadcast, taped in late April 2004, and slated for air on <A href="/wiki/UPN" title="UPN">UPN</A> in May 2004. When negotiations with fellow <A href="/wiki/Viacom" title="Viacom">Viacom</A> property CBS failed (see above) two weeks before the broadcast, and he signed a deal with ESPN, UPN promptly canceled the broadcast, and the show aired on the <A href="/wiki/I_Network" class="mw-redirect" title="I Network">i Network</A> in December 2004 (both UPN and CBS are now owned by <A href="/wiki/CBS_Corporation" title="CBS Corporation">CBS Corporation</A>).</P>
<P>Sanders works at <A href="/wiki/NFL_Network" title="NFL Network">NFL Network</A> as an analyst on a number of the network's shows. Prior to the Sunday night game, Sanders, alongside host <A href="/wiki/Rich_Eisen" title="Rich Eisen">Rich Eisen</A> and <A href="/wiki/Steve_Mariucci" title="Steve Mariucci">Steve Mariucci</A>, breaks down all the action from the afternoon games on <A href="/wiki/NFL_GameDay_(NFL_Network_show)" title="NFL GameDay (NFL Network show)"><I>NFL GameDay</I></A>. At the conclusion of all the action on Sunday, Sanders, Mariucci, Michael Irvin and host Fran Charles recap the day's action with highlights, analysis and postgame interviews. For the 2010 season, Sanders joined Eisen, Mariucci and <A href="/wiki/Marshall_Faulk" title="Marshall Faulk">Marshall Faulk</A> on the road for <I>Thursday Night Kickoff presented by <A href="/wiki/Lexus" title="Lexus">Lexus</A></I>, NFL Network's two-hour pregame show leading into <I><A href="/wiki/Thursday_Night_Football" title="Thursday Night Football">Thursday Night Football</A></I>. The group broadcasts live from the stadium two hours prior to all eight live <I>Thursday Night Football</I> games and returns for the <A href="/wiki/Sprint_Corporation" title="Sprint Corporation">Sprint</A> halftime show and <A href="/wiki/Sterling_Jewelers" title="Sterling Jewelers">Kay Jewelers</A> postgame show. Sanders also has a segment called "Let's Go Primetime" on <A href="/wiki/NFL_Network" title="NFL Network">NFL Network</A>.</P>
<P>In 2008, Sanders and his wife starred in the reality show <I><A href="/wiki/Deion_%26_Pilar:_Prime_Time_Love" title="Deion & Pilar: Prime Time Love">Deion & Pilar: Prime Time Love</A></I>, centering on them and their five children living in the small town of <A href="/wiki/Prosper,_Texas" title="Prosper, Texas">Prosper, Texas</A>.</P>
<P>Sanders appeared as himself in the fourth season of <I><A href="/wiki/The_League" title="The League">The League</A></I>, playing a prospective buyer of Andre's apartment.<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2014, Sanders was featured in an episode of <I><A href="/wiki/Running_Wild_with_Bear_Grylls" title="Running Wild with Bear Grylls">Running Wild with Bear Grylls</A></I>, where he and Grylls hiked in the desert of southern Utah for two days, rappelling down canyon walls and later climbing up a mesa.<SUP id="cite_ref-RWBG_37-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RWBG-37">[37]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Sanders served as an alumni captain for Team Sanders in the <A href="/wiki/2014_Pro_Bowl" title="2014 Pro Bowl">2014 Pro Bowl</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2014, he rejoined <A href="/wiki/The_NFL_Today" title="The NFL Today">CBS Sports</A> as a studio analyst for Thursday games only. He still works for the NFL Network on Sundays.</P>
<P>Sanders and his girlfriend <A href="/wiki/Tracey_Edmonds" title="Tracey Edmonds">Tracey Edmonds</A> were featured together on an episode of <I><A href="/wiki/Tiny_House_Nation" title="Tiny House Nation">Tiny House Nation</A></I> that first aired on January 21, 2017.<SUP id="cite_ref-Deion_Sanders_Goes_Tiny_39-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Deion_Sanders_Goes_Tiny-39">[39]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Other_business_and_entertainment_ventures">Other business and entertainment ventures</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=13&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Other business and entertainment ventures">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>In addition to his sports career, Sanders also had a career in music as a rapper. He released his debut album, <I><A href="/wiki/Prime_Time_(Deion_Sanders_album)" title="Prime Time (Deion Sanders album)">Prime Time</A></I>, through <A href="/wiki/MC_Hammer" title="MC Hammer">Hammer</A>'s <A href="/wiki/MC_Hammer#The_Funky_Headhunter_and_Prime_Time_.281994.29" title="MC Hammer">Bust It Records</A> label via <A href="/wiki/Capitol_Records" title="Capitol Records">Capitol Records</A>, in 1994.</P>
<P>Sanders moved on to other ventures after his retirement. In 2003, Sanders took interest in <A href="/wiki/Devin_Hester" title="Devin Hester">Devin Hester</A>, a <A href="/wiki/Return_specialist" title="Return specialist">return specialist</A> from <A href="/wiki/Miami_Hurricanes_football" title="Miami Hurricanes football">Miami</A>. Sanders mentored Hester, counseling and advising him during various points of his collegiate career. The <A href="/wiki/Chicago_Bears" title="Chicago Bears">Chicago Bears</A> drafted Hester in the second round of the <A href="/wiki/2006_NFL_Draft" title="2006 NFL Draft">2006 NFL Draft</A>. Since then, Hester has broken the record for the most total returns for touchdowns in NFL history with 15 punt returns and 5 kick off returns. Hester has cited Sanders as one of his major inspirations and idols, and thanked him for his training and advice. Hester, also known as "Anytime", occasionally performs Sanders' signature touchdown dance and high-steps in homage to his mentor.<SUP id="cite_ref-Hester_Pilot_40-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Hester_Pilot-40">[40]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Hester_Rams_41-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Hester_Rams-41">[41]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Hester_Q.2FA_42-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Hester_Q.2FA-42">[42]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Sanders also tried to adopt a high school running back, <A href="/wiki/Noel_Devine" title="Noel Devine">Noel Devine</A>, who was one of the top recruits in 2007. Sanders was advised against this, but responded, "He doesn't have parents; they died. God put this young man in my heart. This is not about sports. This is about a kid's life." He now mentors Devine, and was a factor in Devine's extended wait to sign a <A href="/wiki/National_Letter_of_Intent" title="National Letter of Intent">letter-of-intent</A> to <A href="/wiki/West_Virginia_University" title="West Virginia University">West Virginia University</A>. Devine eventually signed to play football for the <A href="/wiki/West_Virginia_Mountaineers_football" title="West Virginia Mountaineers football">Mountaineers</A>. Sanders has also been a mentor to Oakland Raiders wide receiver <A href="/wiki/Michael_Crabtree" title="Michael Crabtree">Michael Crabtree</A>, as well as Dallas Cowboys wide receiver, <A href="/wiki/Dez_Bryant" title="Dez Bryant">Dez Bryant</A>.</P>
<P>In January 2004, Sanders was hired as an assistant coach to the <A href="/wiki/Dallas_Fury" class="mw-redirect" title="Dallas Fury">Dallas Fury</A>, a women's professional <A href="/wiki/Basketball" title="Basketball">basketball</A> team in the <A href="/wiki/National_Women%27s_Basketball_League" title="National Women's Basketball League">National Women's Basketball League</A>, even though Sanders had never played organized basketball either in college or the professional level.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On September 2, 2005, in response to the after-effects of <A href="/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina" title="Hurricane Katrina">Hurricane Katrina</A>, Sanders challenged all professional athletes in the four major sports to donate <A href="/wiki/United_States_dollar" title="United States dollar">$1,000</A> each to relief efforts, hoping to raise between $1.5 and $3 million total. Sanders said "Through unity, we can touch thousands....I have friends and relatives that feel this pain. Help in any way you can."<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2009)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> In April 2006, Sanders became an owner of the <A href="/wiki/Austin_Wranglers" title="Austin Wranglers">Austin Wranglers</A>, an <A href="/wiki/Arena_Football_League" title="Arena Football League">Arena Football League</A> team.<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Sanders has occasionally served as a celebrity spokesperson, such as representing <A href="/wiki/Monitronics" class="mw-redirect" title="Monitronics">Monitronics</A>, a security system firm, at an industry conference in the spring of 2010.<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2012, he co-founded <A href="/wiki/Prime_Prep_Academy" title="Prime Prep Academy">Prime Prep Academy</A>, a grouping of charter schools in Texas. The school was plagued by ethical, legal and financial issues, and closed on January 30, 2015, due to financial insolvency.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Personal_life">Personal life</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Deion_Sanders&action=edit&section=15&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Personal life">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Sanders has been married twice — to Carolyn Chambers (1989–1998), with whom he has two children (Deion Jr. and Deiondra), and Pilar Biggers-Sanders (1999–2013) with whom he has three children (Shilo, Shelomi Golenzer and Shedeur).</P>
<P>Sanders, along with J.M. Black, published his autobiography, <I>Power, Money & Sex: How Success Almost Ruined My Life</I>. World Publishing 1998. The book was inspired after he began counseling with <A href="/wiki/Bishop_T.D._Jakes" class="mw-redirect" title="Bishop T.D. Jakes">Bishop T.D. Jakes</A>. He notes his agent <A href="/wiki/Eugene_E._Parker" class="mw-redirect" title="Eugene E. Parker">Eugene E. Parker</A> as another person who influenced his life.</P>
<P>He appeared with his family on the NBC show <I><A href="/wiki/Celebrity_Family_Feud" title="Celebrity Family Feud">Celebrity Family Feud</A></I> which premiered on June 24, 2008.</P>
<P>On September 22, 2011, he served Pilar Biggers-Sanders with divorce papers. He then backed away from the story and denied he and Pilar would be divorcing. By December 17, 2011, he had followed through with filing for divorce.<SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[46]</A></SUP> On March 12, 2013, he was awarded primary custody of his two sons, Shilo and Shedeur, and Pilar was awarded primary custody of their daughter Shelomi.<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[47]</A></SUP> However, one week later, a judge awarded custody of Shelomi to him as well.<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP> During the divorce battle, Pilar made several accusations of abuse against him on social media and in interviews, leading him to file a Defamation of Character lawsuit against her. In 2015, he was vindicated when the court awarded him a $2.2 million judgment against his ex-wife in the case.<SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[49]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Sanders is a devout Christian.<SUP id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-50">[50]</A></SUP> He has been in a relationship with <A href="/wiki/Tracey_Edmonds" title="Tracey Edmonds">Tracey Edmonds</A> since 2012.<SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[51]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Deion_Sanders_Goes_Tiny_39-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Deion_Sanders_Goes_Tiny-39">[39]</A></SUP></P>

<P>The <B>United States House of Representatives</B> is the <A href="/wiki/Lower_house" title="Lower house">lower chamber</A> of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Congress" title="United States Congress">United States Congress</A>, the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Senate" title="United States Senate">Senate</A> being the <A href="/wiki/Upper_house" title="Upper house">upper chamber</A>. Together they compose the <A href="/wiki/Legislature" title="Legislature">legislature</A> of the <A href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</A>.</P>
<P>The composition and powers of the House are established by <A href="/wiki/Article_One_of_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Article One of the United States Constitution">Article One of the United States Constitution</A>. The House is composed of Representatives who sit in <A href="/wiki/List_of_United_States_congressional_districts" title="List of United States congressional districts">congressional districts</A> that are allocated to each of the 50 states on a basis of population as measured by the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Census" title="United States Census">U.S. Census</A>, with each district entitled to one representative. Since its inception in 1789, all Representatives have been directly elected. The <A href="/wiki/United_States_congressional_apportionment" title="United States congressional apportionment">total number of voting representatives</A> is <A href="/wiki/Apportionment_Act_of_1911" title="Apportionment Act of 1911">fixed by law</A> at 435.<SUP id="cite_ref-USPL_62-5_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-USPL_62-5-1">[1]</A></SUP> As of the <A href="/wiki/2010_United_States_Census" title="2010 United States Census">2010 Census</A>, the largest delegation is that of <A href="/wiki/List_of_United_States_Representatives_from_California" title="List of United States Representatives from California">California</A>, with fifty-three representatives. Seven states have the smallest delegation possible, a single representative: <A href="/wiki/Alaska" title="Alaska">Alaska</A>, <A href="/wiki/Delaware" title="Delaware">Delaware</A>, <A href="/wiki/Montana" title="Montana">Montana</A>, <A href="/wiki/North_Dakota" title="North Dakota">North Dakota</A>, <A href="/wiki/South_Dakota" title="South Dakota">South Dakota</A>, <A href="/wiki/Vermont" title="Vermont">Vermont</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Wyoming" title="Wyoming">Wyoming</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The House is charged with the passage of federal <A href="/wiki/Legislation" title="Legislation">legislation</A>, known as <A href="/wiki/Article_One_of_the_United_States_Constitution#Section_7:_Bills" title="Article One of the United States Constitution">bills</A>, which, after concurrence by the Senate, are sent to the <A href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">President</A> for consideration. In addition to this basic power, the House has certain exclusive powers which include the power to initiate all bills related to revenue, the <A href="/wiki/Impeachment_in_the_United_States" title="Impeachment in the United States">impeachment</A> of federal officers, who are sent to trial in the Senate, and in cases wherein no candidate receives a majority of <A href="/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States)" title="Electoral College (United States)">electors</A> for <A href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">President</A>, the duty falls upon the House to elect one of the top three recipients of electors for that office, with one vote given to each state for that purpose.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The presiding officer is the <A href="/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" title="Speaker of the United States House of Representatives">Speaker of the House</A>, who is elected by the members thereof and is therefore traditionally the leader of the controlling party. He or she and <A href="/wiki/Party_leaders_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" title="Party leaders of the United States House of Representatives">other floor leaders</A> are chosen by the <A href="/wiki/Democratic_Caucus_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" title="Democratic Caucus of the United States House of Representatives">Democratic Caucus</A> or the <A href="/wiki/Republican_Conference_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" title="Republican Conference of the United States House of Representatives">Republican Conference</A>, depending on whichever <A href="/wiki/Party_caucuses_and_conferences_in_the_United_States_Congress" title="Party caucuses and conferences in the United States Congress">party</A> has more voting members. The House meets in the south wing of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Capitol" title="United States Capitol">United States Capitol</A>.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_House_of_Representatives&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" title="History of the United States House of Representatives">History of the United States House of Representatives</A></DIV>
<P>Under the <A href="/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation" title="Articles of Confederation">Articles of Confederation</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation" title="Congress of the Confederation">Congress of the Confederation</A> was a <A href="/wiki/Unicameralism" title="Unicameralism">unicameral</A> body in which each state was equally represented, and in which each state had a veto over most action. After eight years of a more limited <A href="/wiki/Confederation" title="Confederation">confederal</A> government under the Articles, numerous political leaders such as <A href="/wiki/James_Madison" title="James Madison">James Madison</A> and <A href="/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton" title="Alexander Hamilton">Alexander Hamilton</A> initiated the <A href="/wiki/Constitutional_Convention_(United_States)" title="Constitutional Convention (United States)">Constitutional Convention</A> in 1787, which received the Confederation Congress's sanction to "amend the Articles of Confederation". All states except <A href="/wiki/Rhode_Island" title="Rhode Island">Rhode Island</A> agreed to send delegates.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Political_Parties_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Political_Parties_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives.png/220px-Political_Parties_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives.png" width="220" height="95" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Political_Parties_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives.png/330px-Political_Parties_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Political_Parties_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives.png/440px-Political_Parties_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives.png 2x" data-file-width="1907" data-file-height="821" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Political_Parties_in_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Representation of all political parties as percentage in House of Representatives over time</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Combined--Control_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives_-_Control_of_the_U.S._Senate.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Combined--Control_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives_-_Control_of_the_U.S._Senate.png/220px-Combined--Control_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives_-_Control_of_the_U.S._Senate.png" width="220" height="111" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Combined--Control_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives_-_Control_of_the_U.S._Senate.png/330px-Combined--Control_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives_-_Control_of_the_U.S._Senate.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Combined--Control_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives_-_Control_of_the_U.S._Senate.png/440px-Combined--Control_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives_-_Control_of_the_U.S._Senate.png 2x" data-file-width="1399" data-file-height="706" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Combined--Control_of_the_U.S._House_of_Representatives_-_Control_of_the_U.S._Senate.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Historical graph of party control of the Senate and House as well as the presidency<SUP id="cite_ref-uspolitics.about_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-uspolitics.about-5">[5]</A></SUP></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The issue of how to structure Congress was one of the most divisive among the <A href="/wiki/Founding_Fathers_of_the_United_States" title="Founding Fathers of the United States">founders</A> during the Convention. <A href="/wiki/Edmund_Randolph" title="Edmund Randolph">Edmund Randolph</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Virginia_Plan" title="Virginia Plan">Virginia Plan</A> called for a <A href="/wiki/Bicameralism" title="Bicameralism">bicameral</A> Congress: the lower house would be "of the people", elected directly by the people of the United States and representing <A href="/wiki/Public_opinion" title="Public opinion">public opinion</A>, and a more deliberative upper house that would represent the individual states, and would be less susceptible to variations of mass sentiment, would be elected by the lower house.<SUP id="cite_ref-Plans_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Plans-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The House is referred to as the <A href="/wiki/Lower_house" title="Lower house">lower house</A>, with the Senate being the <A href="/wiki/Upper_house" title="Upper house">upper house</A>, although the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Constitution" title="United States Constitution">United States Constitution</A> does not use that terminology. Both houses' approval is necessary for the passage of <A href="/wiki/Legislation" title="Legislation">legislation</A>. The Virginia Plan drew the support of delegates from large states such as <A href="/wiki/Virginia" title="Virginia">Virginia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Massachusetts" title="Massachusetts">Massachusetts</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Pennsylvania" title="Pennsylvania">Pennsylvania</A>, as it called for representation based on population. The smaller states, however, favored the <A href="/wiki/New_Jersey_Plan" title="New Jersey Plan">New Jersey Plan</A>, which called for a unicameral Congress with equal representation for the states.<SUP id="cite_ref-Plans_6-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Plans-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Eventually, the Convention reached the <A href="/wiki/Connecticut_Compromise" title="Connecticut Compromise">Connecticut Compromise</A> or Great Compromise, under which one house of Congress (the House of Representatives) would provide representation proportional to each state's population, whereas the other (the Senate) would provide equal representation amongst the states.<SUP id="cite_ref-Plans_6-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Plans-6">[6]</A></SUP> The Constitution was ratified by the requisite number of states (nine out of the 13) in 1788, but its implementation was set for March 4, 1789. The House began work on April 1, 1789, when it achieved a <A href="/wiki/Quorum" title="Quorum">quorum</A> for the first time.</P>
<P>During the first half of the 19th century, the House was frequently in conflict with the Senate over regionally divisive issues, including <A href="/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States" title="Slavery in the United States">slavery</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Northeastern_United_States" title="Northeastern United States">North</A> was much more populous than the <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_Southern_United_States" title="History of the Southern United States">South</A>, and therefore dominated the House of Representatives. However, the North held no such advantage in the Senate, where the equal representation of states prevailed.</P>
<P>Regional conflict was most pronounced over the issue of slavery. One example of a provision repeatedly supported by the House but blocked by the Senate was the <A href="/wiki/Wilmot_Proviso" title="Wilmot Proviso">Wilmot Proviso</A>, which sought to ban slavery in the land gained during the <A href="/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War" title="Mexican–American War">Mexican–American War</A>. Conflict over slavery and other issues persisted until the <A href="/wiki/American_Civil_War" title="American Civil War">Civil War</A> (1861–1865), which began soon after several southern states attempted to <A href="/wiki/Secession" title="Secession">secede</A> from the Union. The war culminated in the South's defeat and in the abolition of slavery. All southern senators except <A href="/wiki/Andrew_Johnson" title="Andrew Johnson">Andrew Johnson</A> resigned their seats at the beginning of the war, and therefore the Senate did not hold the balance of power between North and South during the war.</P>
<P>The years of <A href="/wiki/Reconstruction_Era" title="Reconstruction Era">Reconstruction</A> that followed witnessed large majorities for the <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_Republican_Party" title="History of the United States Republican Party">Republican Party</A>, which many Americans associated with the Union's victory in the Civil War and the ending of slavery. The Reconstruction period ended in about 1877; the ensuing era, known as the <A href="/wiki/Gilded_Age" title="Gilded Age">Gilded Age</A>, was marked by sharp political divisions in the electorate. The <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_Democratic_Party" title="History of the United States Democratic Party">Democratic Party</A> and Republican Party each held majorities in the House at various times.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:202px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Thomas_Brackett_Reed_-_Brady-Handy.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Thomas_Brackett_Reed_-_Brady-Handy.jpg/200px-Thomas_Brackett_Reed_-_Brady-Handy.jpg" width="200" height="259" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Thomas_Brackett_Reed_-_Brady-Handy.jpg/300px-Thomas_Brackett_Reed_-_Brady-Handy.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Thomas_Brackett_Reed_-_Brady-Handy.jpg/400px-Thomas_Brackett_Reed_-_Brady-Handy.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1000" data-file-height="1297" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">

<A href="/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States)" title="Republican Party (United States)">Republican</A> <A href="/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" title="Speaker of the United States House of Representatives">Speaker of the House</A>, <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Brackett_Reed" title="Thomas Brackett Reed">Thomas Brackett Reed</A> (1895–1899)</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The late 19th and early 20th centuries also saw a dramatic increase in the power of the <A href="/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" title="Speaker of the United States House of Representatives">Speaker of the House</A>. The rise of the Speaker's influence began in the 1890s, during the tenure of Republican <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Brackett_Reed" title="Thomas Brackett Reed">Thomas Brackett Reed</A>. "<A href="/wiki/Czar" class="mw-redirect" title="Czar">Czar</A> Reed", as he was nicknamed, attempted to put into effect his view that "The best system is to have one party govern and the other party watch." The leadership structure of the House also developed during approximately the same period, with the positions of <A href="/wiki/Majority_Leader_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" class="mw-redirect" title="Majority Leader of the United States House of Representatives">Majority Leader</A> and <A href="/wiki/Minority_leader_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" class="mw-redirect" title="Minority leader of the United States House of Representatives">Minority Leader</A> being created in 1899. While the Minority Leader was the head of the minority party, the Majority Leader remained subordinate to the Speaker. The Speakership reached its zenith during the term of Republican <A href="/wiki/Joseph_Gurney_Cannon" title="Joseph Gurney Cannon">Joseph Gurney Cannon</A>, from 1903 to 1911. The powers of the Speaker included chairmanship of the influential <A href="/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Rules" title="United States House Committee on Rules">Rules Committee</A> and the ability to appoint members of other House committees. These powers, however, were curtailed in the "Revolution of 1910" because of the efforts of Democrats and dissatisfied Republicans who opposed Cannon's arguably heavy-handed tactics.</P>
<P>The Democratic Party dominated the House of Representatives during the administration of President <A href="/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt" title="Franklin D. Roosevelt">Franklin D. Roosevelt</A> (1933–1945), often winning over two-thirds of the seats. Both Democrats and Republicans were in power at various times during the next decade. The Democratic Party maintained control of the House from 1955 until 1995. In the mid-1970s, there were major reforms of the House, strengthening the power of sub-committees at the expense of committee chairs and allowing party leaders to nominate committee chairs. These actions were taken to undermine the <A href="/wiki/Seniority_in_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives" title="Seniority in the United States House of Representatives">seniority system</A>, and to reduce the ability of a small number of senior members to obstruct legislation they did not favor. There was also a shift from the 1990s to greater control of the legislative program by the majority party; the power of party leaders (especially the Speaker) grew considerably.</P>
<P>The Republicans <A href="/wiki/Republican_Revolution" title="Republican Revolution">took control of the House</A> in 1995, under the leadership of Speaker <A href="/wiki/Newt_Gingrich" title="Newt Gingrich">Newt Gingrich</A>. Gingrich attempted to pass a major legislative program, the <A href="/wiki/Contract_with_America" title="Contract with America">Contract with America</A>, on which the House Republicans had been elected, and made major reforms of the House, notably reducing the tenure of committee chairs to three two-year terms. Many elements of the Contract did not pass Congress, were vetoed by President <A href="/wiki/Bill_Clinton" title="Bill Clinton">Bill Clinton</A>, or were substantially altered in negotiations with Clinton. The Republicans held on to the House until 2006, when the Democrats won control and <A href="/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi" title="Nancy Pelosi">Nancy Pelosi</A> was subsequently elected by the House as the first female Speaker. The Republicans retook the House in 2011, with the largest shift of power since the 1930s.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
