<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Special_effects">Special effects</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Special effects">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><I>The Fellowship of the Ring</I> makes extensive use of digital, practical and make-up special effects throughout. One noticeable illusion that appears in almost every scene involves setting a proper scale so that the characters are all the correct height. Elijah Wood, who plays Frodo, is 5 ft 6 in (1.68 m) tall in real life, but the character of Frodo Baggins is barely four feet in height. Many different tricks were used to depict the hobbits (and Gimli the Dwarf) as being of diminutive stature. (In a happy coincidence, John-Rhys Davies – who played Gimli – is as tall compared to the Hobbit actors as his character needed to be compared to theirs, so he did not need to be filmed separately as a third variation of height, and is quite taller than Orlando Bloom, who played Legolas.) Large- and small-scale doubles were used in certain scenes, while entire duplicates of certain sets (including <A href="/wiki/Bag_End" class="mw-redirect" title="Bag End">Bag End</A> in Hobbiton) were built at two different scales, so that the characters would appear to be the appropriate size. At one point in the film, Frodo runs along a corridor in Bag End, followed by Gandalf. Elijah Wood and Ian McKellen were filmed in separate versions of the same corridor, built at two different scales, and a fast camera pan conceals the edit between the two. <A href="/wiki/Forced_perspective" title="Forced perspective">Forced perspective</A> was also employed, so that it would look as though the short Hobbits were interacting with taller <A href="/wiki/Man_(Middle-earth)" title="Man (Middle-earth)">Men</A> and Elves. Even the simple use of kneeling down, to the filmmakers' surprise, turned out to be an effective method in creating the illusion.</P>
<P>For the battle between the Last Alliance and Sauron's forces that begins the film, an elaborate <A href="/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery" title="Computer-generated imagery">CGI</A> animation system, called <A href="/wiki/MASSIVE_(software)" title="MASSIVE (software)">MASSIVE</A>, was developed by <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Regelous" title="Stephen Regelous">Stephen Regelous</A>; it allowed thousands of individual animated "characters" in the program to act independently. This helped give the illusion of realism to the battle sequences. The "Making of" Lord of the Rings DVD reports some interesting initial problems: in the first execution of a battle between groups of characters, the wrong groups attacked each other. In another early demo, some of the warriors at the edge of the field could be seen running away. They were initially moving in the wrong direction, and had been programmed to keep running until they encountered an enemy.</P>
<P>The digital creatures were important due to Jackson's requirement of biological plausibility. Their surface was scanned from large <A href="/wiki/Maquette" title="Maquette">maquettes</A> before numerous digital details of their skeletons and muscles were added. In the case of the Balrog, Gray Horsfield created a system that copied recorded imagery of fire.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Score">Score</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Score">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring_(soundtrack)" title="The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (soundtrack)">The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (soundtrack)</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Music_of_The_Lord_of_the_Rings_film_series" title="Music of The Lord of the Rings film series">Music of The Lord of the Rings film series</A></DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Film_score" title="Film score">musical score</A> for <I>The Lord of the Rings</I> films was composed by <A href="/wiki/Howard_Shore" title="Howard Shore">Howard Shore</A>. It was performed by the 100-strong <A href="/wiki/New_Zealand_Symphony_Orchestra" title="New Zealand Symphony Orchestra">New Zealand Symphony Orchestra</A>, the <A href="/wiki/London_Philharmonic_Orchestra" title="London Philharmonic Orchestra">London Philharmonic Orchestra</A>, the <A href="/wiki/London_Voices" title="London Voices">London Voices</A>, The London Oratory School Schola, and the Maori Samoan Choir, and featured several vocal soloists. Shore wrote almost four hours of finalised music for the film (of which just over three hours are used as underscore), featuring a number of non-orchestral instruments, and a large number (49-62) of <A href="/wiki/Leitmotif" title="Leitmotif">leitmotives</A>.</P>
<P>Two original songs, "<A href="/wiki/An%C3%ADron" title="Aníron">Aníron</A>" and the end title theme "<A href="/wiki/May_It_Be" title="May It Be">May It Be</A>", were composed and sung by <A href="/wiki/Enya" title="Enya">Enya</A>, who allowed her label, <A href="/wiki/Reprise_Records" title="Reprise Records">Reprise Records</A>, to release the soundtrack to this and its two sequels. In addition to these songs, Shore composed "<A href="/wiki/In_Dreams_(Howard_Shore_song)" title="In Dreams (Howard Shore song)">In Dreams</A>", which was sung by Edward Ross of the London Oratory School Schola.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Release">Release</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Release">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>A special behind-the-scenes trailer was released in 2000. Two teasers were shown before <I><A href="/wiki/Spy_Kids" title="Spy Kids">Spy Kids</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Pearl_Harbor_(film)" title="Pearl Harbor (film)">Pearl Harbor (film)</A></I>. The final trailer was with the television premiere of <I><A href="/wiki/Angel_(1999_TV_series)" title="Angel (1999 TV series)">Angel</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Harry_Potter_and_the_Philosopher%27s_Stone_(film)" title="Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (film)">Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone</A></I>, and on the DVD and VHS of <I><A href="/wiki/Rush_Hour_2" title="Rush Hour 2">Rush Hour 2</A></I>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Home_media">Home media</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Home media">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><I>The Fellowship of the Ring</I> was released on <A href="/wiki/VHS" title="VHS">VHS</A> and DVD in August 2002.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Theatrical_and_extended_release">Theatrical and extended release</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Theatrical and extended release">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>In November 2002, an extended edition was released on VHS and DVD, with 30 minutes of new material, added special effects and music, plus 20 minutes of fan-club credits, totalling to 228 minutes.<SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[39]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-movies.com_40-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-movies.com-40">[40]</A></SUP> The DVD set included four commentaries and over three hours of supplementary material.</P>
<P>In August 2006, a limited edition of <I>The Fellowship of the Ring</I> was released on DVD. The set included both the film's theatrical and extended editions on a <A href="/wiki/DVD-9" class="mw-redirect" title="DVD-9">double-sided disc</A> along with all-new bonus material.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Blu-ray_edition">Blu-ray edition</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Blu-ray edition">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>The theatrical <A href="/wiki/Blu-ray_Disc" class="mw-redirect" title="Blu-ray Disc">Blu-ray</A> version of <I>The Lord of the Rings</I> was released in the United States in April 2010. There were two separate sets: one with digital copies and one without.<SUP id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-41">[41]</A></SUP> The individual Blu-ray disc of <I>The Fellowship of the Ring</I> was released in September 2010 with the same special features as the complete trilogy release, except there was no digital copy.<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[42]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The extended Blu-ray editions were released in the US in June 2011.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP> This version has a runtime of 238 minutes<SUP id="cite_ref-movies.com_40-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-movies.com-40">[40]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP> (the extended editions include the names of all fan club members at the time of their release; the additional 9 minutes in the Blu-ray version are because of expanded member rolls, not any additional story material).</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Reception">Reception</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Reception">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Box_office">Box office</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Box office">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><I>The Fellowship of the Ring</I> was released on 19 December 2001 in 3,359 cinemas where it grossed $47.2 million on its opening weekend. The world premiere was held at the <A href="/wiki/Odeon_Leicester_Square" title="Odeon Leicester Square">Odeon Leicester Square</A> in London. It went on to make $314.7 million in North America and $555.9 million in the rest of the world for a worldwide total of $870.7 million.<SUP id="cite_ref-boxoffice_45-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-boxoffice-45">[45]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Box_Office_Mojo" title="Box Office Mojo">Box Office Mojo</A> estimates that the film sold over 54 million tickets in the US in its initial theatrical run.<SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[46]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Critical_response">Critical response</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Critical response">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><I>The Fellowship of the Ring</I> was acclaimed by film critics and was one of 2001's best reviewed films.<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[47]</A></SUP> The film holds a 91% approval rating on aggregate review site <A href="/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes" title="Rotten Tomatoes">Rotten Tomatoes</A> based on 227 reviews and an average score of 8.2/10. The site's main consensus reads "Full of eye-popping special effects, and featuring a pitch-perfect cast, <I>The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring</I> brings J.R.R. Tolkien's classic to vivid life".<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP> The film holds a score of 92 out of 100 on <A href="/wiki/Metacritic" title="Metacritic">Metacritic</A> based on 34 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim".<SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[49]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Roger_Ebert" title="Roger Ebert">Roger Ebert</A> gave the film three out of four stars and stating that while it is not "a true visualization of Tolkien's Middle-earth", it is "a work for, and of, our times. It will be embraced, I suspect, by many Tolkien fans and take on aspects of a cult. It is a candidate for many Oscars. It is an awesome production in its daring and breadth, and there are small touches that are just right".<SUP id="cite_ref-Ebert_50-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Ebert-50">[50]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/USA_Today" title="USA Today">USA Today</A></I> also gave the film three out of four stars and wrote, "this movie version of a beloved book should please devotees as well as the uninitiated".<SUP id="cite_ref-Puig_51-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Puig-51">[51]</A></SUP> In his review for <I><A href="/wiki/The_New_York_Times" title="The New York Times">The New York Times</A></I>, <A href="/wiki/Elvis_Mitchell" title="Elvis Mitchell">Elvis Mitchell</A> wrote, "The playful spookiness of Mr. Jackson's direction provides a lively, light touch, a gesture that doesn't normally come to mind when Tolkien's name is mentioned".<SUP id="cite_ref-Mitchell_52-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Mitchell-52">[52]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly" title="Entertainment Weekly">Entertainment Weekly</A></I> magazine gave the film an "A" rating and Lisa Schwarzbaum wrote, "The cast take to their roles with becoming modesty, certainly, but Jackson also makes it easy for them: His <I>Fellowship</I> flows, never lingering for the sake of admiring its own beauty ... Every detail of which engrossed me. I may have never turned a page of Tolkien, but I know enchantment when I see it".<SUP id="cite_ref-Schwarzbaum_53-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Schwarzbaum-53">[53]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In her review for <I><A href="/wiki/The_Washington_Post" title="The Washington Post">The Washington Post</A></I>, Rita Kempley praised the cast, in particular, "Mortensen, as Strider, is a revelation, not to mention downright gorgeous. And McKellen, carrying the burden of thousands of years' worth of the fight against evil, is positively Merlinesque".<SUP id="cite_ref-Kempley_54-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Kempley-54">[54]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/Time_(magazine)" title="Time (magazine)">Time</A></I> magazine's Richard Corliss praised Jackson's work: "His movie achieves what the best fairy tales do: the creation of an alternate world, plausible and persuasive, where the young — and not only the young — can lose themselves. And perhaps, in identifying with the little Hobbit that could, find their better selves".<SUP id="cite_ref-Corliss_55-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Corliss-55">[55]</A></SUP> In his review for <I><A href="/wiki/The_Village_Voice" title="The Village Voice">The Village Voice</A></I>, <A href="/wiki/J._Hoberman" title="J. Hoberman">J. Hoberman</A> wrote, "Peter Jackson's adaptation is certainly successful on its own terms".<SUP id="cite_ref-Hoberman_56-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Hoberman-56">[56]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/Rolling_Stone" title="Rolling Stone">Rolling Stone</A></I> magazine's <A href="/wiki/Peter_Travers" title="Peter Travers">Peter Travers</A> wrote, "It's emotion that makes <I>Fellowship</I> stick hard in the memory... Jackson deserves to revel in his success. He's made a three-hour film that leaves you wanting more".<SUP id="cite_ref-Travers_57-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Travers-57">[57]</A></SUP> However, in his review for <I><A href="/wiki/The_Guardian" title="The Guardian">The Guardian</A></I>, Peter Bradshaw wrote, "there is a strange paucity of plot complication, an absence of anything unfolding, all the more disconcerting because of the clotted and indigestible mythic back story that we have to wade through before anything happens at all".<SUP id="cite_ref-Bradshaw_58-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Bradshaw-58">[58]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/CinemaScore" title="CinemaScore">CinemaScore</A> polls conducted during the opening weekend, cinema audiences gave the film an average grade of "A−" on an A+ to F scale.<SUP id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-59">[59]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Accolades">Accolades</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: Accolades">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/List_of_accolades_received_by_The_Lord_of_the_Rings_film_series" title="List of accolades received by The Lord of the Rings film series">List of accolades received by The Lord of the Rings film series</A></DIV>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/74th_Academy_Awards" title="74th Academy Awards">2002</A>, the film won four <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award" class="mw-redirect" title="Academy Award">Academy Awards</A> from thirteen nominations.<SUP id="cite_ref-Oscars2002_60-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Oscars2002-60">[60]</A></SUP> The winning categories were for <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Cinematography" title="Academy Award for Best Cinematography">Best Cinematography</A>, <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Visual_Effects" title="Academy Award for Best Visual Effects">Best Visual Effects</A>, <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Makeup_and_Hairstyling" title="Academy Award for Best Makeup and Hairstyling">Best Makeup</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Score" title="Academy Award for Best Original Score">Best Original Score</A>. It was also nominated for <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor" title="Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor">Best Actor in a Supporting Role</A> (<A href="/wiki/Ian_McKellen" title="Ian McKellen">Ian McKellen</A>), <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Production_Design" title="Academy Award for Best Production Design">Best Art Direction</A>, <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director" title="Academy Award for Best Director">Best Director</A>, <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Film_Editing" title="Academy Award for Best Film Editing">Best Film Editing</A>, <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Song" title="Academy Award for Best Original Song">Best Original Song</A> (<A href="/wiki/Enya" title="Enya">Enya</A>, <A href="/wiki/Nicky_Ryan" title="Nicky Ryan">Nicky Ryan</A> and <A href="/wiki/Roma_Ryan" title="Roma Ryan">Roma Ryan</A> for "<A href="/wiki/May_It_Be" title="May It Be">May It Be</A>"), <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture" title="Academy Award for Best Picture">Best Picture</A>, <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Sound" class="mw-redirect" title="Academy Award for Best Sound">Best Sound</A> (<A href="/wiki/Christopher_Boyes" title="Christopher Boyes">Christopher Boyes</A>, <A href="/wiki/Michael_Semanick" title="Michael Semanick">Michael Semanick</A>, <A href="/wiki/Gethin_Creagh" title="Gethin Creagh">Gethin Creagh</A> and <A href="/wiki/Hammond_Peek" title="Hammond Peek">Hammond Peek</A>), <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Costume_Design" title="Academy Award for Best Costume Design">Best Costume Design</A> and <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Writing_(Adapted_Screenplay)" class="mw-redirect" title="Academy Award for Best Writing (Adapted Screenplay)">Best Adapted Screenplay</A>.</P>
<P>As of January 2014<SUP class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><A class="external text" href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Fellowship_of_the_Ring&action=edit">[update]</A></SUP>, it is the 31st highest-grossing film worldwide, with US$871,530,324 in worldwide theatrical box office receipts.<SUP id="cite_ref-BOM_3-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BOM-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The film won the 2002 <A href="/wiki/Hugo_Award_for_Best_Dramatic_Presentation" title="Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation">Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation</A>. It also won <I><A href="/wiki/Empire_(film_magazine)" title="Empire (film magazine)">Empire</A></I> readers' Best Film award, as well as five <A href="/wiki/British_Academy_of_Film_and_Television_Arts" title="British Academy of Film and Television Arts">BAFTAs</A>, including <A href="/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Film" title="BAFTA Award for Best Film">Best Film</A>, the <A href="/wiki/David_Lean" title="David Lean">David Lean</A> Award for <A href="/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Direction" title="BAFTA Award for Best Direction">Best Direction</A>, the Audience Award (voted for by the public), <A href="/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Special_Visual_Effects" title="BAFTA Award for Best Special Visual Effects">Best Special Effects</A>, and <A href="/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Makeup_and_Hair" title="BAFTA Award for Best Makeup and Hair">Best Make-up</A>. The film was nominated for an <A href="/wiki/MTV_Movie_Award_for_Best_Fight" title="MTV Movie Award for Best Fight">MTV Movie Award for Best Fight</A> between Gandalf and Saruman.</P>
<P>In June 2008, AFI revealed its "<A href="/wiki/AFI%27s_10_Top_10" title="AFI's 10 Top 10">10 Top 10</A>"—the ten best films in ten "classic" American film genres—after polling over 1,500 people from the creative community. <I>The Fellowship of the Ring</I> was acknowledged as the second best film in the fantasy genre.<SUP id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-61">[61]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-62">[62]</A></SUP> The film was also listed as the 50th best film in the 2007 list <A href="/wiki/AFI%27s_100_Years...100_Movies_(10th_Anniversary_Edition)" title="AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies (10th Anniversary Edition)">AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies (10th Anniversary Edition)</A>.</P>

<P><B>Gilles Marini</B> <SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ʒ/: 's' in 'pleasure'">ʒ</SPAN><SPAN title="/iː/: 'ee' in 'fleece'">iː</SPAN><SPAN title="'l' in 'lie'">l</SPAN></SPAN> <SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="'m' in 'my'">m</SPAN><SPAN title="/ə/: 'a' in 'about'">ə</SPAN><SPAN title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</SPAN><SPAN title="'r' in 'rye'">r</SPAN><SPAN title="/iː/: 'ee' in 'fleece'">iː</SPAN><SPAN title="'n' in 'nigh'">n</SPAN><SPAN title="/i/: 'y' in 'happy'">i</SPAN></SPAN>/</A></SPAN></SPAN> (born January 26, 1976) is a French-American actor, known for his roles in the film <I><A href="/wiki/Sex_and_the_City_(film)" title="Sex and the City (film)">Sex and the City</A></I> and in the American television shows <I><A href="/wiki/Brothers_%26_Sisters_(2006_TV_series)" title="Brothers & Sisters (2006 TV series)">Brothers & Sisters</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Switched_at_Birth_(TV_series)" title="Switched at Birth (TV series)">Switched at Birth</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Devious_Maids" title="Devious Maids">Devious Maids</A></I>. He was also the runner-up in <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_8)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 8)">season 8</A> of <I><A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._TV_series)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. TV series)">Dancing with the Stars</A></I>, and was one of the returning celebrities in <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_15)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 15)">season 15</A>, also a French Co-Host on <I><A href="/wiki/Ultimate_Beastmaster" title="Ultimate Beastmaster">Ultimate Beastmaster</A></I>.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_life">Early life</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Gilles_Marini&action=edit&section=1&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Early life">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Marini was born in <A href="/wiki/Grasse" title="Grasse">Grasse</A>, <A href="/wiki/Alpes-Maritimes" title="Alpes-Maritimes">Alpes-Maritimes</A>, France, to a <A href="/wiki/Greeks" title="Greeks">Greek</A> mother and <A href="/wiki/Italians" title="Italians">Italian</A> father.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> After working as a baker in his father's bakery since he was eight years old and high school, he joined the French army and was stationed in Paris, where he served as a fireman in the <A href="/wiki/Paris_Fire_Brigade" title="Paris Fire Brigade">Paris Fire Brigade</A>. It was in Paris where Marini met Fred Goudon, a photographer who introduced him to the world of modeling. After fulfilling his military duties, he went to the United States to learn English while working as a model. He began his career as a model in his early twenties. One of his first jobs was a television commercial for Bud Light beer. He made his acting debut at the age of 29, in the 2005 horror film <I>Screech of the Decapitated</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Career">Career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Gilles_Marini&action=edit&section=2&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>He played Dante in <I><A href="/wiki/Sex_and_the_City_(film)" title="Sex and the City (film)">Sex and the City: The Movie</A></I>, and has appeared on <I><A href="/wiki/Brothers_%26_Sisters_(TV_series)" class="mw-redirect" title="Brothers & Sisters (TV series)">Brothers & Sisters</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Ugly_Betty" title="Ugly Betty">Ugly Betty</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Dirty_Sexy_Money" title="Dirty Sexy Money">Dirty Sexy Money</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Criminal_Minds" title="Criminal Minds">Criminal Minds</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Nip/Tuck" title="Nip/Tuck">Nip/Tuck</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/The_Bold_and_the_Beautiful" title="The Bold and the Beautiful">The Bold and the Beautiful</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Passions" title="Passions">Passions</A></I>, and <I><A href="/wiki/2_Broke_Girls" title="2 Broke Girls">2 Broke Girls</A></I>. His film credits include <I>One and the Other (L'Une et L'Autre)</I> and <I><A href="/wiki/The_Boys_%26_Girls_Guide_to_Getting_Down" title="The Boys & Girls Guide to Getting Down">The Boys & Girls Guide to Getting Down</A></I>. On February 8, 2009, it was announced that Marini would participate in the <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_8)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 8)">eighth season</A> of <I><A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._TV_series)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. TV series)">Dancing with the Stars</A></I>. His professional partner was <A href="/wiki/Cheryl_Burke" title="Cheryl Burke">Cheryl Burke</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> He also took part in the <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_15)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 15)">fifteenth season</A> of <I>Dancing with the Stars</I> for another chance to win the mirrorball trophy.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> He danced with <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_14)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 14)">season fourteen</A> winner, <A href="/wiki/Peta_Murgatroyd" title="Peta Murgatroyd">Peta Murgatroyd</A>. They were the eighth couple eliminated from the competition, alongside <A href="/wiki/Kirstie_Alley" title="Kirstie Alley">Kirstie Alley</A> and <A href="/wiki/Maksim_Chmerkovskiy" title="Maksim Chmerkovskiy">Maksim Chmerkovskiy</A>.</P>
<P>He was introduced as a recurring character on <A href="/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company" title="American Broadcasting Company">ABC</A>'s family drama <I><A href="/wiki/Brothers_%26_Sisters_(2006_TV_series)" title="Brothers & Sisters (2006 TV series)">Brothers & Sisters</A></I>. He played Luc Laurent, the French love interest of <A href="/wiki/Rachel_Griffiths" title="Rachel Griffiths">Rachel Griffiths</A>' character <A href="/wiki/Sarah_Walker_(Brothers_%26_Sisters)" title="Sarah Walker (Brothers & Sisters)">Sarah Walker</A> in what was originally supposed to be a five-episode arc,<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> but was promoted to a series regular.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> The series was cancelled in May 2011, after the fifth season ended. He also appears as Bay Kennish's biological father, Angelo Sorrento, in <I><A href="/wiki/Switched_at_Birth_(TV_series)" title="Switched at Birth (TV series)">Switched at Birth</A></I>. On September 18, 2012<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP>, it was announced that he would become a series regular for the second season.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Dancing_with_the_Stars_performances"><I>Dancing with the Stars</I> performances</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Gilles_Marini&action=edit&section=3&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Dancing with the Stars performances">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Gilles and his professional partner, <A href="/wiki/Cheryl_Burke" title="Cheryl Burke">Cheryl Burke</A> came in as the runners-up of the American televised <A href="/wiki/Ballroom_dancing" class="mw-redirect" title="Ballroom dancing">ballroom dancing</A> competition, <I><A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_8)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 8)">Dancing with the Stars</A></I>. On May 19, 2009, then seventeen-year-old gymnast <A href="/wiki/Shawn_Johnson" class="mw-redirect" title="Shawn Johnson">Shawn Johnson</A> and her partner, <A href="/wiki/Mark_Ballas" title="Mark Ballas">Mark Ballas</A> were crowned champions of that season, defeating Marini & Burke by 1%.</P>

<P><I><B>The Merchant of Venice</B></I> is a 16th-century play by <A href="/wiki/William_Shakespeare" title="William Shakespeare">William Shakespeare</A> in which a merchant in Venice must default on a large loan provided by an abused Jewish moneylender. It is believed to have been written between 1596 and 1599. Though classified as a <A href="/wiki/Shakespearean_comedy" title="Shakespearean comedy">comedy</A> in the <A href="/wiki/First_Folio" title="First Folio">First Folio</A> and sharing certain aspects with Shakespeare's other <A href="/wiki/Romantic_comedy" class="mw-redirect" title="Romantic comedy">romantic comedies</A>, the play is perhaps most remembered for its dramatic scenes, and it is best known for <A href="/wiki/Shylock" title="Shylock">Shylock</A> and the famous "Hath not a Jew eyes?" speech. Also notable is <A href="/wiki/Portia_(Merchant_of_Venice)" class="mw-redirect" title="Portia (Merchant of Venice)">Portia</A>'s speech about "<A href="/wiki/The_quality_of_mercy_(Shakespeare_quote)" title="The quality of mercy (Shakespeare quote)">the quality of mercy</A>". Critic <A href="/wiki/Harold_Bloom" title="Harold Bloom">Harold Bloom</A> listed it among Shakespeare's great comedies.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Summary">Summary</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Summary">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Gilbert-Shylock.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Gilbert-Shylock.jpg/220px-Gilbert-Shylock.jpg" width="220" height="146" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Gilbert-Shylock.jpg/330px-Gilbert-Shylock.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/dc/Gilbert-Shylock.jpg 2x" data-file-width="423" data-file-height="280" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Gilbert-Shylock.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Gilbert's <I><A href="/wiki/Shylock" title="Shylock">Shylock</A> After the Trial</I>, an illustration to The <I>Merchant of Venice</I>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Bassanio, a young <A href="/wiki/Republic_of_Venice" title="Republic of Venice">Venetian</A> of noble rank, wishes to woo the beautiful and wealthy heiress <A href="/wiki/Portia_(Merchant_of_Venice)" class="mw-redirect" title="Portia (Merchant of Venice)">Portia</A> of Belmont. Having squandered his estate, he needs 3,000 <A href="/wiki/Ducats" class="mw-redirect" title="Ducats">ducats</A> to subsidise his expenditures as a suitor. Bassanio approaches his friend <A href="/wiki/Antonio_(Merchant_of_Venice)" class="mw-redirect" title="Antonio (Merchant of Venice)">Antonio</A>, a wealthy merchant of Venice who has previously and repeatedly bailed him out. Antonio agrees, but since he is cash-poor – his ships and merchandise are busy at sea – he promises to cover a bond if Bassanio can find a lender, so Bassanio turns to the Jewish moneylender Shylock and names Antonio as the loan's guarantor.</P>
<P>Antonio has already antagonized Shylock through his outspoken <A href="/wiki/Antisemitism" title="Antisemitism">antisemitism</A>, and because Antonio's habit of lending money without interest forces Shylock to charge lower rates. Shylock is at first reluctant to grant the loan, citing abuse he has suffered at Antonio's hand. He finally agrees to lend the sum to Bassanio without interest upon one condition: if Antonio is unable to repay it at the specified date, Shylock may take a <A href="/wiki/Pound_(mass)" title="Pound (mass)">pound</A> of Antonio's flesh. Bassanio does not want Antonio to accept such a risky condition; Antonio is surprised by what he sees as the moneylender's generosity (no "usance" – interest – is asked for), and he signs the contract. With money at hand, Bassanio leaves for Belmont with his friend Gratiano, who has asked to accompany him. Gratiano is a likeable young man, but is often flippant, overly talkative, and tactless. Bassanio warns his companion to exercise self-control, and the two leave for Belmont.</P>
<P>Meanwhile, in Belmont, Portia is awash with suitors. Her father left a <A href="/wiki/Will_(law)" class="mw-redirect" title="Will (law)">will</A> stipulating each of her suitors must choose correctly from one of three caskets – one each of gold, silver and lead. If he picks the right casket, he gets Portia. The first suitor, the Prince of Morocco, chooses the gold casket, interpreting its slogan, "Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire", as referring to Portia. The second suitor, the conceited Prince of Arragon, chooses the silver casket, which proclaims, "Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves", as he believes he is full of merit. Both suitors leave empty-handed, having rejected the lead casket because of the baseness of its material and the uninviting nature of its slogan, "Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath". The last suitor is Bassanio, whom Portia wishes to succeed, having met him before. As Bassanio ponders his choice, members of Portia's household sing a song which says that "fancy" (not true love) is "engend'red in the eyes, / With gazing fed";<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> Bassanio chooses the lead casket and wins Portia's hand.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Shakespeare%27s_Heroines_-_Jessica.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Shakespeare%27s_Heroines_-_Jessica.jpg/220px-Shakespeare%27s_Heroines_-_Jessica.jpg" width="220" height="301" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Shakespeare%27s_Heroines_-_Jessica.jpg/330px-Shakespeare%27s_Heroines_-_Jessica.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Shakespeare%27s_Heroines_-_Jessica.jpg/440px-Shakespeare%27s_Heroines_-_Jessica.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4435" data-file-height="6070" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Shakespeare%27s_Heroines_-_Jessica.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
A depiction of Jessica, from <I>The Graphic Gallery of Shakespeare's Heroines</I></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>At Venice, Antonio's ships are reported lost at sea so the merchant cannot repay the bond. Shylock has become more determined to exact revenge from Christians because his daughter Jessica eloped with the Christian Lorenzo and converted. She took a substantial amount of Shylock's wealth with her, as well as a turquoise ring which Shylock had been given by his late wife, Leah. Shylock has Antonio brought before court.</P>
<P>At Belmont, Bassanio receives a letter telling him that Antonio has been unable to repay the loan from Shylock. Portia and Bassanio marry, as do Gratiano and Portia's handmaid Nerissa. Bassanio and Gratiano leave for <A href="/wiki/Venice" title="Venice">Venice</A>, with money from Portia, to save Antonio's life by offering the money to Shylock. Unknown to Bassanio and Gratiano, Portia sent her servant, Balthazar, to seek the counsel of Portia's cousin, Bellario, a lawyer, at <A href="/wiki/Padua" title="Padua">Padua</A>.</P>
<P>The climax of the play takes place in the court of the <A href="/wiki/Doges_of_Venice" class="mw-redirect" title="Doges of Venice">Duke of Venice</A>. Shylock refuses Bassanio's offer of 6,000 ducats, twice the amount of the loan. He demands his pound of flesh from Antonio. The Duke, wishing to save Antonio but unable to nullify a contract, refers the case to a visitor. He identifies himself as Balthazar, a young male "doctor of the law", bearing a letter of recommendation to the Duke from the learned lawyer Bellario. The doctor is Portia in disguise, and the law clerk who accompanies her is Nerissa, also disguised as a man. As Balthazar, Portia repeatedly asks Shylock to show mercy in a <A href="/wiki/The_quality_of_mercy_(Shakespeare_quote)" title="The quality of mercy (Shakespeare quote)">famous speech</A>, advising him that mercy "is twice blest: It blesseth him that gives and him that takes" (IV, i, 185). However, Shylock adamantly refuses any compensations and insists on the pound of flesh.</P>
<P>As the court grants Shylock his bond and Antonio prepares for Shylock's knife, Portia deftly appropriates Shylock's argument for "specific performance". She says that the contract allows Shylock only to remove the <I>flesh</I>, not the "blood", of Antonio (see <A href="/wiki/Quibble_(plot_device)" title="Quibble (plot device)">quibble</A>). Thus, if Shylock were to shed any drop of Antonio's blood, his "lands and goods" would be forfeited under Venetian laws. She tells him that he must cut precisely one pound of flesh, no more, no less; she advises him that "if the scale do turn, But in the estimation of a hair, Thou diest and all thy goods are confiscate."</P>
<P>Defeated, Shylock concedes to accepting Bassanio's offer of money for the defaulted bond, first his offer to pay "the bond thrice", which Portia rebuffs, telling him to take his bond, and then merely the principal, which Portia also prevents him from doing on the ground that he has already refused it "in the open court". She cites a law under which Shylock, as a Jew and therefore an "alien", having attempted to take the life of a citizen, has forfeited his property, half to <A href="/wiki/Venetian_Republic" class="mw-redirect" title="Venetian Republic">the government</A> and half to Antonio, leaving his life at the mercy of the Duke. The Duke pardons Shylock's life. Antonio asks for his share "in use" until Shylock's death, when the principal will be given to Lorenzo and Jessica. At Antonio's request, the Duke grants remission of the state's half of forfeiture, but on the condition that Shylock convert to Christianity and bequeath his entire estate to Lorenzo and Jessica (IV,i).</P>
<P>Bassanio does not recognise his disguised wife, but offers to give a present to the supposed lawyer. First she declines, but after he insists, Portia requests his ring and Antonio's gloves. Antonio parts with his gloves without a second thought, but Bassanio gives the ring only after much persuasion from Antonio, as earlier in the play he promised his wife never to lose, sell or give it. Nerissa, as the lawyer's clerk, succeeds in likewise retrieving her ring from Gratiano, who does not see through her disguise.</P>
<P>At Belmont, Portia and Nerissa taunt and pretend to accuse their husbands before revealing they were really the lawyer and his clerk in disguise (V). After all the other characters make amends, Antonio learns from Portia that three of his ships were not stranded and have returned safely after all.</P>

<P>The forfeit of a merchant's deadly <A href="/wiki/Surety_bond" title="Surety bond">bond</A> after standing surety for a friend's loan was a common tale in England in the late 16th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-Muir2005_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Muir2005-4">[4]</A></SUP> In addition, the test of the suitors at Belmont, the merchant's rescue from the "pound of flesh" penalty by his friend's new wife disguised as a lawyer, and her demand for the betrothal ring in payment are all elements present in the 14th-century tale <I><A href="https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_Pecorone" class="extiw" title="it:Il Pecorone">Il Pecorone</A></I> by <A href="/wiki/Italian_literature#Giovanni_Fiorentino" title="Italian literature">Giovanni Fiorentino</A>, which was published in Milan in 1558.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> Elements of the trial scene are also found in <I>The Orator</I> by <A href="/wiki/Histoires_tragiques" title="Histoires tragiques">Alexandre Sylvane</A>, published in translation in 1596.<SUP id="cite_ref-Muir2005_4-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Muir2005-4">[4]</A></SUP> The story of the three caskets can be found in "Gesta Romanorum", a collection of tales probably compiled at the end of the 13th century.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Date_and_text">Date and text</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Date and text">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The date of composition for <I>The Merchant of Venice</I> is believed to be between 1596 and 1598. The play was mentioned by <A href="/wiki/Francis_Meres" title="Francis Meres">Francis Meres</A> in 1598, so it must have been familiar on the stage by that date. The title page of the first edition in 1600 states that it had been performed "divers times" by that date. Salerino's reference to his ship the <I>Andrew</I> (I,i,27) is thought to be an allusion to the Spanish ship <I>St. Andrew,</I> captured by the English at <A href="/wiki/C%C3%A1diz" title="Cádiz">Cádiz</A> in 1596. A date of 1596–97 is considered consistent with the play's style.</P>
<P>The play was entered in the <A href="/wiki/Stationers%27_Register" title="Stationers' Register">Register</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Worshipful_Company_of_Stationers_and_Newspaper_Makers" title="Worshipful Company of Stationers and Newspaper Makers">Stationers Company</A>, the method at that time of obtaining <A href="/wiki/Copyright" title="Copyright">copyright</A> for a new play, by <A href="/wiki/James_Roberts_(printer)" title="James Roberts (printer)">James Roberts</A> on 22 July 1598 under the title <I>The Merchant of Venice</I>, otherwise called <I>The Jew of Venice</I>. On 28 October 1600 Roberts transferred his right to the play to the stationer <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Heyes" title="Thomas Heyes">Thomas Heyes</A>; Heyes published the first <A href="/wiki/Book_size" title="Book size">quarto</A> before the end of the year. It was printed again in a pirated edition in 1619, as part of William Jaggard's so-called <A href="/wiki/False_Folio" title="False Folio">False Folio</A>. (Afterward, Thomas Heyes' son and heir Laurence Heyes asked for and was granted a confirmation of his right to the play, on 8 July 1619.) The 1600 edition is generally regarded as being accurate and reliable. It is the basis of the text published in the 1623 <A href="/wiki/First_Folio" title="First Folio">First Folio</A>, which adds a number of stage directions, mainly musical cues.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Themes">Themes</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Themes">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Shylock_and_the_antisemitism_debate">Shylock and the antisemitism debate</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Shylock and the antisemitism debate">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The play is frequently staged today, but is potentially troubling to modern audiences due to its central themes, which can easily appear <A href="/wiki/Antisemitism" title="Antisemitism">antisemitic</A>. Critics today still continue to argue over the play's stance on the Jews and Judaism.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">

<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Shylock_as_a_villain">Shylock as a villain</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Shylock as a villain">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>English society in the Elizabethan era has been described as "judeophobic".<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_England" title="History of the Jews in England">English Jews</A> had been <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_England#Expulsion,_1290" title="History of the Jews in England">expelled</A> under <A href="/wiki/King_Edward_I_of_England" class="mw-redirect" title="King Edward I of England">Edward I</A> in 1290 and were not permitted to return until 1656 under the rule of <A href="/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell" title="Oliver Cromwell">Oliver Cromwell</A>. In Venice and in some other places, Jews were required to wear a red hat at all times in public to make sure that they were easily identified, and had to live in a ghetto protected by Christian guards.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Shakespeare's play may be seen as a continuation of this tradition.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> The title page of the <A href="/wiki/Folios_and_Quartos_(Shakespeare)" class="mw-redirect" title="Folios and Quartos (Shakespeare)">Quarto</A> indicates that the play was sometimes known as <I>The Jew of Venice</I> in its day, which suggests that it was seen as similar to Marlowe's <I><A href="/wiki/The_Jew_of_Malta" title="The Jew of Malta">The Jew of Malta</A></I>. One interpretation of the play's structure is that Shakespeare meant to contrast the mercy of the main Christian characters with the vengefulness of a Jew, who lacks the religious <A href="/wiki/Divine_grace" title="Divine grace">grace</A> to comprehend mercy. Similarly, it is possible that Shakespeare meant Shylock's <A href="/wiki/Forced_conversion" title="Forced conversion">forced conversion</A> to Christianity to be a "<A href="/wiki/Happy_ending" title="Happy ending">happy ending</A>" for the character, as, to a Christian audience, it saves his soul and allows him to enter Heaven.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Regardless of what Shakespeare's <A href="/wiki/Authorial_intent" title="Authorial intent">authorial intent</A> may have been, the play has been made use of by antisemites throughout the play's history. The <A href="/wiki/Nazis" class="mw-redirect" title="Nazis">Nazis</A> used the usurious Shylock for their propaganda. Shortly after <A href="/wiki/Kristallnacht" title="Kristallnacht">Kristallnacht</A> in 1938, <I>The Merchant of Venice</I> was broadcast for propagandistic ends over the German airwaves. Productions of the play followed in <A href="/wiki/L%C3%BCbeck" title="Lübeck">Lübeck</A> (1938), <A href="/wiki/Berlin" title="Berlin">Berlin</A> (1940), and elsewhere within the Nazi territory.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In a series of articles called <I>Observer</I>, first published in 1785, British playwright <A href="/wiki/Richard_Cumberland_(dramatist)" title="Richard Cumberland (dramatist)">Richard Cumberland</A> created a character named Abraham Abrahams who is quoted as saying, "I verily believe the odious character of Shylock has brought little less persecution upon us, poor scattered sons of <A href="/wiki/Abraham" title="Abraham">Abraham</A>, than the <A href="/wiki/Inquisition" title="Inquisition">Inquisition</A> itself."<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP> Cumberland later wrote a successful play, <I><A href="/wiki/The_Jew" class="mw-redirect" title="The Jew">The Jew</A></I> (1794), in which his title character, <A href="/wiki/The_Jew" class="mw-redirect" title="The Jew">Sheva</A>, is portrayed sympathetically, as both a kindhearted and generous man. This was the first known attempt by a dramatist to reverse the negative stereotype that Shylock personified.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Stereotypes_of_Jews_in_literature" title="Stereotypes of Jews in literature">depiction of Jews in literature</A> throughout the centuries bears the close imprint of Shylock. With slight variations much of English literature up until the 20th century depicts the Jew as "a monied, cruel, lecherous, avaricious outsider tolerated only because of his golden hoard".<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Shylock_as_a_sympathetic_character">Shylock as a sympathetic character</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Shylock as a sympathetic character">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Portia_and_Shylock.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Portia_and_Shylock.jpg/220px-Portia_and_Shylock.jpg" width="220" height="283" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/eb/Portia_and_Shylock.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="280" data-file-height="360" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Portia_and_Shylock.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
<I>Shylock and Portia</I> (1835) by <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Sully" title="Thomas Sully">Thomas Sully</A>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Many modern readers and theatregoers have read the play as a plea for tolerance, noting that Shylock is a sympathetic character. They cite as evidence that Shylock's "trial" at the end of the play is a mockery of justice, with Portia acting as a judge when she has no right to do so. The characters who berated Shylock for dishonesty resort to trickery in order to win. In addition, Shakespeare gives Shylock one of his most eloquent speeches:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE class="templatequote">
<DIV class="poem">
<P><I>Salerio.</I> Why, I am sure, if he forfeit, thou wilt not take his flesh. What's that good for?<BR />
<I>Shylock.</I> To bait fish withal; if it will feed nothing else, it will feed my revenge. He hath disgraced me and hindered me half a million, laughed at my losses, mocked at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my bargains, cooled my friends, heated mine enemies – and what's his reason? I am a Jew. Hath not a Jew eyes? Hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions; fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian is? If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die? And if you wrong us, shall we not revenge? If we are like you in the rest, we will resemble you in that. If a Jew wrong a Christian, what is his humility? Revenge. If a Christian wrong a Jew, what should his sufferance be by Christian example? Why, revenge. The villainy you teach me, I will execute, and it shall go hard but I will better the instruction.</P>
</DIV>
<DIV class="templatequotecite">— <CITE>Act III, scene I</CITE></DIV>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>It is difficult to know whether the sympathetic reading of Shylock is entirely due to changing sensibilities among readers, or whether Shakespeare, a writer who created complex, multi-faceted characters, deliberately intended this reading.</P>
<P>One of the reasons for this interpretation is that Shylock's painful status in Venetian society is emphasised. To some critics, Shylock's celebrated "Hath not a Jew eyes?" speech redeems him and even makes him into something of a tragic figure; in the speech, Shylock argues that he is no different from the Christian characters.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> Detractors note that Shylock ends the speech with a tone of revenge: "if you wrong us, shall we not revenge?" Those who see the speech as sympathetic point out that Shylock says he learned the desire for revenge from the Christian characters: "If a Christian wrong a Jew, what should his sufferance be by Christian example? Why, revenge. The villainy you teach me, I will execute, and it shall go hard but I will better the instruction."</P>
<P>Even if Shakespeare did not intend the play to be read this way, the fact that it retains its power on stage for audiences who may perceive its central conflicts in radically different terms is an illustration of the subtlety of Shakespeare's characterisations.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> In the trial Shylock represents what Elizabethan Christians believed to be the Jewish desire for "justice", contrasted with their obviously superior Christian value of mercy. The Christians in the courtroom urge Shylock to love his enemies, although they themselves have failed in the past. Jewish critic <A href="/wiki/Harold_Bloom" title="Harold Bloom">Harold Bloom</A> suggests that, although the play gives merit to both cases, the portraits are not even-handed: "Shylock's shrewd indictment of Christian hypocrisy delights us, but … Shakespeare’s intimations do not alleviate the savagery of his portrait of the Jew…"<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></P>

<H3><SPAN id="Antonio.2C_Bassanio"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Antonio,_Bassanio">Antonio, Bassanio</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Antonio, Bassanio">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Antonio's unexplained depression – "In sooth I know not why I am so sad" – and utter devotion to Bassanio has led some critics to theorise that he is suffering from <A href="/wiki/Unrequited_love" title="Unrequited love">unrequited love</A> for Bassanio and is depressed because Bassanio is coming to an age where he will marry a woman. In his plays and poetry Shakespeare often depicted strong male bonds of varying <A href="/wiki/Homosociality" title="Homosociality">homosociality</A>, which has led some critics to infer that Bassanio returns Antonio's affections despite his obligation to marry:<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP></P>
<BLOCKQUOTE class="templatequote">
<DIV class="poem">
<P>ANTONIO: Commend me to your honourable wife:<BR />
Tell her the process of Antonio's end,<BR />
Say how I lov'd you, speak me fair in death;<BR />
And, when the tale is told, bid her be judge<BR />
Whether Bassanio had not once a love.<BR />
BASSANIO: But life itself, my wife, and all the world<BR />
Are not with me esteemed above thy life;<BR />
I would lose all, ay, sacrifice them all<BR />
Here to this devil, to deliver you. (IV,i)</P>
</DIV>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>In his essay "Brothers and Others", published in <I>The Dyer's Hand,</I> <A href="/wiki/W._H._Auden" title="W. H. Auden">W. H. Auden</A> describes Antonio as "a man whose emotional life, though his conduct may be chaste, is concentrated upon a member of his own sex." Antonio's feelings for Bassanio are likened to a couplet from Shakespeare's <I>Sonnets</I>: "But since she pricked thee out for women's pleasure,/ Mine be thy love, and my love's use their treasure." Antonio, says Auden, embodies the words on Portia's leaden casket: "Who chooseth me, must give and hazard all he hath." Antonio has taken this potentially fatal turn because he despairs, not only over the loss of Bassanio in marriage, but also because Bassanio cannot requite what Antonio feels for him. Antonio's frustrated devotion is a form of idolatry: the right to live is yielded for the sake of the loved one. There is one other such idolator in the play: Shylock himself. "Shylock, however unintentionally, did, in fact, hazard all for the sake of destroying the enemy he hated; and Antonio, however unthinkingly he signed the bond, hazarded all to secure the happiness of the man he loved." Both Antonio and Shylock, agreeing to put Antonio's life at a forfeit, stand outside the normal bounds of society. There was, states Auden, a traditional "association of sodomy with usury", reaching back at least as far as <A href="/wiki/Dante" class="mw-redirect" title="Dante">Dante</A>, with which Shakespeare was likely familiar. (Auden sees the theme of <A href="/wiki/Usury" title="Usury">usury</A> in the play as a comment on human relations in a mercantile society.)</P>
<P>Other interpreters of the play regard Auden's conception of Antonio's sexual desire for Bassanio as questionable. Michael Radford, director of the 2004 film version starring <A href="/wiki/Al_Pacino" title="Al Pacino">Al Pacino</A>, explained that although the film contains a scene where Antonio and Bassanio actually kiss, the friendship between the two is platonic, in line with the prevailing view of male friendship at the time. <A href="/wiki/Jeremy_Irons" title="Jeremy Irons">Jeremy Irons</A>, in an interview, concurs with the director's view and states that he did not "play Antonio as gay". <A href="/wiki/Joseph_Fiennes" title="Joseph Fiennes">Joseph Fiennes</A>, however, who plays Bassanio, encouraged a homoerotic interpretation and, in fact, surprised Irons with the kiss on set, which was filmed in one take. Fiennes defended his choice, saying "I would never invent something before doing my detective work in the text. If you look at the choice of language … you'll read very sensuous language. That's the key for me in the relationship. The great thing about Shakespeare and why he's so difficult to pin down is his ambiguity. He's not saying they're gay or they're straight, he's leaving it up to his actors. I feel there has to be a great love between the two characters … there's great attraction. I don't think they have slept together but that's for the audience to decide."<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Performance_history">Performance history</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Performance history">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The earliest performance of which a record has survived was held at the court of <A href="/wiki/James_I_of_England" class="mw-redirect" title="James I of England">King James</A> in the spring of 1605, followed by a second performance a few days later, but there is no record of any further performances in the 17th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP> In 1701, <A href="/wiki/George_Granville" class="mw-redirect" title="George Granville">George Granville</A> staged a successful adaptation, titled <I>The Jew of Venice</I>, with <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Betterton" title="Thomas Betterton">Thomas Betterton</A> as Bassanio. This version (which featured a <A href="/wiki/Masque" title="Masque">masque</A>) was popular, and was acted for the next forty years. Granville cut the clownish <A href="#Characters">Gobbos</A><SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP> in line with <A href="/wiki/Neoclassicism" title="Neoclassicism">neoclassical</A> <A href="/wiki/Decorum" title="Decorum">decorum</A>; he added a jail scene between Shylock and Antonio, and a more extended scene of toasting at a banquet scene. <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Doggett" title="Thomas Doggett">Thomas Doggett</A> was Shylock, playing the role comically, perhaps even farcically. <A href="/wiki/Nicholas_Rowe_(dramatist)" class="mw-redirect" title="Nicholas Rowe (dramatist)">Rowe</A> expressed doubts about this interpretation as early as 1709; Doggett's success in the role meant that later productions would feature the troupe clown as Shylock.</P>
<P>In 1741, <A href="/wiki/Charles_Macklin" title="Charles Macklin">Charles Macklin</A> returned to the original text in a very successful production at <A href="/wiki/Theatre_Royal,_Drury_Lane" title="Theatre Royal, Drury Lane">Drury Lane</A>, paving the way for <A href="/wiki/Edmund_Kean" title="Edmund Kean">Edmund Kean</A> seventy years later (see below).<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Arthur_Sullivan" title="Arthur Sullivan">Arthur Sullivan</A> wrote <A href="/wiki/Incidental_music" title="Incidental music">incidental music</A> for the play in 1871.<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP></P>

<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Edmund_Kean_as_Shylock.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Edmund_Kean_as_Shylock.jpg/220px-Edmund_Kean_as_Shylock.jpg" width="220" height="341" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Edmund_Kean_as_Shylock.jpg/330px-Edmund_Kean_as_Shylock.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Edmund_Kean_as_Shylock.jpg/440px-Edmund_Kean_as_Shylock.jpg 2x" data-file-width="991" data-file-height="1536" /></A>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Shylock_on_stage">Shylock on stage</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Shylock on stage">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Shylock" title="Shylock">Shylock</A></DIV>
<P>Jewish actor <A href="/wiki/Jacob_Pavlovitch_Adler" class="mw-redirect" title="Jacob Pavlovitch Adler">Jacob Adler</A> and others report that the tradition of playing Shylock sympathetically began in the first half of the 19th century with <A href="/wiki/Edmund_Kean" title="Edmund Kean">Edmund Kean</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP> and that previously the role had been played "by a comedian as a repulsive <A href="/wiki/Clown" title="Clown">clown</A> or, alternatively, as a monster of unrelieved evil." Kean's Shylock established his reputation as an actor.<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<P>From Kean's time forward, all of the actors who have famously played the role, with the exception of <A href="/wiki/Edwin_Booth" title="Edwin Booth">Edwin Booth</A>, who played Shylock as a simple villain, have chosen a sympathetic approach to the character; even Booth's father, <A href="/wiki/Junius_Brutus_Booth" title="Junius Brutus Booth">Junius Brutus Booth</A>, played the role sympathetically. <A href="/wiki/Henry_Irving" title="Henry Irving">Henry Irving</A>'s portrayal of an aristocratic, proud Shylock (first seen at the Lyceum in 1879, with Portia played by <A href="/wiki/Ellen_Terry" title="Ellen Terry">Ellen Terry</A>) has been called "the summit of his career".<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP> Jacob Adler was the most notable of the early 20th century: Adler played the role in <A href="/wiki/Yiddish_theatre" title="Yiddish theatre">Yiddish</A>-language translation, first in <A href="/wiki/Manhattan" title="Manhattan">Manhattan</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Yiddish_Theater_District" class="mw-redirect" title="Yiddish Theater District">Yiddish Theater District</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Lower_East_Side,_Manhattan" class="mw-redirect" title="Lower East Side, Manhattan">Lower East Side</A>, and later on <A href="/wiki/Broadway_theatre" title="Broadway theatre">Broadway</A>, where, to great acclaim, he performed the role in <A href="/wiki/Yiddish" title="Yiddish">Yiddish</A> in an otherwise English-language production.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Kean and Irving presented a Shylock justified in wanting his <A href="/wiki/Revenge" title="Revenge">revenge</A>; Adler's Shylock evolved over the years he played the role, first as a stock Shakespearean villain, then as a man whose better nature was overcome by a desire for revenge, and finally as a man who operated not from revenge but from <A href="/wiki/Pride" title="Pride">pride</A>. In a 1902 interview with <I>Theater</I> magazine, Adler pointed out that Shylock is a wealthy man, "rich enough to forgo the interest on three thousand ducats" and that Antonio is "far from the chivalrous gentleman he is made to appear. He has insulted the Jew and spat on him, yet he comes with hypocritical politeness to borrow money of him." Shylock's fatal flaw is to depend on the law, but "would he not walk out of that courtroom head erect, the very apotheosis of defiant hatred and scorn?"<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Some modern productions take further pains to show the sources of Shylock's thirst for vengeance. For instance, in the <A href="/wiki/The_Merchant_of_Venice_(2004_film)" title="The Merchant of Venice (2004 film)">2004 film adaptation</A> directed by <A href="/wiki/Michael_Radford" title="Michael Radford">Michael Radford</A> and starring <A href="/wiki/Al_Pacino" title="Al Pacino">Al Pacino</A> as Shylock, the film begins with text and a montage of how <A href="/wiki/Venice_Ghetto" class="mw-redirect" title="Venice Ghetto">Venetian Jews</A> are cruelly abused by bigoted Christians. One of the last shots of the film also brings attention to the fact that, as a convert, Shylock would have been cast out of the Jewish community in Venice, no longer allowed to live in the ghetto. Another interpretation of Shylock and a vision of how "must he be acted" appears at the conclusion of the autobiography of <A href="/wiki/Alexander_Granach" title="Alexander Granach">Alexander Granach</A>, a noted Jewish stage and film actor in Weimar Germany (and later in Hollywood and on Broadway).<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP></P>
