<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Operas">Operas</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Operas">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Josef_Bohuslav_Foerster" title="Josef Bohuslav Foerster">Josef Bohuslav Foerster</A>'s three-act Czech opera <I>Jessika</I> was first performed at the <A href="/wiki/National_Theatre_(Prague)" title="National Theatre (Prague)">Prague National Theatre</A> on 16 April 1905.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Reynaldo_Hahn" title="Reynaldo Hahn">Reynaldo Hahn</A>'s three-act French opera <I><A href="/wiki/Le_marchand_de_Venise" title="Le marchand de Venise">Le marchand de Venise</A></I> was first performed at the <A href="/wiki/Paris_Op%C3%A9ra" class="mw-redirect" title="Paris Opéra">Paris Opéra</A> on 25 March 1935.</LI>
<LI>The late <A href="/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Tchaikowsky" title="André Tchaikowsky">André Tchaikowsky</A>'s (1935–1982) opera <I>The Merchant of Venice</I> premiered at the <A href="/wiki/Bregenz_Festival" class="mw-redirect" title="Bregenz Festival">Bregenz Festival</A><SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP> on 18 July 2013.</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Cultural_references">Cultural references</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Merchant_of_Venice&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Cultural references">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The play contains the earliest known use of the phrase "with bated breath" (by Shylock, in Act I, Scene 3, "Shall I bend low and, in a bondman's key, / With bated breath and whisp'ring humbleness, / Say this ..."), which has come into common use to convey the idea of restraining one's breathing in anticipation or supplicance (in which the archaic <I>"<A href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/bated" class="extiw" title="wikt:bated">bated</A>"</I> is often misidentified as <I>"<A href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/baited" class="extiw" title="wikt:baited">baited</A>"</I> in modern usage).<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[35]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Arnold_Wesker" title="Arnold Wesker">Arnold Wesker</A>'s play <I>The Merchant</I> tells the same story from Shylock's point of view. In this retelling, Shylock and Antonio are fast friends bound by a mutual love of books and culture and a disdain for the crass anti-Semitism of the Christian community's laws. They make the bond in defiant mockery of the Christian establishment, never anticipating that the bond might become forfeit. When it does, the play argues, Shylock must carry through on the letter of the law or jeopardise the scant legal security of the entire Jewish community. He is, therefore, quite as grateful as Antonio when Portia, as in Shakespeare's play, shows the legal way out. The play received its American premiere on 16 November 1977 at New York's <A href="/wiki/Plymouth_Theatre" class="mw-redirect" title="Plymouth Theatre">Plymouth Theatre</A>, with Joseph Leon as Shylock and <A href="/wiki/Marian_Seldes" title="Marian Seldes">Marian Seldes</A> as Shylock's sister Rivka. This production had a challenging history in previews on the road, culminating (after the first night out of town in Philadelphia on 8 September 1977) with the death of the larger-than-life Broadway star <A href="/wiki/Zero_Mostel" title="Zero Mostel">Zero Mostel</A>, who was initially cast as Shylock. The play's author, <A href="/wiki/Arnold_Wesker" title="Arnold Wesker">Arnold Wesker</A>, wrote a book chronicling the out-of-town tribulations that beset the play and Zero's death called <I>The Birth of Shylock and the Death of Zero Mostel</I>.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/David_Henry_Wilson" title="David Henry Wilson">David Henry Wilson</A>'s play <I>Shylock's Revenge</I>, which was first performed by The University Players at the <A href="/wiki/Audimax_(University_of_Hamburg)" title="Audimax (University of Hamburg)">Audimax (University of Hamburg)</A> on 9 June 1989, can be seen as a full-length sequel to Shakespeare's drama.</P>
<P>The title of the film <I><A href="/wiki/Seven_Pounds" title="Seven Pounds">Seven Pounds</A></I> is a reference to the "pound of flesh" from the play.</P>
<P>Edmond Haraucourt, the French playwright and poet, was commissioned in the 1880s by the actor and theatrical director Paul Porel to make a French-verse adaptation of <I>The Merchant of Venice</I>. His play <I>Shylock</I>, first performed at the <A href="/wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_de_l%27Od%C3%A9on" class="mw-redirect" title="Théâtre de l'Odéon">Théâtre de l'Odéon</A> in December 1889, had incidental music by the French composer <A href="/wiki/Gabriel_Faur%C3%A9" title="Gabriel Fauré">Gabriel Fauré</A>, later incorporated into an orchestral suite of the same name.<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP></P>
<P>One of the four short stories comprising <A href="/wiki/Alan_Isler" title="Alan Isler">Alan Isler</A>'s <I>Op Non Cit</I> is also told from Shylock's point of view. In this story, Antonio was a boy of Jewish origin kidnapped at an early age by priests.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Ralph_Vaughan_Williams" title="Ralph Vaughan Williams">Ralph Vaughan Williams</A>' choral work <I><A href="/wiki/Serenade_to_Music" title="Serenade to Music">Serenade to Music</A></I> draws its text from the discussion about music and the music of the spheres in Act V, scene 1.</P>
<P>In both versions of the comic film <I><A href="/wiki/To_Be_or_Not_to_Be_(1983_film)" title="To Be or Not to Be (1983 film)">To Be or Not to Be</A></I> the character "Greenberg", specified as a Jew only in the later version, gives a recitation of the "Hath Not a Jew eyes?" speech to Nazi soldiers.<SUP id="cite_ref-Bernardi2001_37-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Bernardi2001-37">[37]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In <I><A href="/wiki/The_Pianist_(memoir)" title="The Pianist (memoir)">The Pianist</A></I>, Henryk Szpilman quotes a passage from Shylock's "Hath Not a Jew eyes?" speech to his brother <A href="/wiki/W%C5%82adys%C5%82aw_Szpilman" title="Władysław Szpilman">Władysław Szpilman</A> in a Jewish ghetto in <A href="/wiki/Warsaw,_Poland" class="mw-redirect" title="Warsaw, Poland">Warsaw, Poland</A>, during the <A href="/wiki/Occupation_of_Poland_(1939%E2%80%931945)" title="Occupation of Poland (1939–1945)">Nazi occupation</A> in <A href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</A>. Given the questioning of Antisemitism in the speech and also the Nazi use of the play for antisemitic propaganda purposes, the quote is seen as particularly poignant and symbolic.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Steven_Spielberg" title="Steven Spielberg">Steven Spielberg</A>'s <I><A href="/wiki/Schindler%27s_List" title="Schindler's List">Schindler's List</A></I> depicts SS Lieutenant <A href="/wiki/Amon_G%C3%B6th" title="Amon Göth">Amon Göth</A> quoting Shylock's "Hath Not a Jew eyes?" speech when deciding whether or not to rape his Jewish maid.</P>
<P>The rock musical <I><A href="/w/index.php?title=Fire_Angel&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Fire Angel (page does not exist)">Fire Angel</A></I> was based on the story of the play, with the scene changed to the Little Italy district of New York. It was performed in <A href="/wiki/Edinburgh" title="Edinburgh">Edinburgh</A> in 1974 and in a revised form at <A href="/wiki/Her_Majesty%27s_Theatre" title="Her Majesty's Theatre">Her Majesty's Theatre</A>, London, in 1977.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Christopher_Moore_(author)" title="Christopher Moore (author)">Christopher Moore</A> combines <I>The Merchant of Venice</I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Othello" title="Othello">Othello</A></I> in his 2014 comic novel <I>The Serpent of Venice</I>, in which he makes Portia (from <I>The Merchant of Venice</I>) and Desdemona (from <I>Othello</I>) sisters. All of the characters come from those two plays with the exception of Pocket, the Fool, who comes from Moore's earlier novel based on <I><A href="/wiki/King_Lear" title="King Lear">King Lear</A></I>.</P>
<P>Jane Lindskold's book <I><A href="/wiki/Changer" title="Changer">Changer</A></I> contains a scene in which the protagonists consider "using Portia's gambit from <I>The Merchant of Venice</I>" to escape from a situation and binding contract analogous to Antonio's.</P>
<P>In its article "Unconventional Director Sets Shakespeare Play In Time, Place Shakespeare Intended", the online satirical news site <I><A href="/wiki/The_Onion" title="The Onion">The Onion</A></I> satirized the contemporary fashion of altering the play's setting.<SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The play has been quoted and paraphrased several times in the <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Trek" title="Star Trek">Star Trek</A></I> Universe:</P>
<UL>
<LI>In <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Trek_VI:_The_Undiscovered_Country" title="Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country">Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country</A></I>, while attacking the <A href="/wiki/USS_Enterprise_(NCC-1701-A)" title="USS Enterprise (NCC-1701-A)">USS Enterprise</A> in a cloaked <A href="/wiki/Klingon" title="Klingon">Klingon</A> <A href="/wiki/Bird_of_Prey_(Star_Trek)" class="mw-redirect" title="Bird of Prey (Star Trek)"><I>Bird of Prey</I></A>, <A href="/wiki/General" class="mw-redirect" title="General">General</A> <A href="/wiki/Chang_(Star_Trek)" title="Chang (Star Trek)">Chang</A> says the following: "Tickle us, do we not laugh? Prick us, do we not bleed? Wrong us, shall we not revenge?"</LI>
<LI>In "<A href="/wiki/The_Naked_Now" title="The Naked Now">The Naked Now</A>", the second episode of <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Trek:_The_Next_Generation" title="Star Trek: The Next Generation">Star Trek: The Next Generation</A></I>, an "intoxicated" Lt. Cmdr. <A href="/wiki/Data_(Star_Trek)" title="Data (Star Trek)">Data</A> paraphrases Shylock when explaining to <A href="/wiki/Jean-Luc_Picard" title="Jean-Luc Picard">Captain Picard</A> how an advanced <A href="/wiki/Android_(robot)" title="Android (robot)">android</A> can become affected similarly to a biological entity, saying, "I have pores, humans have pores. I have fingerprints, humans have fingerprints. My chemical nutrients are like your blood. If you prick me, do I not...leak?"</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Diane_Duane" title="Diane Duane">Diane Duane</A>'s novel, <I><A href="/wiki/Dark_Mirror_(Star_Trek_novel)" title="Dark Mirror (Star Trek novel)">Dark Mirror</A></I>, contains quotes from a <A href="/wiki/Mirror_Universe" title="Mirror Universe">Mirror Universe</A> version of the play. In it, Portia successfully argues that Antonio does indeed owe Shylock a pound of flesh, a sentence which is actually carried out (Antonio's heart is cut out and given to Shylock). Portia's speech is also much more authoritarian – "The quality of mercy must be earned, and not strewn gratis on the common ground..."</LI>
</UL>
<P>In the film <A href="/wiki/OSS_117:_Lost_in_Rio" title="OSS 117: Lost in Rio">OSS 117: Lost in Rio</A>, the final speech of Von Zimmel parodies Shylock's tirade.</P>
<P>In the Brazilian film <I><A href="/wiki/A_Dog%27s_Will" title="A Dog's Will">A Dog's Will</A></I>, the marriage bargain involving a lump-sum payment or the skin off Chicó's back is foiled by reference to the legal contrivance familiar from the play — that is, the skin may be owing but not a drop of blood must be taken with it.</P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Hey_Arnold!" title="Hey Arnold!">Hey Arnold!</A> episode, "Eating Contest / Rhonda's Glasses," Rhonda, becoming fed up with the treatment toward the geeks, yells “If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh?,” a direct quote from <A href="/wiki/Shylock" title="Shylock">Shylock</A>'s famous speech.</P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/David_Fincher" title="David Fincher">David Fincher</A>'s 1995 film, <I><A href="/wiki/Seven_(1995_film)" title="Seven (1995 film)">Seven</A></I>, John Doe coerces the lawyer, Eli Gould, to remove a pound of flesh and place it on a scale (symbolizing the scales of justice) prior to murdering him.</P>

<P><I><B>Rocky</B></I> is a 1976 American <A href="/wiki/Sports_film" title="Sports film">sports</A> <A href="/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television)" title="Drama (film and television)">drama film</A> directed by <A href="/wiki/John_G._Avildsen" title="John G. Avildsen">John G. Avildsen</A> and both written by and starring <A href="/wiki/Sylvester_Stallone" title="Sylvester Stallone">Sylvester Stallone</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Rocky_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rocky-2">[2]</A></SUP> It tells the <A href="/wiki/Rags_to_riches" title="Rags to riches">rags to riches</A> <A href="/wiki/American_Dream" title="American Dream">American Dream</A> story of <A href="/wiki/Rocky_Balboa" title="Rocky Balboa">Rocky Balboa</A>, an uneducated but kind-hearted <A href="/wiki/Working_class" title="Working class">working class</A> <A href="/wiki/Italian-American" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian-American">Italian-American</A> boxer working as a debt collector for a <A href="/wiki/Loan_shark" title="Loan shark">loan shark</A> in the slums of <A href="/wiki/Philadelphia" title="Philadelphia">Philadelphia</A>. Rocky starts out as a small-time <A href="/wiki/Club_fighter" title="Club fighter">club fighter</A>, and later gets a shot at the <A href="/wiki/List_of_heavyweight_boxing_champions" title="List of heavyweight boxing champions">world heavyweight championship</A>. The film also stars <A href="/wiki/Talia_Shire" title="Talia Shire">Talia Shire</A> as Adrian, <A href="/wiki/Burt_Young" title="Burt Young">Burt Young</A> as Adrian's brother Paulie, <A href="/wiki/Burgess_Meredith" title="Burgess Meredith">Burgess Meredith</A> as Rocky's trainer <A href="/wiki/Mickey_Goldmill" title="Mickey Goldmill">Mickey Goldmill</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Carl_Weathers" title="Carl Weathers">Carl Weathers</A> as the champion, <A href="/wiki/Apollo_Creed" title="Apollo Creed">Apollo Creed</A>.</P>
<P>The film, made on a budget of just over $1 million, was a <A href="/wiki/Sleeper_hit" title="Sleeper hit">sleeper hit</A>; it earned $225 million in global box office receipts, becoming the <A href="/wiki/1976_in_film" title="1976 in film">highest-grossing film of 1976</A>, and went on to win three <A href="/wiki/Academy_Awards" title="Academy Awards">Oscars</A>, including <A href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture" title="Academy Award for Best Picture">Best Picture</A>. The film received many positive reviews and turned Stallone into a major star.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> In 2006, the film was selected for preservation in the United States <A href="/wiki/National_Film_Registry" title="National Film Registry">National Film Registry</A> by the <A href="/wiki/Library_of_Congress" title="Library of Congress">Library of Congress</A> as being "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant". <I>Rocky</I> is considered to be one of <A href="/wiki/List_of_films_considered_the_best#Sports" title="List of films considered the best">the greatest sports films ever made</A> and was ranked as the second-best in the genre, after <I><A href="/wiki/Raging_Bull" title="Raging Bull">Raging Bull</A></I>, by the <A href="/wiki/American_Film_Institute" title="American Film Institute">American Film Institute</A> in 2008.</P>
<P>The film has spawned <A href="/wiki/Rocky_(film_series)" title="Rocky (film series)">six sequels</A>: <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_II" title="Rocky II">Rocky II</A></I> (1979), <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_III" title="Rocky III">Rocky III</A></I> (1982), <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_IV" title="Rocky IV">Rocky IV</A></I> (1985), <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_V" title="Rocky V">Rocky V</A></I> (1990), <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_Balboa_(film)" title="Rocky Balboa (film)">Rocky Balboa</A></I> (2006) and <I><A href="/wiki/Creed_(film)" title="Creed (film)">Creed</A></I> (2015). Stallone portrays Rocky in all six sequels, wrote the first five, and directed four (Avildsen returned to direct <I>Rocky V</I> and <A href="/wiki/Ryan_Coogler" title="Ryan Coogler">Ryan Coogler</A> directed <I>Creed</I>).</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Plot">Plot</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Plot">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>In late 1975, the <A href="/wiki/Heavyweight" title="Heavyweight">heavyweight</A> <A href="/wiki/Boxing" title="Boxing">boxing</A> world champion, Apollo Creed, announces plans to hold a <A href="/wiki/Title_bout" class="mw-redirect" title="Title bout">title bout</A> in <A href="/wiki/Philadelphia" title="Philadelphia">Philadelphia</A> during the upcoming <A href="/wiki/United_States_Bicentennial" title="United States Bicentennial">United States Bicentennial</A>. However, he is informed five weeks from the fight date that his scheduled opponent is unable to compete due to an injured hand. With all other potential replacements booked up or otherwise unavailable, Creed decides to spice things up by giving a local contender a chance to challenge him. He settles in on <A href="/wiki/Rocky_Balboa" title="Rocky Balboa">Rocky Balboa</A>, an aspiring <A href="/wiki/Southpaw_stance" title="Southpaw stance">southpaw</A> boxer from an Italian neighborhood of Philadelphia, known by the nickname "The Italian Stallion".</P>
<P>Rocky meets with <A href="/wiki/Promoter_(entertainment)" title="Promoter (entertainment)">promoter</A> Miles Jergens, unexpectedly presuming Creed is seeking local sparring partners. Reluctant at first, Rocky eventually agrees to the fight which will pay him $150,000. After several weeks of training, using whatever he can find, including meat carcasses as <A href="/wiki/Punching_bag" title="Punching bag">punching bags</A>, Rocky accepts an offer of assistance from former boxer Mickey "Mighty Mick" Goldmill, a respected trainer and former <A href="/wiki/Bantamweight" title="Bantamweight">bantamweight</A> fighter from the 1920s, who always criticized Rocky for wasting his potential.</P>
<P>Meanwhile, Rocky meets Adrian Pennino, who is working part-time at the J&M Tropical Fish <A href="/wiki/Pet_store" title="Pet store">pet store</A>. He begins to build a romantic relationship with Adrian, culminating in a kiss. Adrian's brother, Paulie, becomes jealous of Rocky's success, but Rocky calms him by agreeing to advertise his <A href="/wiki/Meat_packing_industry" title="Meat packing industry">meatpacking business</A> before the upcoming fight. The night before the fight, Rocky begins to lose confidence after touring the arena. He confesses to Adrian that he does not expect to win, but is content to <A href="/wiki/The_distance_(boxing)" title="The distance (boxing)">go the distance</A> against Creed and prove himself to everyone.</P>
<P>On <A href="/wiki/New_Year%27s_Day" title="New Year's Day">New Year's Day</A>, the fight is held, with Creed making a dramatic entrance dressed as <A href="/wiki/George_Washington" title="George Washington">George Washington</A> and then <A href="/wiki/Uncle_Sam" title="Uncle Sam">Uncle Sam</A>. Taking advantage of his overconfidence, Rocky knocks him down in the first round—the first time that Creed has ever been knocked down. Humiliated, Creed takes Rocky more seriously for the rest of the fight, though his ego never fully fades. The fight goes on for the full fifteen rounds, with both combatants sustaining various injuries. As the fight progresses, Creed's superior skill is countered by Rocky's apparently unlimited ability to absorb punches, and his dogged refusal to go down. As the final round bell sounds, with both fighters locked in each other's arms, they promise to each other that there will be no rematch.</P>
<P>After the fight, the sportscasters and the audience go wild. Jergens announces over the loudspeaker that the fight was "the greatest exhibition of guts and stamina in the history of the ring", and Rocky calls out repeatedly for Adrian, who runs down and comes into the ring as Paulie distracts arena security. As Jergens declares Creed the winner by virtue of a split decision (8:7, 7:8, 9:6), Adrian and Rocky embrace and profess their love to each other, not caring about the result of the fight.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Production">Production</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Production">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Development">Development</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Development">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Sylvester_Stallone" title="Sylvester Stallone">Sylvester Stallone</A> wrote the screenplay for <I>Rocky</I> in three and a half days, shortly after watching the championship match between <A href="/wiki/Muhammad_Ali" title="Muhammad Ali">Muhammad Ali</A> and <A href="/wiki/Chuck_Wepner" title="Chuck Wepner">Chuck Wepner</A> that took place at <A href="/wiki/Richfield_Coliseum" title="Richfield Coliseum">Richfield Coliseum</A> in <A href="/wiki/Richfield,_Ohio" title="Richfield, Ohio">Richfield, Ohio</A> on March 24, 1975. Wepner was TKO'd in the 15th round of the match by Ali, but nobody ever expected him to last as long as he did. Despite the fact that the match motivated Stallone to begin work on <I>Rocky</I>,<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> he has subsequently denied that Wepner provided any inspiration for the script.<SUP id="cite_ref-ESPN_Wepner_Recognized_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ESPN_Wepner_Recognized-5">[5]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-The_Real_Rocky_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_Real_Rocky-6">[6]</A></SUP> Other possible inspirations for the film may have included characteristics of real-life boxers <A href="/wiki/Rocky_Marciano" title="Rocky Marciano">Rocky Marciano</A> and <A href="/wiki/Joe_Frazier" title="Joe Frazier">Joe Frazier</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> as well as <A href="/wiki/Rocky_Graziano" title="Rocky Graziano">Rocky Graziano</A>'s autobiography <I>Somebody Up There Likes Me</I> and <A href="/wiki/Somebody_Up_There_Likes_Me_(1956_film)" title="Somebody Up There Likes Me (1956 film)">the movie of the same name</A>. Wepner filed a lawsuit which was eventually settled with Stallone for an undisclosed amount.<SUP id="cite_ref-The_Real_Rocky_6-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_Real_Rocky-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/United_Artists" title="United Artists">United Artists</A> liked Stallone's script, and viewed it as a possible vehicle for a well-established star such as <A href="/wiki/Robert_Redford" title="Robert Redford">Robert Redford</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ryan_O%27Neal" title="Ryan O'Neal">Ryan O'Neal</A>, <A href="/wiki/Burt_Reynolds" title="Burt Reynolds">Burt Reynolds</A>, or <A href="/wiki/James_Caan" title="James Caan">James Caan</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> Stallone insisted upon portraying the title character himself, to the point of issuing an ultimatum. Stallone later said that he would never have forgiven himself, had the film become a success with somebody else in the lead. He also knew that producers <A href="/wiki/Irwin_Winkler" title="Irwin Winkler">Irwin Winkler</A> and <A href="/wiki/Robert_Chartoff" title="Robert Chartoff">Robert Chartoff</A>'s contract with the studio enabled them to "greenlight" a project if the budget was kept low enough. The producers also collateralized any possible losses with their big-budget entry, <I><A href="/wiki/New_York,_New_York_(1977_film)" title="New York, New York (1977 film)">New York, New York</A></I> (whose eventual losses were ironically covered by <I>Rocky</I><SPAN class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'s</SPAN> success).<SUP id="cite_ref-EW_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-EW-10">[10]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> The film's production budget ended up being $1,075,000, with a further $100,000 spent on producers' fees and $4.2 million on advertising costs.<SUP id="cite_ref-BlockWilson583_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BlockWilson583-12">[12]</A></SUP></P>

<P>Although Chartoff and Winkler were enthusiastic about the script and the idea of Stallone playing the lead character, they were hesitant about having an unknown headline the film. The producers also had trouble casting other major characters in the story, with Apollo Creed and Adrian cast unusually late by production standards (both were ultimately cast on the same day). Real-life boxer <A href="/wiki/Ken_Norton" title="Ken Norton">Ken Norton</A> was initially sought for the role of <A href="/wiki/Apollo_Creed" title="Apollo Creed">Apollo Creed</A>, but he pulled out and the role was ultimately given to <A href="/wiki/Carl_Weathers" title="Carl Weathers">Carl Weathers</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP> Norton had had three fights with <A href="/wiki/Muhammad_Ali" title="Muhammad Ali">Muhammad Ali</A>, upon whom Creed was loosely based. According to <I>The Rocky Scrapbook</I>, <A href="/wiki/Carrie_Snodgress" title="Carrie Snodgress">Carrie Snodgress</A> was originally chosen to play Adrian, but a money dispute forced the producers to look elsewhere. <A href="/wiki/Susan_Sarandon" title="Susan Sarandon">Susan Sarandon</A> auditioned for the role but was deemed too pretty for the character. After <A href="/wiki/Talia_Shire" title="Talia Shire">Talia Shire</A>'s ensuing audition, Chartoff and Winkler, along with Avildsen, insisted that she play the part.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (April 2007)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>Boxer <A href="/wiki/Joe_Frazier" title="Joe Frazier">Joe Frazier</A> has a <A href="/wiki/Cameo_appearance" title="Cameo appearance">cameo appearance</A> in the film. The character of Apollo Creed was influenced by outspoken boxer <A href="/wiki/Muhammad_Ali" title="Muhammad Ali">Muhammad Ali</A> who fought Frazier three times. During the <A href="/wiki/49th_Academy_Awards" title="49th Academy Awards">49th Academy Awards</A> ceremony in 1977, Ali and Stallone staged a brief comic confrontation to show Ali was not offended by the film. Some of the plot's most memorable moments—Rocky's carcass-punching scenes and Rocky running up the steps of the <A href="/wiki/Philadelphia_Museum_of_Art" title="Philadelphia Museum of Art">Philadelphia Museum of Art</A>, as part of his training regimen—are taken from the real-life exploits of Joe Frazier, for which he received no credit.<SUP id="cite_ref-Joe_Frazier_Inspiration_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Joe_Frazier_Inspiration-14">[14]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Due to the film's comparatively low budget, members of Stallone's family played minor roles. His father rings the bell to signal the start and end of a round, his brother <A href="/wiki/Frank_Stallone" title="Frank Stallone">Frank</A> plays a street corner singer, and his first wife, Sasha, was <A href="/wiki/Unit_still_photographer" title="Unit still photographer">stills photographer</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Stalone's_wife_Rocky_photographer_15-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Stalone's_wife_Rocky_photographer-15">[15]</A></SUP> Other cameos include former Philadelphia and then-current Los Angeles television <A href="/wiki/Sports_commentator" title="Sports commentator">sportscaster</A> <A href="/wiki/Stu_Nahan" title="Stu Nahan">Stu Nahan</A> playing himself, alongside radio and TV broadcaster Bill Baldwin; and <A href="/wiki/Lloyd_Kaufman" title="Lloyd Kaufman">Lloyd Kaufman</A>, founder of the independent film company <A href="/wiki/Troma_Entertainment" title="Troma Entertainment">Troma</A>, appearing as a drunk. Diana Lewis, then a news anchor in Los Angeles and later in Detroit, has a small scene as a TV news reporter. <A href="/wiki/Tony_Burton" title="Tony Burton">Tony Burton</A> appeared as Apollo Creed's trainer, <A href="/wiki/Tony_%22Duke%22_Evers" title="Tony "Duke" Evers">Tony "Duke" Evers</A>, a role he would reprise in the entire <I>Rocky</I> series, though he is not given an official name until <I>Rocky II</I>. Though uncredited, <A href="/wiki/Michael_Dorn" title="Michael Dorn">Michael Dorn</A>, who would later gain fame as the <A href="/wiki/Klingon" title="Klingon">Klingon</A> <A href="/wiki/Worf" title="Worf">Worf</A> in <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Trek:_The_Next_Generation" title="Star Trek: The Next Generation">Star Trek: The Next Generation</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Trek:_Deep_Space_Nine" title="Star Trek: Deep Space Nine">Star Trek: Deep Space Nine</A></I>, made his acting debut as Creed's bodyguard.<SUP id="cite_ref-Trek_16-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Trek-16">[16]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Filming">Filming</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Filming">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Principal photography for <I>Rocky</I> began on January 9, 1976.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP> Filming took place primarily throughout <A href="/wiki/Philadelphia" title="Philadelphia">Philadelphia</A>, with a few scenes being shot in <A href="/wiki/Los_Angeles" title="Los Angeles">Los Angeles</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> Inventor/operator <A href="/wiki/Garrett_Brown" title="Garrett Brown">Garrett Brown</A>'s new <A href="/wiki/Steadicam" title="Steadicam">Steadicam</A> was used to accomplish smooth photography while running alongside Rocky during the film's Philadelphia street jogging/training sequences and the run up the Art Museum's flight of stairs, now colloquially known as the <A href="/wiki/Rocky_Steps" title="Rocky Steps">Rocky Steps</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP> It was also used for some of the shots in the fight scenes and can be seen at the ringside during some wide shots of the final fight. <I>Rocky</I> is often erroneously cited as the first film to use the Steadicam, although it was actually the third, after <I><A href="/wiki/Bound_for_Glory_(film)" title="Bound for Glory (film)">Bound for Glory</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Marathon_Man_(film)" title="Marathon Man (film)">Marathon Man</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Certain elements of the story were altered during filming. The original script had a darker tone: Mickey was portrayed as <A href="/wiki/Racism" title="Racism">racist</A>, and the script ended with Rocky throwing the fight after realizing he did not want to be part of the <A href="/wiki/Professional_boxing" title="Professional boxing">professional boxing</A> world after all.<SUP id="cite_ref-EW_10-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-EW-10">[10]</A></SUP></P>
<P>During filming, both Stallone and Weathers suffered injuries during the shooting of the final fight; Stallone suffered bruised ribs and Weathers suffered a damaged nose, the opposite injuries of what their characters had.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The first date between Rocky and Adrian, in which Rocky bribes a janitor to allow them to skate after closing hours in a deserted ice skating rink, was shot that way only because of budgetary pressures. This scene was originally scheduled to be shot in a skating rink during regular business hours. However, the producers decided that they could not afford to hire the hundreds of extras that would have been necessary for that scene.<SUP id="cite_ref-ReelLife_22-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ReelLife-22">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The poster seen above the ring before Rocky fights Apollo Creed shows Rocky wearing red shorts with a white stripe when he actually wears white shorts with a red stripe. When Rocky points this out, he is told that "it doesn't really matter, does it?" According to director Avildsen's DVD commentary, this was an actual mistake made by the props department that they could not afford to rectify, so Stallone wrote the brief scene to ensure the audience did not see it as a goof.<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> (Carl Weathers, coincidentally, wore white-striped red shorts for the Creed-Balboa rematch in <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_II" title="Rocky II">Rocky II</A></I>). Avildsen said that the same situation arose with Rocky's robe. When it came back from the costume department, it was far too baggy for Stallone. Because the robe arrived on the day of filming the scene and there was no chance of replacing or altering it, instead of ignoring this and risking the audience laughing at it, Stallone wrote the dialogue where Rocky himself points out the robe is too big.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Music">Music</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Music">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Rocky_(soundtrack)" title="Rocky (soundtrack)">Rocky (soundtrack)</A></DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Film_score" title="Film score">musical score</A> for <I>Rocky</I> was composed by <A href="/wiki/Bill_Conti" title="Bill Conti">Bill Conti</A>, who previously composed a score for director <A href="/wiki/John_G._Avildsen" title="John G. Avildsen">John G. Avildsen</A>'s <I><A href="/wiki/W.W._and_the_Dixie_Dancekings" title="W.W. and the Dixie Dancekings">W.W. and the Dixie Dancekings</A></I> (1975) that was ultimately rejected by the studio.<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP> In fact, <A href="/wiki/David_Shire" title="David Shire">David Shire</A> (then-husband of Talia Shire) was the first to be offered the chance to compose the music for <I>Rocky</I> but had to turn it down due to prior commitments.<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP> Thus, Avildsen reached out to Conti without any studio intervention due to the film's relatively low budget. "The budget for the music was 25 grand," said Avildsen. "And that was for everything: The composer's fee, that was to pay the musicians, that was to rent the studio, that was to buy the tape that it was going to be recorded on."<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The main <A href="/wiki/Theme_music" title="Theme music">theme song</A>, "<A href="/wiki/Gonna_Fly_Now" title="Gonna Fly Now">Gonna Fly Now</A>", made it to number one on the <I><A href="/wiki/Billboard_(magazine)" title="Billboard (magazine)">Billboard</A></I> magazine's <A href="/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100" title="Billboard Hot 100">Hot 100</A> list for one week (from July 2 to July 8, 1977) and the <A href="/wiki/American_Film_Institute" title="American Film Institute">American Film Institute</A> placed it 58th on its <A href="/wiki/AFI%27s_100_Years...100_Songs" title="AFI's 100 Years...100 Songs">AFI's 100 Years...100 Songs</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP> A soundtrack album was released on November 12, 1976 by <A href="/wiki/United_Artists_Records" title="United Artists Records">United Artists Records</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP> The album was re-released in 1988 by <A href="/wiki/EMI" title="EMI">EMI</A> on <A href="/wiki/Compact_Disc" class="mw-redirect" title="Compact Disc">CD</A> and <A href="/wiki/Compact_Cassette" title="Compact Cassette">cassette</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Reception">Reception</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Reception">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Box_office">Box office</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Box office">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><I>Rocky</I> grossed $5 million during its opening weekend and eventually reached $117 million at the North American box office.<SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP> Adjusted for inflation, the film has earned nearly $460 million in North America at 2015 prices.<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[33]</A></SUP> Overseas <I>Rocky</I> fared just as well, grossing $107 million for a worldwide box office accumulation of $225 million.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[35]</A></SUP> With its production budget of $1 million, <I>Rocky</I> is notable for its worldwide <A href="/wiki/Rate_of_return" title="Rate of return">percentage return</A> of over 11,000 percent.<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP> It was the highest-grossing film of <A href="/wiki/1976_in_film" title="1976 in film">1976</A> in the United States.<SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[37]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Critical_response">Critical response</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Critical response">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><I>Rocky</I> received positive reviews at the time of its release. <A href="/wiki/Roger_Ebert" title="Roger Ebert">Roger Ebert</A> of the <I><A href="/wiki/Chicago_Sun-Times" title="Chicago Sun-Times">Chicago Sun-Times</A></I> gave it 4 out of 4 stars and said that Stallone reminded him of "the young <A href="/wiki/Marlon_Brando" title="Marlon Brando">Marlon Brando</A>."<SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP> <I>Box Office Magazine</I> claimed that audiences would be "touting Sylvester 'Sly' Stallone as a new star".<SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[39]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[40]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Frank_Rich" title="Frank Rich">Frank Rich</A> liked the film, calling it "almost 100 per cent <A href="/wiki/Schmaltz" title="Schmaltz">schmaltz</A>," but favoring it over the cynicism that was prevalent in movies at that time, although he referred to the plot as "gimmicky" and the script "heavy-handed".<SUP id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-41">[41]</A></SUP> Several reviews, including <A href="/wiki/Richard_Eder" title="Richard Eder">Richard Eder</A>'s (as well as Canby's negative review), compared the work to that of <A href="/wiki/Frank_Capra" title="Frank Capra">Frank Capra</A>.</P>
<P>The film, however, did not escape criticism. <A href="/wiki/Vincent_Canby" title="Vincent Canby">Vincent Canby</A>, of <I><A href="/wiki/The_New_York_Times" title="The New York Times">The New York Times</A></I>, called it "pure '30s make believe" and dismissed both Stallone's acting and Avildsen's directing, calling the latter "none too decisive".<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[42]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Andrew_Sarris" title="Andrew Sarris">Andrew Sarris</A> found the Capra comparisons disingenuous: "Capra's movies projected more despair deep down than a movie like <I>Rocky</I> could envisage, and most previous ring movies have been much more cynical about the fight scene," and, commenting on Rocky's work as a loan shark, says that the film "teeters on the edge of sentimentalizing gangsters." Sarris also found Meredith "oddly cast in the kind of part the late <A href="/wiki/James_Gleason" title="James Gleason">James Gleason</A> used to pick his teeth."<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Four decades later, the film enjoys a reputation as a classic and still receives nearly universal praise; <I>Rocky</I> holds a 93% "Certified Fresh" rating on <A href="/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes" title="Rotten Tomatoes">Rotten Tomatoes</A>, based on 54 reviews, with an average rating of 8.4/10. The site's consensus states: "This story of a down-on-his-luck boxer is thoroughly predictable, but Sylvester Stallone's script and stunning performance in the title role brush aside complaints."<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP> One of the positive online reviews came from the <A href="/wiki/BBC" title="BBC">BBC</A> Films website, with both reviewer Almar Haflidason and BBC online users giving it 5/5 stars.<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP> In Steven J. Schneider's <I>1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die</I>, Schneider says the film is "often overlooked as schmaltz."<SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[46]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2006, <I>Rocky</I> was selected for preservation in the United States <A href="/wiki/National_Film_Registry" title="National Film Registry">National Film Registry</A> by the <A href="/wiki/Library_of_Congress" title="Library of Congress">Library of Congress</A> as being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[47]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP></P>

<P>The <A href="/wiki/Directors_Guild_of_America" title="Directors Guild of America">Directors Guild of America</A> awarded <I>Rocky</I> its <A href="/wiki/Directors_Guild_of_America_Award" title="Directors Guild of America Award">annual award</A> for best film of the year in 1976, and in 2006, Sylvester Stallone's original screenplay for <I>Rocky</I> was selected for the <A href="/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America_Award" title="Writers Guild of America Award">Writers Guild of America Award</A> as the 78th best screenplay of all time.<SUP id="cite_ref-Screenplay_50-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Screenplay-50">[50]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In June 2008, AFI revealed its "<A href="/wiki/AFI%27s_10_Top_10" title="AFI's 10 Top 10">Ten top Ten</A>"—the best ten films in ten "classic" American film genres—after polling over 1,500 people from the creative community. <I>Rocky</I> was acknowledged as the second-best film in the sports genre, after <I><A href="/wiki/Raging_Bull" title="Raging Bull">Raging Bull</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[51]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[52]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2008, <I>Rocky</I> was chosen by British film magazine <I><A href="/wiki/Empire_(film_magazine)" title="Empire (film magazine)">Empire</A></I> as one of <I>The 500 Greatest Movies of All Time</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[53]</A></SUP> In contrast, in a 2005 poll by <I><A href="/wiki/Empire_(film_magazine)" title="Empire (film magazine)">Empire</A></I>, Rocky was No. 9 on their list of "The Top 10 Worst Pictures to Win Best Picture Oscar".<SUP id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-54">[54]</A></SUP></P>
<P><I>Rocky</I> has also appeared on several of the <A href="/wiki/American_Film_Institute" title="American Film Institute">American Film Institute</A>'s <I><A href="/wiki/AFI_100_Years..._series" title="AFI 100 Years... series">100 Years</A></I> lists.</P>

<P>The famous scene of Rocky running up the steps of the <A href="/wiki/Philadelphia_Museum_of_Art" title="Philadelphia Museum of Art">Philadelphia Museum of Art</A> has become a cultural icon, with the steps acquiring the vernacular title of "Rocky Steps".<SUP id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-59">[59]</A></SUP> In 1982, a statue of Rocky, commissioned by Stallone for <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_III" title="Rocky III">Rocky III</A></I>, was placed at the top of the <A href="/wiki/Rocky_Steps" title="Rocky Steps">Rocky Steps</A>. City Commerce Director <A href="/wiki/Dick_Doran" title="Dick Doran">Dick Doran</A> claimed that Stallone and Rocky had done more for the city's image than "anyone since <A href="/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin" title="Benjamin Franklin">Ben Franklin</A>."<SUP id="cite_ref-RockyStatue_60-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RockyStatue-60">[60]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Differing opinions of the statue and its placement led to a relocation to the sidewalk outside the Spectrum Arena, although the statue was temporarily returned to the top of the steps in 1990 for <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_V" title="Rocky V">Rocky V</A></I>, and again in 2006 for the 30th anniversary of the original <I>Rocky</I> (although this time it was placed at the bottom of the steps). Later that year, it was permanently moved to a spot next to the steps.<SUP id="cite_ref-RockyStatue_60-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RockyStatue-60">[60]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The scene is frequently parodied in the media. In the 2008 movie <I><A href="/wiki/You_Don%27t_Mess_with_the_Zohan" title="You Don't Mess with the Zohan">You Don't Mess with the Zohan</A></I>, Zohan's nemesis, Phantom, goes through a parodied training sequence finishing with him running up a desert dune and raising his hands in victory. In the fourth-season finale of <I><A href="/wiki/The_Fresh_Prince_of_Bel-Air" title="The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air">The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air</A></I>, as the credits roll at the end of the episode, Will is seen running up the same steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art; however, as he celebrates after finishing his climb, he passes out in exhaustion, and while he lies unconscious on the ground, a pickpocket steals his wallet and his wool hat. In <I><A href="/wiki/The_Nutty_Professor_(1996_film)" title="The Nutty Professor (1996 film)">The Nutty Professor</A></I>, there is a scene where Sherman Klump (<A href="/wiki/Eddie_Murphy" title="Eddie Murphy">Eddie Murphy</A>) struggles to and eventually succeeds at running up a lengthy flight of steps on his college campus, victoriously throwing punches at the top.</P>
<P>In 2006, <A href="/wiki/E!" title="E!">E!</A> named the "Rocky Steps" scene #13 in its <I>101 Most Awesome Moments in Entertainment</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-61">[61]</A></SUP></P>
<P>During the <A href="/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics" title="1996 Summer Olympics">1996 Summer Olympics</A> torch relay, Philadelphia native <A href="/wiki/Dawn_Staley" title="Dawn Staley">Dawn Staley</A> was chosen to run up the museum steps. In <A href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_election,_2004" title="United States presidential election, 2004">2004, Presidential candidate</A> <A href="/wiki/John_Kerry" title="John Kerry">John Kerry</A> ended his pre-convention campaign at the foot of the steps before going to Boston to accept his party's nomination for President.<SUP id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-62">[62]</A></SUP></P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Adaptations_and_merchandise">Adaptations and merchandise</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Adaptations and merchandise">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Upon the film's release, a paperback <A href="/wiki/Novelization" title="Novelization">novelization</A> of the screenplay was written by <A href="/wiki/Rosalyn_Drexler" title="Rosalyn Drexler">Rosalyn Drexler</A> under the pseudonym Julia Sorel and published by <A href="/wiki/Ballantine_Books" title="Ballantine Books">Ballantine Books</A> in 1976. <SUP id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-65">[65]</A></SUP> Several <A href="/wiki/Video_game" title="Video game">video games</A> have also been made based on the film. The first <I>Rocky</I> video game was released by <A href="/wiki/Coleco" title="Coleco">Coleco</A> for <A href="/wiki/ColecoVision" title="ColecoVision">ColecoVision</A> in August 1983 titled <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_Super_Action_Boxing" title="Rocky Super Action Boxing">Rocky Super Action Boxing</A></I>; the principal designer was Coleco staffer B. Dennis Sustare. <A href="/wiki/Rocky_(1987_video_game)" title="Rocky (1987 video game)">Another</A> was released in 1987 for the <A href="/wiki/Sega_Master_System" class="mw-redirect" title="Sega Master System">Sega Master System</A>. In 1985, <A href="/wiki/Dinamic_Multimedia" title="Dinamic Multimedia">Dinamic Software</A> released a boxing game for the <A href="/wiki/ZX_Spectrum" title="ZX Spectrum">Sinclair ZX Spectrum</A> (also advertised for and/or published on the Sega Master System, Amstrad CPC and MSX) called <I>Rocky</I>. Due to copyright reasons it was quickly renamed "Rocco".<SUP id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-66">[66]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 1988, William T. Naud released a low budget parody entitled <I><A href="/wiki/Ricky_1_(film)" title="Ricky 1 (film)">Ricky 1</A></I>.</P>
<P>More recently, a <A href="/wiki/Rocky_(2002_video_game)" title="Rocky (2002 video game)"><I>Rocky</I> video game</A> was released in 2002 for the <A href="/wiki/Nintendo_GameCube" class="mw-redirect" title="Nintendo GameCube">Nintendo GameCube</A>, <A href="/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance" title="Game Boy Advance">Game Boy Advance</A>, <A href="/wiki/PlayStation_2" title="PlayStation 2">PlayStation 2</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Xbox_(console)" title="Xbox (console)">Xbox</A>, and a <A href="/wiki/Sequel" title="Sequel">sequel</A>, <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_Legends" title="Rocky Legends">Rocky Legends</A></I>, was released in 2004 for the PlayStation 2 and Xbox. In 2007, a video game called <I><A href="/wiki/Rocky_Balboa_(video_game)" title="Rocky Balboa (video game)">Rocky Balboa</A></I> was released for PSP. In 2016, <A href="/wiki/Tapinator" title="Tapinator">Tapinator, Inc.</A> released a mobile game named <I>ROCKY</I> for the iOS platform, with a planned 2017 release for Google Play and Amazon platforms.<SUP id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-67">[67]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Theatre">Theatre</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Rocky&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Theatre">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Rocky_the_Musical" title="Rocky the Musical">Rocky the Musical</A></DIV>
<P>A musical was written by <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Flaherty" title="Stephen Flaherty">Stephen Flaherty</A> and <A href="/wiki/Lynn_Ahrens" title="Lynn Ahrens">Lynn Ahrens</A> (lyrics and music), with the book by <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Meehan_(writer)" title="Thomas Meehan (writer)">Thomas Meehan</A>, based on the film. The musical premiered in <A href="/wiki/Hamburg" title="Hamburg">Hamburg</A>, Germany in October 2012. It began performances at the <A href="/wiki/Winter_Garden_Theater" class="mw-redirect" title="Winter Garden Theater">Winter Garden Theater</A> on <A href="/wiki/Broadway_theatre" title="Broadway theatre">Broadway</A> on February 11, 2014, and officially opened on March 13, 2014.<SUP id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-68">[68]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-69">[69]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-70">[70]</A></SUP></P>

<P><I><B>The Path</B></I> is an American drama <A href="/wiki/Web_television" title="Web television">web television</A> series created by <A href="/wiki/Jessica_Goldberg" title="Jessica Goldberg">Jessica Goldberg</A> and starring <A href="/wiki/Aaron_Paul" title="Aaron Paul">Aaron Paul</A>, <A href="/wiki/Michelle_Monaghan" title="Michelle Monaghan">Michelle Monaghan</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Hugh_Dancy" title="Hugh Dancy">Hugh Dancy</A>. The show portrays members of a <A href="/wiki/List_of_fictional_religions" title="List of fictional religions">fictional religion</A> known as <A href="#Meyerism">Meyerism</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The series was ordered by <A href="/wiki/Hulu" title="Hulu">Hulu</A> in March 2015 with a straight 10-episode order.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> The series was originally titled <I>The Way</I>, but was changed to <I>The Path</I> in September 2015 due to its similarity to real-life ministry and alleged cult, <A href="/wiki/The_Way_International" title="The Way International">The Way International</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> The show debuted on March 30, 2016.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> On May 4, 2016, Hulu renewed the series for a second season, which premiered on January 25, 2017.<SUP id="cite_ref-AndreevaRenewed_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AndreevaRenewed-7">[7]</A></SUP> On April 12, 2017, Hulu renewed the series for a 13-episode third season,<SUP id="cite_ref-PetskiRenewed_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-PetskiRenewed-8">[8]</A></SUP> which premiered on January 17, 2018.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On April 23, 2018, Jessica Goldberg announced via Twitter that <I>The Path</I> will not be renewed for a fourth season.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Premise">Premise</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Path_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Premise">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Eddie Lane lives in <A href="/wiki/Upstate_New_York" title="Upstate New York">Upstate New York</A> with his wife Sarah and their two children, Hawk and Summer. They are all members of the Meyerist Movement, which combines aspects of <A href="/wiki/New_Age" title="New Age">New Age</A> philosophy, <A href="/wiki/Shaman" class="mw-redirect" title="Shaman">shamanism</A>, <A href="/wiki/Scientology" title="Scientology">Scientology</A>, <A href="/wiki/Christian_mysticism" title="Christian mysticism">Christian mysticism</A> and <A href="/wiki/Utopia#Utopianism" title="Utopia">Utopianism</A> with a few elements from the <A href="/wiki/Shakers" title="Shakers">Shakers</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sufism" title="Sufism">Sufism</A>, <A href="/wiki/Tibetan_Buddhism" title="Tibetan Buddhism">Tibetan Buddhism</A> and <A href="/wiki/Freemasonry" title="Freemasonry">Freemasonry</A> ritual. Eddie returns from Peru, where he had undergone a spiritual retreat designed to advance him further up Meyerism's spiritual ladder. Unbeknownst to his family, while in Peru, Eddie experienced a revelation which causes him to question his faith in Meyerism. Meanwhile, Cal Roberts, a friend of Sarah's and one of Meyerism's top leaders, is looking to expand their influence and deal with the imminent death of their founder, Doctor Stephen Meyer.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Meyerism">Meyerism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Path_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Meyerism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Meyerism is a fictional movement in the series founded by Dr. Stephen Meyer. In the show's mythology, on October 28, 1974, Meyer literally climbed a ladder of burning light to receive the message of universal truth. Meyer gave to his followers the instructions for their spiritual development, written in the first book of Meyerism, <I>The Ladder</I>. Meyerists believe that all people are damaged which is the cause of the world's suffering. Through personal enlightenment, they seek to become aware of suffering in themselves and others, and to heal the world, caring deeply about family, humanity and the environment. In this way and others, they create the heavenly Garden of Meyer's vision here on earth. However, <I>The Ladder</I> foretells that their efforts will be thwarted by non-believers or Ignorant Systemites (I.S.) whose selfish actions will result in an apocalypse; but those who ascend The Ladder of Enlightenment will live forever in The Garden.</P>
<P>The Movement claims 6000 members with facilities located in <A href="/wiki/San_Diego" title="San Diego">San Diego, California</A>, and <A href="/wiki/New_York_(state)" title="New York (state)">Parksdale, New York</A>, with a <A href="/wiki/Retreat_(spiritual)" title="Retreat (spiritual)">retreat center</A> located in <A href="/wiki/Cusco" title="Cusco">Cusco, Peru</A>. Most practice Meyerism in everyday lives, while others have taken vows of service and dedicate themselves to counseling, recruitment and outreach programs. However, founder Stephen Meyer warned against media attention, that the movement should remain small and publicity should be kept to a minimum. Spiritual progress is evaluated on an ascending series of rungs from 1R to 10R, with many decisions made by the senior membership or Upper Rungs (U.R.). Meyerists practice meditation and use biofeedback devices and drugs—including <A href="/wiki/Ayahuasca" title="Ayahuasca">ayahuasca</A> and <A href="/wiki/Cannabis" title="Cannabis">cannabis</A>—to aid in reaching deeper levels of consciousness, and put considerable stock in visions and intuition which are believed to be The Light trying to communicate with them.</P>
<P>A <I>Vanity Fair</I> analysis of the show's first episode described Meyerism as "inspired by a grab bag of religious practices and cult beliefs".<SUP id="cite_ref-vanityfair_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-vanityfair-11">[11]</A></SUP> The show's creator, <A href="/wiki/Jessica_Goldberg" title="Jessica Goldberg">Jessica Goldberg</A>, specifically refutes comparisons to <A href="/wiki/Scientology" title="Scientology">Scientology</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-hulu_to_know_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hulu_to_know-12">[12]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-hwr_refutes_13-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hwr_refutes-13">[13]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-hwr_i_lost_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hwr_i_lost-14">[14]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Cast_and_characters">Cast and characters</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Path_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Cast and characters">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Main">Main</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Path_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Main">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Aaron_Paul" title="Aaron Paul">Aaron Paul</A> as Eddie Lane: A convert to <A href="#Meyerism">Meyerism</A> with a wayward past. Eddie suffers a crisis of faith when all that he has come to accept as truth is fundamentally challenged.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Hugh_Dancy" title="Hugh Dancy">Hugh Dancy</A> as Calvin "Cal" Roberts: The charismatic, unofficial leader of The Meyerist Movement. His ambition puts him at odds with the organization's existing leadership and roils Sarah and Eddie's already turbulent marriage.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Michelle_Monaghan" title="Michelle Monaghan">Michelle Monaghan</A> as Sarah Lane (née Armstrong): Born into a Meyerist family, Sarah's compassion and authority have made her an important figure in The Movement. Her devotion, however, is tested when she uncovers her husband's falsehoods.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Emma_Greenwell" title="Emma Greenwell">Emma Greenwell</A> as Mary Cox: An addict who's been saved by Cal and a team of Meyerists after a <A href="/wiki/Tornado" title="Tornado">tornado</A> leveled her hometown. Now freed from a life of abuse, she becomes infatuated with Cal and devotes herself entirely to The Movement.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Rockmond_Dunbar" title="Rockmond Dunbar">Rockmond Dunbar</A> as Agent Abe Gaines (seasons 1-2): An <A href="/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation" title="Federal Bureau of Investigation">FBI</A> investigator who seems to be the only agent suspicious of the mysterious religious sect that recently responded to a natural disaster. As he delves deeper into the investigation, he faces personal troubles at home and is forced to reflect on his own faith.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>Kyle Allen as Hawk Lane: Eddie and Sarah's devoted teenage son who wants nothing more than to drop out of high school and join The Movement full-time. His loyalty wavers when a popular classmate pursues a relationship with him.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>Amy Forsyth as Ashley Fields (starring season 1; recurring season 2): A popular girl at Hawk's school who would normally have nothing to do with "a weird cult kid." After a financial crisis hits home, she turns to Hawk and his family for help.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Sarah_Jones_(screen_actress)" title="Sarah Jones (screen actress)">Sarah Jones</A> as Alison Kemp (season 1): A defector of Meyerism who holds The Movement responsible for the mysterious death of her husband. She employs Eddie's help in a search for answers and redemptions.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Paul_James_(actor)" title="Paul James (actor)">Paul James</A> as Sean Egan (recurring season 1, starring season 2): A novice member of the Meyerist Movement who begins to date Mary when she joins the Movement. Sean's sister was shot and killed in a school shooting, which led him to join the Movement.<SUP id="cite_ref-PetskiJames_23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-PetskiJames-23">[23]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Freida_Pinto" title="Freida Pinto">Freida Pinto</A> as Vera Stephans (season 3): Eddie's publicist.</LI>
</UL>

<DIV class="div-col columns column-count column-count-2" style="-moz-column-count: 2; -webkit-column-count: 2; column-count: 2;">
<UL>

<LI><A href="/wiki/Deirdre_O%27Connell_(actress)" title="Deirdre O'Connell (actress)">Deirdre O'Connell</A> as Gab Armstrong</LI>

<H3><SPAN id="Season_1_.282016.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Season_1_(2016)">Season 1 (2016)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Path_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Season 1 (2016)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<TABLE class="wikitable plainrowheaders wikiepisodetable" style="width:100%">
<TBODY><TR style="color:black;text-align:center">

overall</TH>
<TH scope="col" style="background:#DAA520;width:5%"><ABBR title="Number">No.</ABBR> in<BR />
season</TH>
<TH scope="col" style="background:#DAA520">Title</TH>
<TH scope="col" style="background:#DAA520">Directed by</TH>
<TH scope="col" style="background:#DAA520">Written by</TH>
