<P>The <B>Michigan Wolverines men's basketball</B> team is the <A href="/wiki/College_basketball" title="College basketball">intercollegiate men's basketball</A> program representing the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Michigan" title="University of Michigan">University of Michigan</A>. The school competes in the <A href="/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference" title="Big Ten Conference">Big Ten Conference</A> in <A href="/wiki/NCAA_Division_I" title="NCAA Division I">Division I</A> of the <A href="/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association" title="National Collegiate Athletic Association">National Collegiate Athletic Association</A> (NCAA). The <A href="/wiki/Michigan_Wolverines" title="Michigan Wolverines">Wolverines</A> play home basketball games at the <A href="/wiki/Crisler_Arena" class="mw-redirect" title="Crisler Arena">Crisler Center</A> in <A href="/wiki/Ann_Arbor,_Michigan" title="Ann Arbor, Michigan">Ann Arbor, Michigan</A> on the university campus. Michigan has won one <A href="/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men%27s_Basketball_Championship" class="mw-redirect" title="NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Championship">NCAA Championship</A> as well as two <A href="/wiki/National_Invitation_Tournament" title="National Invitation Tournament">National Invitation Tournaments</A> (NIT), 14 <A href="/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference" title="Big Ten Conference">Big Ten Conference</A> championships and two <A href="/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="Big Ten Conference Men's Basketball Tournament">Big Ten Tournament</A> titles. In addition, it has won an NIT title and a Big Ten Tournament that were vacated due to NCAA sanctions.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p5_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p5-2">[2]</A></SUP> The team is currently coached by <A href="/wiki/John_Beilein" title="John Beilein">John Beilein</A>.</P>
<P>Michigan has had 31 <A href="/wiki/All-America" title="All-America">All-Americans</A>, selected 44 times. Eight of these have been consensus All-Americans, which are <A href="/wiki/Cazzie_Russell" title="Cazzie Russell">Cazzie Russell</A> (two times), <A href="/wiki/Rickey_Green" title="Rickey Green">Rickey Green</A>, <A href="/wiki/Gary_Grant" title="Gary Grant">Gary Grant</A>, <A href="/wiki/Chris_Webber" title="Chris Webber">Chris Webber</A>, <A href="/wiki/Trey_Burke" title="Trey Burke">Trey Burke</A>, as well as <A href="/wiki/Harry_Kipke" title="Harry Kipke">Harry Kipke</A>, Richard Doyle and <A href="/wiki/Bennie_Oosterbaan" title="Bennie Oosterbaan">Bennie Oosterbaan</A> (two-times) who were retroactively selected by the Helms Foundation.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p145_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p145-3">[3]</A></SUP> Twelve All-Americans have been at least two-time honorees. Russell was the only three-time All-American.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p13_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p13-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Michigan basketball players have been successful in professional basketball. Fifty-eight have been drafted into the <A href="/wiki/National_Basketball_Association" title="National Basketball Association">National Basketball Association</A> (NBA); twenty-six of those were first round draft picks, including both <A href="/wiki/Cazzie_Russell" title="Cazzie Russell">Cazzie Russell</A> and <A href="/wiki/Chris_Webber" title="Chris Webber">Chris Webber</A> who were drafted <A href="/wiki/List_of_first_overall_NBA_draft_picks" title="List of first overall NBA draft picks">first overall</A>. The <A href="/wiki/1990_NBA_draft" title="1990 NBA draft">1990 NBA draft</A> in which <A href="/wiki/Rumeal_Robinson" title="Rumeal Robinson">Rumeal Robinson</A> was selected 10th, <A href="/wiki/Loy_Vaught" title="Loy Vaught">Loy Vaught</A> was selected 13th, and <A href="/wiki/Terry_Mills_(basketball)" title="Terry Mills (basketball)">Terry Mills</A> was selected 16th made Michigan the third of only ten schools that have ever had three or more players selected in the first round of the same draft.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p22-3_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p22-3-5">[5]</A></SUP> Five players have gone on to become <A href="/wiki/List_of_NBA_Champions" class="mw-redirect" title="List of NBA Champions">NBA champions</A> for a total of nine times and eight players have become <A href="/wiki/NBA_All-Star_Game" title="NBA All-Star Game">NBA All-Stars</A> a total of 17 times. <A href="/wiki/Rudy_Tomjanovich" title="Rudy Tomjanovich">Rudy Tomjanovich</A> coached both the <A href="/wiki/1994_NBA_Finals" title="1994 NBA Finals">1994</A> and <A href="/wiki/1995_NBA_Finals" title="1995 NBA Finals">1995</A> NBA Finals Champions.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p22-3_5-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p22-3-5">[5]</A></SUP> Not only has <A href="/wiki/Glen_Rice" title="Glen Rice">Glen Rice</A> won both an NBA and NCAA championship, he is also one of only nine basketball players to have won a state high school championship, NCAA title and <A href="/wiki/2000_NBA_Finals" title="2000 NBA Finals">NBA championship</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P>During the 1990s Michigan endured an <A href="/wiki/University_of_Michigan_basketball_scandal" title="University of Michigan basketball scandal">NCAA violations scandal</A>, described as involving one of the largest amounts of illicit money in NCAA history, when Ed Martin loaned four players a reported total of <A href="/wiki/U.S._Dollar" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Dollar">$</A>616,000.<SUP id="cite_ref-AfFtrNtcMc_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AfFtrNtcMc-7">[7]</A></SUP> Due to NCAA sanctions, records from the 1992 <A href="/wiki/Final_Four" class="mw-redirect" title="Final Four">Final Four</A>, the 1992–93 season, and 1995–99 seasons have been vacated.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p8_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p8-8">[8]</A></SUP> Throughout this article asterisks denote awards, records and honors that have been vacated.</P>

<H2><SPAN id="Michigan.27s_history"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Michigan's_history">Michigan's history</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Michigan's history">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/List_of_Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball_seasons" title="List of Michigan Wolverines men's basketball seasons">List of Michigan Wolverines men's basketball seasons</A></DIV>
<H3><SPAN id="Early_years_.281908.E2.80.9319.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_years_(1908–19)">Early years (1908–19)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Early years (1908–19)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:212px;"><A href="/wiki/File:University_of_Michigan_basketball_1909.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/University_of_Michigan_basketball_1909.png/210px-University_of_Michigan_basketball_1909.png" width="210" height="160" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/University_of_Michigan_basketball_1909.png/315px-University_of_Michigan_basketball_1909.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/University_of_Michigan_basketball_1909.png/420px-University_of_Michigan_basketball_1909.png 2x" data-file-width="969" data-file-height="739" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:University_of_Michigan_basketball_1909.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
1909 Michigan basketball team</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:157px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Richard_F._Doyle.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Richard_F._Doyle.png/155px-Richard_F._Doyle.png" width="155" height="241" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Richard_F._Doyle.png/233px-Richard_F._Doyle.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Richard_F._Doyle.png/310px-Richard_F._Doyle.png 2x" data-file-width="388" data-file-height="603" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Richard_F._Doyle.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Richard Doyle, Michigan's First All-American basketball player</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>As a result of public and alumni demand for a basketball team, Michigan fielded a team of members of the then-current student body and achieved a 1–4 record for the 1908–09 season. However, after three years of demanding a basketball program, the student body did not attend the games and the program was terminated due to low attendance.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p190_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p190-9">[9]</A></SUP> Basketball returned in 1917 in what was considered the inaugural season of <A href="/wiki/Varsity_team" title="Varsity team">varsity</A> basketball. The team was coached by <A href="/wiki/Elmer_Mitchell" title="Elmer Mitchell">Elmer Mitchell</A> who instituted the intramural sports program at Michigan. The team finished 6–12 overall (0–10, Big Ten). The following year Mitchell led the team to a 16–8 (5–5) record.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p190_9-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p190-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Mather_era_.281919.E2.80.9328.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Mather_era_(1919–28)">Mather era (1919–28)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Mather era (1919–28)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/E._J._Mather" title="E. J. Mather">E. J. Mather</A> coached the team to three Big Ten titles in his nine seasons as coach. After inheriting Mitchell's team, which he led to a 10–13 overall (3–9, Big Ten) record during the 1919–20 season, he led the team to an 18–4 overall (8–4, Big Ten) record during the 1920–21 season.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p190_9-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p190-9">[9]</A></SUP> This 1921 team won its first eight and last eight games to tie the <A href="/wiki/Wisconsin_Badgers_men%27s_basketball" title="Wisconsin Badgers men's basketball">Wisconsin Badgers</A> and <A href="/wiki/Purdue_Boilermakers_men%27s_basketball" title="Purdue Boilermakers men's basketball">Purdue Boilermakers</A> for the Big Ten title.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p10_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p10-10">[10]</A></SUP> The team won back-to-back championships in 1925–26 and 1926–27.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p190_9-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p190-9">[9]</A></SUP> The 1926 squad, which was <A href="/wiki/Captain_(sports)" title="Captain (sports)">captained</A> by Richard Doyle who became the team's first <A href="/wiki/All-American" class="mw-redirect" title="All-American">All-American</A>, tied with Purdue, the <A href="/wiki/Iowa_Hawkeyes_men%27s_basketball" title="Iowa Hawkeyes men's basketball">Iowa Hawkeyes</A> and <A href="/wiki/Indiana_Hoosiers_men%27s_basketball" title="Indiana Hoosiers men's basketball">Indiana Hoosiers</A> for the conference championship. The 1927 team had a new All-American, <A href="/wiki/Bennie_Oosterbaan" title="Bennie Oosterbaan">Bennie Oosterbaan</A>, and won the school's first back-to-back championships and first outright championship with a 14–3 overall (10–2, Big Ten) record.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p190_9-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p190-9">[9]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p10_10-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p10-10">[10]</A></SUP> Mather died after a lengthy battle with cancer in August 1928.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p190_9-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p190-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Veenker_era_.281928.E2.80.9331.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Veenker_era_(1928–31)">Veenker era (1928–31)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Veenker era (1928–31)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/George_F._Veenker" title="George F. Veenker">George F. Veenker</A> compiled the highest overall and highest Big Ten winning percentages of any coach in school history during his three years as coach. He earned 1st(tied), 3rd and 2nd(tied) finishes during his three seasons, which included the 1928–29 conference championship. During Veenker's first season his team compiled a 13–3 overall (10–2, Big Ten) record to win the conference, and Veenker continues to be the only coach in school history to win a conference championship in his first season.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p10_10-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p10-10">[10]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p191_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p191-11">[11]</A></SUP> The championship team, which finished tied with Wisconsin, was captained by the school's third All-American <A href="/wiki/Ernie_McCoy_(athletic_director)" title="Ernie McCoy (athletic director)">Ernie McCoy</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p10_10-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p10-10">[10]</A></SUP> Veenker resigned to become the <A href="/wiki/Iowa_State_Cyclones_football" title="Iowa State Cyclones football">Iowa State Cyclones football</A> head coach.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p191_11-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p191-11">[11]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Cappon_era_.281931.E2.80.9338.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Cappon_era_(1931–38)">Cappon era (1931–38)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Cappon era (1931–38)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Franklin_Cappon" title="Franklin Cappon">Franklin Cappon</A> had a long history of association with Michigan athletics starting with his service as a four-time <A href="/wiki/Varsity_letter" title="Varsity letter">letterman</A> in football and basketball from 1919 to 1923. In 1928, he became assistant football and basketball coach and in 1929 he served as <A href="/wiki/Fielding_H._Yost" title="Fielding H. Yost">Fielding H. Yost</A>'s assistant Athletic Director.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p192_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p192-12">[12]</A></SUP> Although the highlight of Cappon's tenure as coach was a 16–4 (9–3) third place 1936–37 Big Ten finish, he coached <A href="/wiki/John_Townsend_(basketball)" title="John Townsend (basketball)">John Townsend</A> who in his 1937–38 senior season became last All-American for at least 10 years.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p13_4-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p13-4">[4]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p192-3_13-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p192-3-13">[13]</A></SUP> The team finished third in two other seasons with less impressive records of 10–8 overall (8–4, Big Ten) in 1932–33 and 15–5 overall (7–5, Big Ten) 1935–36,<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p193_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p193-14">[14]</A></SUP> and Cappon's overall record was 78–57 overall (44–40, Big Ten).<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p192_12-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p192-12">[12]</A></SUP> A notable captain during the Cappon era was 1933–34 captain <A href="/wiki/Ted_Petoskey" title="Ted Petoskey">Ted Petoskey</A>, a two-time <A href="/wiki/American_football" title="American football">football</A> All-American <A href="/wiki/End_(football)" class="mw-redirect" title="End (football)">end</A> and eventual <A href="/wiki/Major_League_Baseball" title="Major League Baseball">Major League Baseball</A> player.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p154_15-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p154-15">[15]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Oosterbaan_era_.281938.E2.80.9346.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Oosterbaan_era_(1938–46)">Oosterbaan era (1938–46)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Oosterbaan era (1938–46)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In 1938 Michigan coaching duties were assumed by one of its greatest athletes. <A href="/wiki/Bennie_Oosterbaan" title="Bennie Oosterbaan">Bennie Oosterbaan</A> had been an All-American in both football and basketball and held various coaching positions at Michigan in both of those sports as well as <A href="/wiki/Baseball" title="Baseball">baseball</A>. In basketball, he implemented a fast-paced attack as coach, and his teams' best overall record was 13–7 in 1939–40. That season he tied with his final season for his best Big Ten record at 6–6. He resigned after eight seasons to concentrate on his football coaching duties.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p192_12-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p192-12">[12]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Cowles_era_.281946.E2.80.9348.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Cowles_era_(1946–48)">Cowles era (1946–48)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Cowles era (1946–48)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Under <A href="/wiki/Ozzie_Cowles" class="mw-redirect" title="Ozzie Cowles">Ozzie Cowles</A>, during the 1947–48 season, Michigan ended the longest (19 years) consecutive year period without a conference championship in school history. They also became the first contestants in the <A href="/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament">NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament</A> during Cowles second of two seasons.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p11_16-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p11-16">[16]</A></SUP> The 1947–48 team posted a 16–6 overall (10–2, Big Ten) record. This team also posted the first undefeated home performance in school history with a 9–0 overall (6–0, Big Ten) record.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p193_14-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p193-14">[14]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="McCoy_era_.281948.E2.80.9352.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="McCoy_era_(1948–52)">McCoy era (1948–52)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: McCoy era (1948–52)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Ernie_McCoy_(athletic_director)" title="Ernie McCoy (athletic director)">Ernie McCoy</A> became the second former All-American Wolverine player to coach the team.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p145_3-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p145-3">[3]</A></SUP> Like Oosterbaan before him, he became a football and baseball coach at Michigan. He also served as assistant Athletic Director under <A href="/wiki/Fritz_Crisler" title="Fritz Crisler">Fritz Crisler</A>. During his four seasons as basketball coach, Michigan's best finish was during the 1948–49 season when they finished 15–6 overall (7–5, Big Ten) and earned a third place Big Ten Conference finish. He coached Michigan's first All-Big Ten basketball players that season in <A href="/wiki/Pete_Elliot" class="mw-redirect" title="Pete Elliot">Pete Elliot</A> and captain <A href="/wiki/Bob_Harrison_(basketball)" title="Bob Harrison (basketball)">Bob Harrison</A> who were both selected to the first team.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p194_17-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p194-17">[17]</A></SUP> Harrison returned the following season as the first repeat first-team All-Big Ten basketball player and Elliot was a second-team honoree.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p147_18-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p147-18">[18]</A></SUP> McCoy served as a football <A href="/wiki/Scout_(sport)" title="Scout (sport)">scout</A> at the same time.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p194_17-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p194-17">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Perigo_era_.281952.E2.80.9360.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Perigo_era_(1952–60)">Perigo era (1952–60)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Perigo era (1952–60)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Bill_Perigo" class="mw-redirect" title="Bill Perigo">Bill Perigo</A> took over the Michigan coaching job after having served three seasons as <A href="/wiki/Western_Michigan_Broncos_men%27s_basketball" title="Western Michigan Broncos men's basketball">Western Michigan</A> basketball coach. Despite previous success as a conference basketball champion coach at Western and subsequent success as a <A href="/wiki/Michigan_High_School_Athletic_Association" title="Michigan High School Athletic Association">Michigan High School Athletic Association</A> (MHSAA) champion basketball coach, his Michigan teams endured several mediocre seasons.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p194_17-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p194-17">[17]</A></SUP> His best Big Ten records came in 1956–57 and 1958–59 when his teams compiled 8–6 conference records. The latter team was tied for second in the conference and was 15–7 overall (8–6, Big Ten).<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p195_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p195-19">[19]</A></SUP> It also had Perigo's only first-team All-Big Ten athlete in <A href="/wiki/M._C._Burton" class="mw-redirect" title="M. C. Burton">M. C. Burton</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p147_18-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p147-18">[18]</A></SUP> Team captain and two-time football consensus All-American <A href="/wiki/Ron_Kramer" title="Ron Kramer">Ron Kramer</A> was third-team All-Big Ten in 1957 after being second-team All-Big Ten in both 1955 and 1956.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p147_18-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p147-18">[18]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Strack_era_.281960.E2.80.9368.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Strack_era_(1960–68)">Strack era (1960–68)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Strack era (1960–68)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Dave_Strack" title="Dave Strack">Dave Strack</A>, a former team 1945–46 captain, had become the freshman basketball team coach in 1948 and later had become a variety assistant to Perigo.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p195-6_20-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p195-6-20">[20]</A></SUP> He led the team to three consecutive Big Ten Championships from 1963–66 and a third-place finish in the 1964 NCAA tournament. During 1964–65 the team compiled a 24–4 overall (13–1, Big Ten) record while completing an undefeated 11–0 overall (7–0, Big Ten) home season and was the national runner-up, falling to John Wooden's UCLA in the 1965 championship game. Strack earned <A href="/wiki/United_Press_International" title="United Press International">United Press International</A> (UPI) National <A href="/wiki/UPI_College_Basketball_Coach_of_the_Year" title="UPI College Basketball Coach of the Year">Coach of the Year</A> honors. The team ended the season listed number one in both the UPI and <A href="/wiki/Associated_Press" title="Associated Press">Associated Press</A> (AP) national rankings. He recruited All-Americans Russell and Buntin to anchor his mid-1960s teams.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p195-6_20-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p195-6-20">[20]</A></SUP> Tomjanovich also became a Wolverine at the end of Strack's career and became second team All-Big Ten in 1968 subsequent later stardom.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p147_18-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p147-18">[18]</A></SUP> The 1964 team, which went 23–5 overall (11–3, Big Ten), tied with <A href="/wiki/Ohio_State_Buckeyes_men%27s_basketball" title="Ohio State Buckeyes men's basketball">Ohio State</A> with sophomore Russell and junior Buntin. In 1965, Buntin became the first Wolverine to be drafted by the NBA. In 1966, Russell led the team to its third straight conference championship and NCAA selection on his way to National <A href="/wiki/Player_of_the_Year" class="mw-redirect" title="Player of the Year">Player of the Year</A> honors.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p11_16-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p11-16">[16]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Orr_era_.281968.E2.80.9380.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Orr_era_(1968–80)">Orr era (1968–80)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Orr era (1968–80)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Orr_(basketball,_born_1927)" title="Johnny Orr (basketball, born 1927)">Johnny Orr</A>'s twelve seasons, he twice (1973–74 and 1976–77) earned Big Ten Coach of the Year honors with Big Ten championships. His teams earned four consecutive NCAA selections from 1974–77. The 25–7 overall (14–4, Big Ten) 1976 team lost to an undefeated Indiana team in the NCAA championship game, and Orr earned <A href="/wiki/National_Association_of_Basketball_Coaches" title="National Association of Basketball Coaches">National Association of Basketball Coaches</A> Coach of the Year honors that season. The 26–4 overall (16–2, Big Ten) 1977 team finished first in both the AP and UPI national rankings, and Orr won Basketball Weekly National Coach of the Year honors.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p196-8_21-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p196-8-21">[21]</A></SUP> During Orr's tenure, six players earned a total of seven All-American recognitions, which is the most of any Michigan coach.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p145_3-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p145-3">[3]</A></SUP> Steve Grote became Michigan's only three-time first-team Academic All-American from 1975–77 and with a second team All Big Ten as well as three honorable mentions was the first four-time All-Big Ten honoree.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p146-7_22-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p146-7-22">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Frieder_era_.281980.E2.80.9389.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Frieder_era_(1980–89)">Frieder era (1980–89)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Frieder era (1980–89)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Bill_Frieder" title="Bill Frieder">Bill Frieder</A>, who had been an assistant coach for seven years, took over from Orr in 1980. He coached the school's first post-season basketball champions during the 1983–84 season and the following two teams were back-to-back conference champions. The 1983–84 team compiled a 24–9 overall (11–7, Big Ten) record on their way to a NIT championship victory over <A href="/wiki/Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_men%27s_basketball" title="Notre Dame Fighting Irish men's basketball">Notre Dame</A>. The 1984–85 team went 26–4 overall (16–2, Big Ten), which earned Frieder Big Ten and AP National Coach of the Year honors. The 1985–86 team, which finished 28–5 overall (14–4, Big Ten), started the season with sixteen victories to make a total of thirty-three consecutive regular season victories. Frieder earned five of Michigan's six consecutive NCAA births from 1985–90, currently the longest streak in program history.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p12_23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p12-23">[23]</A></SUP> Roy Tarpley led the 1985 team as Big Ten MVP.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p12_23-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p12-23">[23]</A></SUP> Frieder resigned, upon request,<SUP id="cite_ref-FIDFTANJ_24-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FIDFTANJ-24">[24]</A></SUP> immediately prior to the 1989 NCAA tournament to assume the coaching job for the <A href="/wiki/Arizona_State_Sun_Devils_men%27s_basketball" title="Arizona State Sun Devils men's basketball">Arizona State Sun Devils men's basketball</A> team.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p198-200_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p198-200-25">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Fisher_era_.281989.E2.80.9397.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Fisher_era_(1989–97)">Fisher era (1989–97)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Fisher era (1989–97)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Steve_Fisher" title="Steve Fisher">Steve Fisher</A> assumed the coaching position immediately before the 1989 NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament from Frieder after having served and led the team to six straight victories and the championship. Fisher also signed the most famous recruiting class known as the <A href="/wiki/Fab_Five_(University_of_Michigan)" title="Fab Five (University of Michigan)">Fab Five</A> (<A href="/wiki/Chris_Webber" title="Chris Webber">Chris Webber</A>, <A href="/wiki/Juwan_Howard" title="Juwan Howard">Juwan Howard</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jalen_Rose" title="Jalen Rose">Jalen Rose</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jimmy_King" title="Jimmy King">Jimmy King</A> and <A href="/wiki/Ray_Jackson_(basketball)" title="Ray Jackson (basketball)">Ray Jackson</A>). He would take these players to the NCAA championship game as Freshmen and Sophomores.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p200-1_26-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p200-1-26">[26]</A></SUP> In their sophomore 1992–93 season they compiled a 31–5 overall (15–3, Big Ten) record,<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p200-1_26-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p200-1-26">[26]</A></SUP> which has since been vacated. Fisher also won the 1997 NIT tournament with a team that compiled a 25–9 overall (11–5) record.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p200-1_26-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p200-1-26">[26]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p152_27-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p152-27">[27]</A></SUP> Many of Fisher's accomplishments were tarnished by NCAA sanctions. He left the job due to the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Michigan_basketball_scandal" title="University of Michigan basketball scandal">University of Michigan basketball scandal</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-FfbpnhsGs_28-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FfbpnhsGs-28">[28]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Ellerbe_era_.281997.E2.80.932001.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Ellerbe_era_(1997–2001)">Ellerbe era (1997–2001)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Ellerbe era (1997–2001)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Brian_Ellerbe" title="Brian Ellerbe">Brian Ellerbe</A> assumed the title of interim coach less than five months after becoming an assistant coach. He was named full-time coach following the 25–9 (11–5) 1997–98 season in which he led the team to victories over Iowa, <A href="/wiki/Minnesota_Golden_Gophers_men%27s_basketball" title="Minnesota Golden Gophers men's basketball">Minnesota</A> and Purdue to capture the <A href="/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="Big Ten Conference Men's Basketball Tournament">Big Ten Conference Men's Basketball Tournament</A> championship. His subsequent teams never finished better than seventh in the conference.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p202_29-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p202-29">[29]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Amaker_era_.282001.E2.80.9307.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Amaker_era_(2001–07)">Amaker era (2001–07)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Amaker era (2001–07)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Tommy_Amaker" title="Tommy Amaker">Tommy Amaker</A> inherited a team that imposed sanctions on itself after his first year at the helm of the program.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP> Nonetheless, he coached the team to the postseason three times including both an NIT championship in 2004 and a runner-up finish in 2006. During the 2005–06, when the team compiled a 22–11 overall (8–8, Big Ten) record, he led them to their first national ranking in eight years when they reached the #20 position.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p202-3_31-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p202-3-31">[31]</A></SUP> Despite his successes, the team never won a Big Ten Championship and never made the NCAA tournament, which led to his firing after six seasons.<SUP id="cite_ref-AfFtrNtcMc_7-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AfFtrNtcMc-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Beilein_era_.282007.E2.80.93present.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Beilein_era_(2007–present)">Beilein era (2007–present)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: Beilein era (2007–present)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/John_Beilein" title="John Beilein">John Beilein</A>'s 10–22 overall (5–13 Big Ten) inaugural season featured the most losses in Michigan's history. However, in Beilein's second season, the team posted impressive non-conference victories over top-five ranked opponents UCLA and Duke. Beilein led Michigan to the 2009 NCAA Tournament, its first appearance since 1998 and the first that was not vacated since 1995.<SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP> After upsetting <A href="/wiki/Clemson_Tigers" title="Clemson Tigers">Clemson</A> in the first round, the Wolverines were eliminated by <A href="/wiki/Oklahoma_Sooners" title="Oklahoma Sooners">Oklahoma</A> in Round 2 by a final score of 73–63.<SUP id="cite_ref-N7O7M6_33-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-N7O7M6-33">[33]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Following a disappointing 15–17 season in 2009–10, the Wolverines bounced back to return to the NCAA Tournament in 2011, advancing to the round of 32 before losing to top-seeded <A href="/wiki/Duke_Blue_Devils_men%27s_basketball" title="Duke Blue Devils men's basketball">Duke</A>, 73–71. The <A href="/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2010–11 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team">2010–11 Wolverines</A>, who swept rival Michigan State for the first time since 1997, finished the season 21–14. In the <A href="/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2011–12 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team">2011–12 season</A>, Michigan split the season series with both Ohio State and Michigan State and went on to be co-Big Ten champs along with the Buckeyes and Spartans. It was the program's first Big Ten title for Michigan since 1986. The Wolverines finished the season 24-10 and 13-5 in conference play, losing in the opening round of the NCAA Tournament.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2012–13 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team">2012–13</A> Michigan team earned a #1 ranking in the <A href="/wiki/AP_Poll" title="AP Poll">AP Poll</A> on January 28, 2013, marking the first time since November 30, 1992, that Michigan held that position.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP> The team also made program history for the best season start, at 21–2. On March 31, The Wolverines defeated <A href="/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Florida_Gators_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2012–13 Florida Gators men's basketball team">Florida</A> by a score of 79–59 to make their first Final Four appearance since the 1992–93 season. The Wolverines then defeated <A href="/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Syracuse_Orange_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2012–13 Syracuse Orange men's basketball team">Syracuse</A> by a score of 61–56 in the Final Four. In the 2013 National Championship game, the Wolverines lost against <A href="/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Louisville_Cardinals_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2012–13 Louisville Cardinals men's basketball team">Louisville</A> by the score of 82–76.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2013–14 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team">2013–14</A> team had another strong season, winning Michigan's first outright Big Ten championship since 1986 and advancing to the Elite Eight of the NCAA tournament, where it lost to <A href="/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_Kentucky_Wildcats_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2013–14 Kentucky Wildcats men's basketball team">Kentucky</A>, 75–72.</P>
<P>During the <A href="/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2016–17 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team">2016–17</A> season, Beilein became the winningest coach in school history, passing <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Orr_(basketball,_born_1927)" title="Johnny Orr (basketball, born 1927)">Johnny Orr</A> with his 210th win, 75–55 over Illinois on March 9 in the opening round of the <A href="/wiki/2017_Big_Ten_Conference_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="2017 Big Ten Conference Men's Basketball Tournament">2017 Big Ten Tournament</A>. Michigan went on to win the tournament, its first since the vacated 1998 title, winning four games in four days as the #8 seed and capping it off with a 71–56 championship victory over <A href="/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Wisconsin_Badgers_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2016–17 Wisconsin Badgers men's basketball team">Wisconsin</A>.</P>
<P>During the <A href="/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2017–18 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team">2017–18</A> season, Beilein's Wolverines again won four games in four days to win back-to-back Big Ten Tournament championships for the first time in school history. The team went on to win the West regional title and advance to the Final Four following its win over <A href="/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Florida_State_Seminoles_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2017–18 Florida State Seminoles men's basketball team">Florida State</A>, 58-54. The win improved the team's record to 32-7, marking a new school record for victories. The <A href="/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball_team" title="2017–18 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team">2017–18 Michigan Wolverines men's basketball team</A> moved on to the NCAA tournament championship, where they lost against Villanova to a score of 79-62.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Fab_Five">Fab Five</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=24" title="Edit section: Fab Five">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:402px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Fab_Five_original_crop.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Fab_Five_original_crop.jpg/400px-Fab_Five_original_crop.jpg" width="400" height="156" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Fab_Five_original_crop.jpg/600px-Fab_Five_original_crop.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Fab_Five_original_crop.jpg/800px-Fab_Five_original_crop.jpg 2x" data-file-width="893" data-file-height="348" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Fab_Five_original_crop.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
The Fab Five during their sophomore year, Crisler Arena, Ann Arbor, Michigan. From left to right, Jimmy King, Jalen Rose, Chris Webber, Ray Jackson, Juwan Howard.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The Fab Five, the 1991 recruiting class of five freshman starters, were <A href="/wiki/Chris_Webber" title="Chris Webber">Chris Webber</A>, <A href="/wiki/Juwan_Howard" title="Juwan Howard">Juwan Howard</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jalen_Rose" title="Jalen Rose">Jalen Rose</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jimmy_King" title="Jimmy King">Jimmy King</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Ray_Jackson_(basketball)" title="Ray Jackson (basketball)">Ray Jackson</A>. They were notable for having gone to the championship game of the <A href="/wiki/1992_NCAA_Division_I_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="1992 NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament">1992</A> and <A href="/wiki/1993_NCAA_Division_I_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="1993 NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament">1993 NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament</A> as freshmen and sophomores, for having started the trend of wearing baggy <A href="/wiki/Gym_shorts" title="Gym shorts">gym shorts</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[37]</A></SUP> which was later popularized by <A href="/wiki/Michael_Jordan" title="Michael Jordan">Michael Jordan</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-FFLHiaHL_38-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FFLHiaHL-38">[38]</A></SUP> and for wearing black <A href="/wiki/Sock" title="Sock">athletic socks</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-FFLHiaHL_38-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FFLHiaHL-38">[38]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[39]</A></SUP> Due to the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Michigan_basketball_scandal" title="University of Michigan basketball scandal">Ed Martin scandal</A>, the records from their 1992 Final Four appearance and the entire following season have been forfeited.<SUP id="cite_ref-FFLHiaHL_38-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FFLHiaHL-38">[38]</A></SUP> Although Webber was the only member of the Fab Five officially implicated with the scandal, the reputation of the whole group has been tarnished.<SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[40]</A></SUP> Webber (1993), Howard (1994) and Rose (1992, 1994) were college basketball All-Americans.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p145_3-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p145-3">[3]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p13-21_41-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p13-21-41">[41]</A></SUP> and both King (1995 3rd team and 1993 & 1994 honorable mention) and Jackson (1995 2nd team & 1994 honorable mention) achieved All-Big Ten honors.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p147_18-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p147-18">[18]</A></SUP> All but Jackson played in the NBA.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p24-5_42-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p24-5-42">[42]</A></SUP> They were the subject of <A href="/wiki/Mitch_Albom" title="Mitch Albom">Mitch Albom</A>'s book entitled <I>Fab Five: Basketball, Trash Talk, the American Dream</I>,<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP> which at one point was under development by <A href="/wiki/Fox_Television" class="mw-redirect" title="Fox Television">Fox Television</A> as a made-for-television movie.<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP> In March 2011 <A href="/wiki/ESPN" title="ESPN">ESPN</A> broadcast a documentary, <I><A href="/wiki/The_Fab_Five_(film)" title="The Fab Five (film)">Fab Five</A></I>, that was the network's highest-rated in its history.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Ed_Martin_scandal">Ed Martin scandal</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Michigan_Wolverines_men%27s_basketball&action=edit&section=25" title="Edit section: Ed Martin scandal">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/University_of_Michigan_basketball_scandal" title="University of Michigan basketball scandal">University of Michigan basketball scandal</A></DIV>
<P>During the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Michigan_basketball_scandal" title="University of Michigan basketball scandal">University of Michigan basketball scandal</A> the Big Ten Conference, National Collegiate Athletic Association, <A href="/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation" title="Federal Bureau of Investigation">Federal Bureau of Investigation</A>, <A href="/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Service" title="Internal Revenue Service">Internal Revenue Service</A>, and <A href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice" title="United States Department of Justice">United States Department of Justice</A> investigated the relationship between the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Michigan" title="University of Michigan">University of Michigan</A>, its men's basketball teams and <A href="/wiki/Booster_(sports)" class="mw-redirect" title="Booster (sports)">basketball team booster</A> Ed Martin. The program was punished for NCAA rules violations, principally involving payments booster Martin made to several players to <A href="/wiki/Money_laundering" title="Money laundering">launder money</A> from an illegal <A href="/wiki/Gambling" title="Gambling">gambling</A> operation. It is one of the largest incidents involving payments to college athletes in American collegiate history.<SUP id="cite_ref-SwkAfrM_45-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SwkAfrM-45">[45]</A></SUP> It was described as one of the three or four worst violations of NCAA <A href="/wiki/Bylaws" class="mw-redirect" title="Bylaws">bylaws</A> in history up to that time by the NCAA infractions committee chairman and the largest athlete payment scandal ever by <A href="/wiki/ESPN" title="ESPN">ESPN</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-SwkAfrM_45-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SwkAfrM-45">[45]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-CNBMFNP_46-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CNBMFNP-46">[46]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The case began when the investigation of an automobile rollover accident during <A href="/wiki/Mateen_Cleaves" title="Mateen Cleaves">Mateen Cleaves</A>' 1996 <A href="/wiki/Michigan_Wolverines" title="Michigan Wolverines">Michigan Wolverines</A> recruiting trip revealed a curious relationship between Martin and the team. Several Michigan basketball players were implicated over the next few years and by 1999 several were called before a federal grand jury. Four eventual professional basketball players (<A href="/wiki/Chris_Webber" title="Chris Webber">Chris Webber</A>, <A href="/wiki/Maurice_Taylor" title="Maurice Taylor">Maurice Taylor</A>, <A href="/wiki/Robert_Traylor" title="Robert Traylor">Robert Traylor</A> and <A href="/wiki/Louis_Bullock" title="Louis Bullock">Louis Bullock</A>) were discovered to have borrowed a total of $616,000 from Martin.<SUP id="cite_ref-SwkAfrM_45-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SwkAfrM-45">[45]</A></SUP> During the investigation, Webber claimed not to have had any financial relationship with Martin. Eventually he confessed to having accepted some of the money he was charged with having borrowed. For his <A href="/wiki/Perjury" title="Perjury">perjury</A> during a federal grand jury investigation, he was both fined in the legal system and briefly suspended by <A href="/wiki/National_Basketball_Association" title="National Basketball Association">National Basketball Association</A> after performing public service.<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[47]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2002, the University punished itself when it became apparent that its players were guilty by declaring itself ineligible for post season play immediately, returning post season play monetary rewards, vacating five seasons of games, removing commemorative banners, and placing itself on a two-year probation.<SUP id="cite_ref-BMPBP_49-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BMPBP-49">[49]</A></SUP> The following year, the NCAA accepted these punishments, doubled both the probation period and the post-season ineligibility, penalized the school one scholarship for four seasons, and ordered disassociation from the four guilty players until 2012.<SUP id="cite_ref-CNBMFNP_46-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CNBMFNP-46">[46]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-slaps_U-M_50-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-slaps_U-M-50">[50]</A></SUP> The disasociation formally ended on May 8, 2013.<SUP id="cite_ref-AFFPMITTP_51-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AFFPMITTP-51">[51]</A></SUP> The additional year of post-season ineligibility was overturned on appeal.<SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[52]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[53]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The punishment cost the 17–13 2002–03 team its post-season eligibility, cost past teams the <A href="/wiki/1997_National_Invitation_Tournament" title="1997 National Invitation Tournament">1997 National Invitation Tournament</A> and the 1998 <A href="/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="Big Ten Conference Men's Basketball Tournament">Big Ten Tournament</A> championships as well as <A href="/wiki/1992_NCAA_Division_I_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="1992 NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament">1992</A> and <A href="/wiki/1993_NCAA_Division_I_Men%27s_Basketball_Tournament" title="1993 NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament">1993 NCAA Division I Men's Basketball Tournament</A> Final Four recognition. It cost Traylor his MVP awards in the 1997 NIT and 1998 Big Ten Tournament, as well as Bullock's standing as the school's third all-time leading scorer and all-time leader in 3-point field goals. <A href="/wiki/Steve_Fisher" title="Steve Fisher">Steve Fisher</A> lost his job as Michigan <A href="/wiki/Head_coach" title="Head coach">head coach</A> as a result of the scandal.<SUP id="cite_ref-MB07-8p8_8-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MB07-8p8-8">[8]</A></SUP></P>

<P><I><B>Cozonac</B></I> (<SMALL>Romanian pronunciation: </SMALL><SPAN title="Representation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)" class="IPA"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Romanian" title="Help:IPA/Romanian">[kozoˈnak]</A></SPAN>) or <I><B>Kozunak</B></I> (<A href="/wiki/Bulgarian_language" title="Bulgarian language">Bulgarian</A>: <SPAN lang="bg" xml:lang="bg">козунак</SPAN>, <SMALL>Bulgarian pronunciation: </SMALL><SPAN title="Representation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)" class="IPA"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Bulgarian_and_Macedonian" title="Help:IPA/Bulgarian and Macedonian">[kozuˈnak]</A></SPAN>), from <A href="/wiki/Greek_language" title="Greek language">Greek</A>: <SPAN lang="el" xml:lang="el">ϰοσώνα</SPAN> ('doll', i.e. "doll-shaped sweet bread"), is a traditional <A href="/wiki/Bulgaria" title="Bulgaria">Bulgarian</A> and <A href="/wiki/Romania" title="Romania">Romanian</A> sweet leavened bread, which is a type of <A href="/wiki/Stollen" title="Stollen">Stollen</A>. It is usually prepared for <A href="/wiki/Easter" title="Easter">Easter</A> in <A href="/wiki/Bulgaria" title="Bulgaria">Bulgaria</A>, and mostly for every major holiday (<A href="/wiki/Christmas" title="Christmas">Christmas</A>, <A href="/wiki/Easter" title="Easter">Easter</A>, New Year's Day, <A href="/wiki/Pentecost" title="Pentecost">Pentecost</A>) in <A href="/wiki/Romania" title="Romania">Romania</A> and <A href="/wiki/Moldova" title="Moldova">Moldova</A>.</P>
<P>The dessert is also known as <I><A href="/wiki/Tsoureki" title="Tsoureki">tsoureki</A></I> (<A href="/wiki/Greek_language" title="Greek language">Greek</A>: <SPAN lang="el" xml:lang="el">τσουρέκι</SPAN>), شوريك (<A href="/wiki/Arabic_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Arabic language">Arabic</A>), <I>panarët</I> (<A href="/wiki/Arb%C3%ABresh_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Arbëresh language">Arbërisht</A>), <I>choreg</I> or <I>chorek</I> (<A href="/wiki/Armenian_language" title="Armenian language">Armenian</A>: չորեկ), <I>çörək</I> (<A href="/wiki/Azerbaijani_language" title="Azerbaijani language">Azerbaijani</A>), or <I>çörek</I> (<A href="/wiki/Turkish_language" title="Turkish language">Turkish</A>). It is a sweet, egg-enriched bread, which is rooted in the cuisines of <A href="/wiki/Western_Asia" title="Western Asia">Western</A> and <A href="/wiki/Central_Asia" title="Central Asia">Central Asia</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> Such rich <A href="/wiki/Brioche" title="Brioche">brioche</A>-like breads are also traditional in many other countries, such as <A href="/wiki/Hungary" title="Hungary">Hungary</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Czech_Republic" title="Czech Republic">Czech Republic</A>. Examples of similar breads from other cultures include <I>badnji kruh</I> in <A href="/wiki/Croatian_cuisine" title="Croatian cuisine">Croatian cuisine</A>, <I>folar de páscoa</I> in <A href="/wiki/Portuguese_cuisine" title="Portuguese cuisine">Portuguese cuisine</A>, <I><A href="/wiki/Brioche" title="Brioche">brioche</A></I> in <A href="/wiki/French_cuisine" title="French cuisine">French cuisine</A>, <I><A href="/wiki/Kulich" title="Kulich">kulich</A></I> in <A href="/wiki/Russian_cuisine" title="Russian cuisine">Russian cuisine</A>, <I><A href="/wiki/Panettone" title="Panettone">panettone</A></I> in <A href="/wiki/Italian_cuisine" title="Italian cuisine">Italian cuisine</A>, and <I><A href="/wiki/Challah" title="Challah">challah</A></I> in <A href="/wiki/Jewish_cuisine" title="Jewish cuisine">Jewish cuisine</A>.</P>
<P><I>Cozonac</I> is a sweet bread, into which <A href="/wiki/Milk" title="Milk">milk</A>, <A href="/wiki/Baker%27s_yeast" title="Baker's yeast">yeast</A>, <A href="/wiki/Egg_(food)" class="mw-redirect" title="Egg (food)">eggs</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sugar" title="Sugar">sugar</A>, <A href="/wiki/Butter" title="Butter">butter</A>, and other ingredients are mixed together and allowed to rise before baking. In <A href="/wiki/Bulgaria" title="Bulgaria">Bulgaria</A>, the <I>kozunak</I> is prepared by adding lemon zest to the dough mixture, just as the Romanian version. The Italian <I><A href="/wiki/Panettone" title="Panettone">Panettone</A></I> is very similar to the basic <I>cozonac</I>, the most visible difference being their shapes.</P>
<P>In Romania, the recipes for trimmings differ rather significantly between regions. The dough is essentially similar throughout the country; a plain sweet bread made from <A href="/wiki/Wheat_flour" title="Wheat flour">flour</A>, eggs, milk, butter, sugar and salt. Depending on the region, one may add to it any of the following: <A href="/wiki/Raisin" title="Raisin">raisins</A>, <I><A href="/wiki/Turkish_delight" title="Turkish delight">rahat</A></I>, grated <A href="/wiki/Orange_(fruit)" title="Orange (fruit)">orange</A> or <A href="/wiki/Lemon" title="Lemon">lemon</A> zest, <A href="/wiki/Walnut" title="Walnut">walnuts</A> or <A href="/wiki/Hazelnut" title="Hazelnut">hazelnuts</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Vanilla" title="Vanilla">vanilla</A> or <A href="/wiki/Rum" title="Rum">rum</A> flavor. Cozonac may be sprinkled with <A href="/wiki/Poppy_seed" title="Poppy seed">poppy seeds</A> on top. Other styles dictate the use of a filling, usually a ground walnut mixture with ground poppy seeds, cocoa powder, rum essence, or raisins. The dough is rolled flat with a pin, the filling is spread and the whole is rolled back into a shape vaguely resembling a pinwheel. In the baked product, the filling forms a swirl adding to the character of the bread.</P>
<P>It was the sweet chosen to represent Romania in the <A href="/wiki/Caf%C3%A9_Europe" title="Café Europe">Café Europe</A> initiative of the Austrian presidency of the <A href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</A>, on <A href="/wiki/Europe_Day" title="Europe Day">Europe Day</A> 2006.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Origins">Origins</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Cozonac&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Origins">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>It is possible that the first <I>cozonac</I> has been made in Ancient <A href="/wiki/Egypt" title="Egypt">Egypt</A>. Perhaps it was sweetened with <A href="/wiki/Honey" title="Honey">honey</A> and filled with seeds. The <A href="/wiki/Greeks" title="Greeks">Greeks</A> took from the <A href="/wiki/Egyptians" title="Egyptians">Egyptians</A> their interest in cuisine, the <A href="/wiki/Yeast" title="Yeast">yeast</A>, and the leavened doughs. Certainly the Greeks have eaten <I>cozonac</I>. They made it with honey, raisins and walnuts. The Greek <I>cozonac</I> is called <I>plakoús</I> (πλακούς). Yeast and implicitly leavened breads, such as <I>cozonac</I>, were "stolen" from the Greeks by the <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">Romans</A>, where they added dried fruits to the <I>cozonac</I>. At first there were only two varieties called <I>libum</I> and <I>placenta</I>. <I>Libum</I> was a small cake, used as an offering to the gods. Later appeared versions were also consumed by people, not only by the gods. <I>Placenta</I>, more elaborate, is a <I>cozonac</I> made from cheese, raisins and peanuts, which was served with a sweet <A href="/wiki/Wine" title="Wine">wine</A>. Although, they took the ready-made yeast from the Greeks and the Egyptians, the Romans were the ones who discovered all the possibilities offered by the yeast added to doughs, thus becoming true masters of pastry. In the Middle Ages, European bakers often made <I>cozonac</I> with dried fruits, because they lasted longer.</P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Great_Britain" title="Great Britain">Great Britain</A>, the first recipe of <I>cozonac</I> appears in a cookbook in 1718, with the recommendation to be baked in long and narrow forms, a recommendation that remains valid nowadays. The <A href="/wiki/French_people" title="French people">French people</A>, those who in the 19th century added the third kind of meal, the dessert, are those who put forward the <I>cozonac</I>, more than others.</P>
<P>Today, this dessert with a long history is prepared mainly in the southeastern <A href="/wiki/Europe" title="Europe">European</A> countries, especially in <A href="/wiki/Romania" title="Romania">Romania</A>, <A href="/wiki/Moldova" title="Moldova">Moldova</A> and <A href="/wiki/Bulgaria" title="Bulgaria">Bulgaria</A>, where it is considered a traditional food.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>

<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">American entry into World War I</H1>			<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">
				<DIV id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</DIV>				<DIV id="contentSub"></DIV>
								<DIV id="jump-to-nav" class="mw-jump">
					Jump to:					<A href="#mw-head">navigation</A>, 					<A href="#p-search">search</A>
				</DIV>
				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><P>The <A href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">American</A> entry into <A href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</A> came in April 1917, after more than two and a half years of efforts by <A href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">President</A> <A href="/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson" title="Woodrow Wilson">Woodrow Wilson</A> to keep the <A href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</A> out of the war. Apart from an <A href="/wiki/Anglophile" title="Anglophile">Anglophile</A> element urging early support for the <A href="/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland" title="United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland">British</A>, American public opinion reflected that of the president: the sentiment for neutrality was particularly strong among <A href="/wiki/Irish_Americans" title="Irish Americans">Irish Americans</A>, <A href="/wiki/German_Americans" title="German Americans">German Americans</A> and <A href="/wiki/Scandinavian_Americans" title="Scandinavian Americans">Scandinavian Americans</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> as well as among church leaders and among women in general. On the other hand, even before <A href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</A> had broken out, American opinion had been more negative toward <A href="/wiki/German_Empire" title="German Empire">Germany</A> than towards any other country in Europe.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> Over time, especially after reports of <A href="/wiki/The_Rape_of_Belgium" class="mw-redirect" title="The Rape of Belgium">atrocities in Belgium</A> in 1914 and following the <A href="/wiki/Sinking_of_the_RMS_Lusitania" title="Sinking of the RMS Lusitania">sinking of the passenger liner <I>RMS Lusitania</I></A> in 1915, the American people increasingly came to see Germany as the aggressor in Europe.</P>
<P>As U.S. president, it was Wilson who made the key policy decisions over foreign affairs: while the country was at peace, the domestic economy ran on a <I><A href="/wiki/Laissez-faire" title="Laissez-faire">laissez-faire</A></I> basis, with American banks making huge loans to <A href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">Britain</A> and <A href="/wiki/French_Third_Republic" title="French Third Republic">France</A> — funds that were in large part used to buy munitions, raw materials, and food from across the Atlantic. Until 1917, Wilson made minimal preparations for a land war and kept the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Army" title="United States Army">United States Army</A> on a small peacetime footing, despite increasing demands for enhanced preparedness. He did however expand the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Navy" title="United States Navy">United States Navy</A>.</P>
<P>In 1917, with Russia <A href="/wiki/Russian_Revolution" title="Russian Revolution">experiencing political upheaval</A> following widespread disillusionment there over the war, and with Britain and France low on credit, Germany appeared to have the upper hand in Europe,<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> while Germany's ally, the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A>, <A href="/wiki/Middle_Eastern_theater_of_World_War_I" class="mw-redirect" title="Middle Eastern theater of World War I">clung stubbornly to its possessions in the Middle East</A>. In the same year, Germany decided to resume <A href="/wiki/Unrestricted_submarine_warfare_(February_1917)" class="mw-redirect" title="Unrestricted submarine warfare (February 1917)">unrestricted submarine warfare</A> against any vessel approaching British waters; this attempt to starve Britain into surrender was balanced against the knowledge that it would almost certainly bring the United States into the war. Germany also made a secret offer to help Mexico regain territories lost in the <A href="/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War" title="Mexican–American War">Mexican–American War</A> in an encoded telegram known as the <A href="/wiki/Zimmermann_Telegram" title="Zimmermann Telegram">Zimmermann Telegram</A>, which was intercepted by British Intelligence. Publication of that communique outraged Americans just as German <A href="/wiki/U-boat" title="U-boat">U-boats</A> started sinking American merchant ships in the <A href="/wiki/North_Atlantic" class="mw-redirect" title="North Atlantic">North Atlantic</A>. Wilson then asked <A href="/wiki/United_States_Congress" title="United States Congress">Congress</A> for "a <A href="/wiki/The_war_to_end_war" title="The war to end war">war to end all wars</A>" that would "make the world safe for democracy", and Congress voted to <A href="/wiki/United_States_declaration_of_war_on_Germany_(1917)" title="United States declaration of war on Germany (1917)">declare war on Germany on April 6, 1917</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On December 7, 1917, <A href="/wiki/United_States_declaration_of_war_on_Austria-Hungary" title="United States declaration of war on Austria-Hungary">the U.S. declared war</A> on <A href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austria-Hungary</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-AHS1_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AHS1-5">[5]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-ElseaWeed_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ElseaWeed-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P>U.S. troops began arriving on the <A href="/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_I)" title="Western Front (World War I)">Western Front</A> in large numbers in 1918.</P>
<P></P>
