<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Main_issues">Main issues</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Main issues">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <A href="/wiki/Diplomatic_history_of_World_War_I" title="Diplomatic history of World War I">Diplomatic history of World War I</A> and <A href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Woodrow_Wilson" title="Presidency of Woodrow Wilson">Presidency of Woodrow Wilson</A></DIV>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Naval_blockade">Naval blockade</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Naval blockade">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Britain used its large navy to prevent cargo vessels entering German ports, mainly by intercepting them in the <A href="/wiki/North_Sea" title="North Sea">North Sea</A> between the coasts of Scotland and Norway. The wider sea approaches to Britain and France, their distance from German harbours and the smaller size of the German surface fleet all made it harder for Germany to reciprocate. Instead, Germany used <A href="/wiki/Submarine" title="Submarine">submarines</A> to lie in wait for, and then sink, merchant ships heading for enemy ports.</P>
<P>The United States insisted on maintaining the traditional rights of ships registered in neutral countries and protested strongly against American ships being intercepted or sunk: the British seized American ships for supposed violations, while the Germans sank them — often without warning, in violation of international law that said sailors must be allowed an opportunity to reach their lifeboats. After several violations, Germany stopped this practice but in early 1917 she decided to resume unrestricted submarine warfare, in the hope that this would starve out the British before the Americans could make any effective military retaliation.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="The_strategy_behind_the_blockade">The strategy behind the blockade</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: The strategy behind the blockade">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>The British <A href="/wiki/Royal_Navy" title="Royal Navy">Royal Navy</A> successfully stopped the shipment of most war supplies and food to Germany. Neutral American ships that tried to trade with Germany were seized or turned back by the Royal Navy who viewed such trade as in direct conflict with the Allies' war efforts. The strangulation came about very slowly, because Germany and <A href="/wiki/Central_Powers" title="Central Powers">its allies</A> controlled extensive farmlands and raw materials. It was eventually successful because Germany and <A href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austria-Hungary</A> had decimated their agricultural production by taking so many farmers into their armies. By 1918, German cities were on the verge of starvation; the front-line soldiers were on short rations and were running out of essential supplies.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Germany also considered a blockade. "England wants to starve us", said Admiral <A href="/wiki/Alfred_von_Tirpitz" title="Alfred von Tirpitz">Alfred von Tirpitz</A>, the man who built the German fleet and who remained a key advisor to the <A href="/wiki/Wilhelm_II,_German_Emperor" title="Wilhelm II, German Emperor">Kaiser Wilhelm II</A>. "We can play the same game. We can bottle her up and destroy every ship that endeavors to break the blockade".<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> Unable to challenge the more powerful Royal Navy on the surface, Tirpitz wanted to scare off merchant and passenger ships en route to Britain. He reasoned that since the island of Britain depended on imports of food, raw materials, and manufactured goods, scaring off a substantial number of the ships would effectively undercut its long-term ability to maintain an army on the <A href="/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_I)" title="Western Front (World War I)">Western Front</A>. While Germany had only nine long-range <A href="/wiki/U-boat" title="U-boat">U-boats</A> at the start of the war, it had ample shipyard capacity to build the hundreds needed. However, the United States demanded that Germany respect the international agreements upon "<A href="/wiki/Freedom_of_the_seas" title="Freedom of the seas">freedom of the seas</A>", which protected neutral American ships on the high seas from seizure or sinking by either belligerent. Furthermore, Americans insisted that the drowning of innocent civilians was barbaric and grounds for a declaration of war. The British frequently violated America's neutral rights by seizing ships.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> Wilson's top advisor, Colonel <A href="/wiki/Edward_M._House" title="Edward M. House">Edward M. House</A> commented that, "The British have gone as far as they possibly could in violating neutral rights, though they have done it in the most courteous way".<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> When Wilson protested British violations of American neutrality, the British backed down.</P>
<P>German submarines torpedoed ships without warning, causing sailors and passengers to drown. Berlin explained that submarines were so vulnerable that they dared not surface near merchant ships that might be carrying guns and which were too small to rescue submarine crews. Britain armed most of its merchant ships with medium calibre guns that could sink a submarine, making above-water attacks too risky. In February 1915, the United States warned Germany about misuse of submarines. On April 22, the German Imperial Embassy warned U.S. citizens against boarding vessels to Britain, which would have to face German attack. On May 7, Germany torpedoed the British passenger liner <A href="/wiki/Sinking_of_the_RMS_Lusitania" title="Sinking of the RMS Lusitania"><I>RMS Lusitania</I>, sinking her</A>. This act of aggression caused the loss of 1,198 civilian lives, including 128 Americans. The sinking of a large, unarmed passenger ship, combined with the previous stories of atrocities in Belgium, shocked Americans and turned public opinion hostile to Germany, although not yet to the point of war. Wilson issued a warning to Germany that it would face "strict accountability" if it sank more neutral U.S. passenger ships.<SUP id="cite_ref-http://www.firstworldwar.com/wilsonwarning_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-http://www.firstworldwar.com/wilsonwarning-11">[11]</A></SUP> Berlin acquiesced, ordering its submarines to avoid passenger ships.</P>
<P>By January 1917, however, <A href="/wiki/Field_Marshal" class="mw-redirect" title="Field Marshal">Field Marshal</A> <A href="/wiki/Paul_von_Hindenburg" title="Paul von Hindenburg">Paul von Hindenburg</A> and <A href="/wiki/General" class="mw-redirect" title="General">General</A> <A href="/wiki/Erich_Ludendorff" title="Erich Ludendorff">Erich Ludendorff</A> decided that an unrestricted submarine blockade was the only way to achieve a decisive victory. They demanded that Kaiser Wilhelm order unrestricted submarine warfare be resumed. Germany knew this decision meant war with the United States, but they gambled that they could win before America's potential strength could be mobilized.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP> However, they overestimated how many ships they could sink and thus the extent Britain would be weakened. Finally, they did not foresee that <A href="/wiki/Convoy" title="Convoy">convoys</A> could and would be used to defeat their efforts. They believed that the United States was so weak militarily that it could not be a factor on the Western Front for more than a year. The civilian government in Berlin objected, but the Kaiser sided with his military.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Business_considerations">Business considerations</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Business considerations">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The beginning of war in Europe coincided with the end of the Recession of 1913–1914 in America. Exports to belligerent nations rose rapidly over the first four years of the War from $824.8 million in 1913 to $2.25 billion in 1917.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP> Loans from American financial institutions to the Allied nations in Europe also increased dramatically over the same period.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP> Economic activity towards the end of this period boomed as government resources aided the production of the private sector. Between 1914 and 1917, industrial production increased 32% and GNP increased by almost 20%.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> The improvements to industrial production in the United States outlasted the war. The capital build-up that had allowed American companies to supply belligerents and the American army resulted in a greater long-run rate of production even after the war had ended in 1918.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 1913, <A href="/wiki/J._P._Morgan,_Jr." class="mw-redirect" title="J. P. Morgan, Jr.">J. P. Morgan, Jr.</A> took over the <A href="/wiki/House_of_Morgan" class="mw-redirect" title="House of Morgan">House of Morgan</A>, an American-based investment bank consisting of separate banking operations in New York, London, and Paris, after the death of his father, <A href="/wiki/J._Pierpont_Morgan" class="mw-redirect" title="J. Pierpont Morgan">J. Pierpont Morgan</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP> The House of Morgan offered assistance in the wartime financing of Britain and France from the earliest stages of the war in 1914 through America's entrance in 1917. J.P. Morgan & Co., the House of Morgan's bank in New York, was designated as the primary financial agent to the British government in 1914 after successful lobbying by the British ambassador, <A href="/wiki/Cecil_Spring_Rice" title="Cecil Spring Rice">Sir Cecil Spring Rice</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP> The same bank would later take a similar role in France and would offer extensive financial assistance to both warring nations. J.P. Morgan &Co. became the primary issuer of loans to the French government by raising money from American investors.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP> Morgan, Harjes, the House of Morgan's French affiliated bank, controlled the majority of the wartime financial dealings between the House of Morgan and the French government after primary issuances of debt in American markets.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP> Relations between the House of Morgan and the French government became tense as the war raged on with no end in sight.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP> France's ability to borrow from other sources diminished, leading to greater lending rates and a depressing of the value of the franc. After the war, in 1918, J.P. Morgan & Co. continued to aid the French government financially through monetary stabilization and debt relief.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Because America was still a declared neutral state, the financial dealings of American banks in Europe caused a great deal of contention between Wall Street and the U.S. government. Secretary of State <A href="/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan" title="William Jennings Bryan">William Jennings Bryan</A> strictly opposed financial support of warring nations and wanted to ban loans to the belligerents in August 1914.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP> He told President Wilson that "refusal to loan to any belligerent would naturally tend to hasten a conclusion of the war." Wilson at first agreed, but then reversed himself when France argued that if it was legal to buy American goods then it was legal to take out credits on the purchase.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP></P>
<P>J.P. Morgan issued loans to France including one in March 1915 and, following negotiations with the <A href="/wiki/Anglo-French_Financial_Commission" title="Anglo-French Financial Commission">Anglo-French Financial Commission</A>, another joint loan to Britain and France in October 1915, the latter amounting to US$500,000,000.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP> Although the stance of the U.S. government was that stopping such financial assistance could hasten the end of the war and therefore save lives, little was done to insure adherence to the ban on loans, in part due to pressure from Allied governments and American business interests.<SUP id="cite_ref-Horn_2000_85–112_15-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Horn_2000_85–112-15">[15]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The American steel industry had faced difficulties and declining profits during the Recession of 1913–1914.<SUP id="cite_ref-Cuff_1970_291–306_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cuff_1970_291–306-19">[19]</A></SUP> As war began in Europe, however, the increased demand for tools of war began a period of heightened productivity that alleviated many U.S. industrial companies from the low-growth environment of the recession. <A href="/wiki/Bethlehem_Steel" title="Bethlehem Steel">Bethlehem Steel</A> took particular advantage of the increased demand for armaments abroad. Prior to American entrance into the War, these companies benefitted from unrestricted commerce with sovereign customers abroad. After President Wilson issued his declaration of war, the companies were subjected to price controls created by the U.S. Trade Commission in order to insure that the U.S. military would have access to the necessary armaments.<SUP id="cite_ref-Cuff_1970_291–306_19-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cuff_1970_291–306-19">[19]</A></SUP></P>
<P>By the end of the war in 1918, Bethlehem Steel had produced 65,000 pounds of forged military products and 70 million pounds of armor plate, 1.1 billion pounds of steel for shells, and 20.1 million rounds of artillery ammunition for Britain and France.<SUP id="cite_ref-Metz_2006_10–15_20-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Metz_2006_10–15-20">[20]</A></SUP> Bethlehem Steel took advantage of the domestic armaments market and produced 60% of the American weaponry and 40% of the artillery shells used in the War.<SUP id="cite_ref-Metz_2006_10–15_20-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Metz_2006_10–15-20">[20]</A></SUP> Even with price controls and a lower profit margin on manufactured goods, the profits resulting from wartime sales expanded the company into the third largest manufacturing company in the country. Bethlehem Steel became the primary arms supplier for the United States and other allied powers again in 1939.<SUP id="cite_ref-Metz_2006_10–15_20-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Metz_2006_10–15-20">[20]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Views_of_the_elites">Views of the elites</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Views of the elites">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Historians divide the views of American political and social leaders into four distinct groupings—the camps were mostly informal:</P>
<P>The first of these were the <A href="/wiki/Non-interventionism" title="Non-interventionism">Non-Interventionists</A>, a loosely affiliated and politically diverse anti-war movement which sought to keep the United States out of the war altogether. Members of this group tended to view the war as a clash between <A href="/wiki/British_imperialism" class="mw-redirect" title="British imperialism">British imperialism</A> and <A href="/wiki/German_militarism" class="mw-redirect" title="German militarism">German militarism</A>, both of which they regarded as equally corrupt. Others were <A href="/wiki/Pacifists" class="mw-redirect" title="Pacifists">pacifists</A>, who objected on moral grounds. Prominent leaders included Democrats like former Secretary of State <A href="/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan" title="William Jennings Bryan">William Jennings Bryan</A>, industrialist <A href="/wiki/Henry_Ford" title="Henry Ford">Henry Ford</A> and publisher <A href="/wiki/William_Randolph_Hearst" title="William Randolph Hearst">William Randolph Hearst</A>; Republicans <A href="/wiki/Robert_M._La_Follette,_Sr." class="mw-redirect" title="Robert M. La Follette, Sr.">Robert M. La Follette</A>, Senator from Wisconsin and <A href="/wiki/George_W._Norris" title="George W. Norris">George W. Norris</A>, Senator from Nebraska; and Progressive Party activist <A href="/wiki/Jane_Addams" title="Jane Addams">Jane Addams</A>.</P>
<P>At the far-left end of the political spectrum the <A href="/wiki/Socialist_Party_of_America" title="Socialist Party of America">Socialists</A>, led by their <A href="/wiki/Perennial_candidate" title="Perennial candidate">perennial candidate</A> for President <A href="/wiki/Eugene_V._Debs" title="Eugene V. Debs">Eugene V. Debs</A> and movement veterans like <A href="/wiki/Victor_L._Berger" title="Victor L. Berger">Victor L. Berger</A> and <A href="/wiki/Morris_Hillquit" title="Morris Hillquit">Morris Hillquit</A>, were staunch <A href="/wiki/Antimilitarism" title="Antimilitarism">anti-militarists</A> and opposed to any US intervention, branding the conflict as a "capitalist war" that American workers should avoid. However, after the US did join the war in April, 1917 a schism developed between the anti-war Party majority and a pro-war faction of Socialist writers, journalists and intellectuals led by <A href="/wiki/John_Spargo" title="John Spargo">John Spargo</A>, <A href="/wiki/William_English_Walling" title="William English Walling">William English Walling</A> and <A href="/wiki/E._Haldeman-Julius" title="E. Haldeman-Julius">E. Haldeman-Julius</A>. This group founded the rival <A href="/wiki/Social_Democratic_League_of_America" title="Social Democratic League of America">Social Democratic League of America</A> to promote the war effort among their fellow Socialists.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Next were the more moderate <A href="/wiki/Liberal_internationalism" title="Liberal internationalism">Liberal-Internationalists</A>. This bipartisan group reluctantly supported a declaration of war against Germany with the postwar goal of establishing collective international security institutions designed to peacefully resolve future conflicts between nations and to promote <A href="/wiki/Liberal_democracy" title="Liberal democracy">liberal democratic</A> values more broadly. This groups's views were advocated by interest groups such as the <A href="/wiki/League_to_Enforce_Peace" title="League to Enforce Peace">League to Enforce Peace</A>. Adherents included US President <A href="/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson" title="Woodrow Wilson">Woodrow Wilson</A>, his influential advisor <A href="/wiki/Edward_M._House" title="Edward M. House">Edward M. House</A>, former President <A href="/wiki/William_Howard_Taft" title="William Howard Taft">William Howard Taft</A>, famed inventor <A href="/wiki/Alexander_Graham_Bell" title="Alexander Graham Bell">Alexander Graham Bell</A>, Wall Street financier <A href="/wiki/Bernard_Baruch" title="Bernard Baruch">Bernard Baruch</A> and Harvard University President <A href="/wiki/Abbott_Lawrence_Lowell" title="Abbott Lawrence Lowell">Abbott Lawrence Lowell</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Cuff_1970_291–306_19-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cuff_1970_291–306-19">[19]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Finally, there were the so-called <A href="/wiki/Atlanticism" title="Atlanticism">Atlanticists</A>. Ardently pro-<A href="/wiki/Triple_Entente" title="Triple Entente">Entente</A>, they had strongly championed American <A href="/wiki/Interventionism_(politics)" title="Interventionism (politics)">intervention</A> in the war since 1915. Their primary political motivation was to both prepare the US for war with Germany and to forge an enduring military alliance with Great Britain. This group actively supported the <A href="/wiki/Preparedness_Movement" title="Preparedness Movement">Preparedness Movement</A> and was strong among the <A href="/wiki/Anglophile" title="Anglophile">Anglophile</A> political <A href="/wiki/The_Establishment" title="The Establishment">establishment</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Northeastern_United_States" title="Northeastern United States">northeast</A>, boasting such luminaries as former President <A href="/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt" title="Theodore Roosevelt">Theodore Roosevelt</A>, Major General <A href="/wiki/Leonard_Wood" title="Leonard Wood">Leonard Wood</A>, prominent attorney and diplomat <A href="/wiki/Joseph_Hodges_Choate" title="Joseph Hodges Choate">Joseph Hodges Choate</A>, former Secretary of War <A href="/wiki/Henry_Stimson" class="mw-redirect" title="Henry Stimson">Henry Stimson</A>, journalist <A href="/wiki/Walter_Lippman" class="mw-redirect" title="Walter Lippman">Walter Lippman</A> and Senators <A href="/wiki/Henry_Cabot_Lodge,_Sr." class="mw-redirect" title="Henry Cabot Lodge, Sr.">Henry Cabot Lodge, Sr.</A> of Massachusetts and <A href="/wiki/Elihu_Root" title="Elihu Root">Elihu Root</A> of New York.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Public_opinion">Public opinion</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Public opinion">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>A cosmopolitan group of upper and upper-middle class businessmen based in the largest cities took the lead in promoting military preparedness and in defining how far America could be pushed around before it would fight back. Many public figures hated war—Secretary of State <A href="/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan" title="William Jennings Bryan">William Jennings Bryan</A> was the most prominent, and he resigned when he thought Wilson had become too bellicose.<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Grassroots" title="Grassroots">Grassroots</A> opposition to American entry came especially from German and Irish elements.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Parties">Parties</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Parties">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>A surprising factor in the development of American public opinion was how little the political parties became involved. Wilson and the Democrats in 1916 campaigned on the slogan "He kept us out of war!", saying a Republican victory would mean war with both Mexico and Germany. His position probably was critical in winning the Western states.<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Charles_Evans_Hughes" title="Charles Evans Hughes">Charles Evans Hughes</A>, the GOP candidate, insisted on downplaying the war issue.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Socialist party talked peace. Socialist rhetoric declared the European conflict to be "an imperialist war". It won 2% of the 1916 vote for <A href="/wiki/Eugene_V._Debs" title="Eugene V. Debs">Eugene V. Debs</A>, blamed the war on capitalism and pledged total opposition. "A bayonet", its propaganda said, "was a weapon with a worker at each end".<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP> When war began, however, about half the Socialists, typified by Congressman <A href="/wiki/Meyer_London" title="Meyer London">Meyer London</A>, supported the decision and sided with the pro-Allied efforts. The rest, led by Debs, remained ideological and die-hard opponents.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP> Many socialists came under investigation from the <A href="/wiki/Espionage_Act_of_1917" title="Espionage Act of 1917">Espionage Act of 1917</A> and many suspected of treason were arrested, including Debs. This would only increase the Socialist's anti-war groups in resentment toward the American government.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Workers.2C_farmers.2C_and_African_Americans"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Workers,_farmers,_and_African_Americans">Workers, farmers, and African Americans</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Workers, farmers, and African Americans">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The working class was relatively quiet, and tended to divide along ethnic lines. At the beginning of the war, neither working men nor farmers took a large interest in the debates on war preparation.<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[33]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Gompers" title="Samuel Gompers">Samuel Gompers</A>, head of the AFL labor movement, denounced the war in 1914 as "unnatural, unjustified, and unholy", but by 1916 he was supporting Wilson's limited preparedness program, against the objections of Socialist union activists. In 1916 the labor unions supported Wilson on domestic issues and ignored the war question.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The war at first disrupted the cotton market; Britain blockaded shipments to Germany, and prices fell from 11 cents a pound to only 4 cents. By 1916, however, the British decided to bolster the price to 10 cents to avoid losing Southern support. The cotton growers seem to have moved from neutrality to intervention at about the same pace as the rest of the nation.<SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[35]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP> Midwestern farmers generally opposed the war, especially those of German and Scandinavian descent. The Midwest became the stronghold of isolationism; other remote rural areas also saw no need for war.<SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[37]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The African-American community did not take a strong position one way or the other. A month after congress declared war, <A href="/wiki/W._E._B._Du_Bois" title="W. E. B. Du Bois">W. E. B. Du Bois</A> called on African-Americans to "fight shoulder to shoulder with the world to gain a world where war shall be no more".<SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP> Once war began and black men were drafted, they worked to achieve equality.<SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[39]</A></SUP> Many had hoped the community's help in the war efforts abroad would earn civil rights at home. When such civil liberties were still not granted, many African-Americans grew tired of waiting for recognition of their rights as American citizens.<SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[40]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="South">South</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: South">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>There was a strong antiwar element in the white South and border states. In rural Missouri for example, distrust of powerful Eastern influences focused on the risk that Wall Street would lead America into war.<SUP id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-41">[41]</A></SUP> Across the South poor white farmers warned each other that "a rich man's war meant a poor man's fight," and they wanted nothing of it.<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[42]</A></SUP> Congressman James Hay, Democrat of Virginia was the powerful chairman of the House Committee on Military Affairs. He repeatedly blocked prewar efforts to modernize and enlarge the army. Preparedness was not needed because Americans were already safe, he insisted in January 1915:</P>
<DL>
<DD>Isolated as we are, safe in our vastness, protected by a great navy, and possessed of an army sufficient for any emergency that may arise, we may disregard the lamentations and predictions of the militarists.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="German_Americans">German Americans</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: German Americans">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/German_Americans" title="German Americans">German Americans</A> by this time usually had only weak ties to Germany; however, they were fearful of negative treatment they might receive if the United States entered the war (such mistreatment was already happening to German-descent citizens in Canada and Australia). Almost none called for intervening on Germany's side, instead calling for neutrality and speaking of the superiority of German culture. As more nations were drawn into the conflict, however, the English-languages press increasingly supporting Britain, while the German-American media called for neutrality while also defending Germany's position. Chicago's Germans worked to secure a complete embargo on all arms shipments to Europe. In 1916, large crowds in Chicago's Germania celebrated the Kaiser's birthday, something they had not done before the war.<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP> German Americans in early 1917 still called for neutrality, but proclaimed that if a war came they would be loyal to the United States. By this point, they had been excluded almost entirely from national discourse on the subject.<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP> Once war started, they were harassed in so many ways that historian Carl Wittke noted in 1936, it was "one of the most difficult and humiliating experiences suffered by an ethnic group in American history."<SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[46]</A></SUP> German-American Socialists in <A href="/wiki/Milwaukee" title="Milwaukee">Milwaukee</A>, <A href="/wiki/Wisconsin" title="Wisconsin">Wisconsin</A> actively campaigned against entry into the war.<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[47]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Christian_churches_and_pacifists">Christian churches and pacifists</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Christian churches and pacifists">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Come_on_in_America.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Come_on_in_America.jpg/220px-Come_on_in_America.jpg" width="220" height="272" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Come_on_in_America.jpg/330px-Come_on_in_America.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f5/Come_on_in_America.jpg 2x" data-file-width="440" data-file-height="544" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Come_on_in_America.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
<I>Come on in, America, the Blood's Fine!</I> (1917) by M.A. Kempf.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Leaders of most religious groups (except the Episcopalians) tended to pacifism, as did leaders of the woman's movement. The Methodists and Quakers among others were vocal opponents of the war.<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP> President Wilson, who was a devout Presbyterian, would often frame the war in terms of good and evil in an appeal for religious support of the war.<SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[49]</A></SUP></P>
<P>A concerted effort was made by pacifists including <A href="/wiki/Jane_Addams" title="Jane Addams">Jane Addams</A>, <A href="/wiki/Oswald_Garrison_Villard" title="Oswald Garrison Villard">Oswald Garrison Villard</A>, <A href="/wiki/David_Starr_Jordan" title="David Starr Jordan">David Starr Jordan</A>, <A href="/wiki/Henry_Ford" title="Henry Ford">Henry Ford</A>, <A href="/wiki/Lillian_Wald" title="Lillian Wald">Lillian Wald</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Carrie_Chapman_Catt" title="Carrie Chapman Catt">Carrie Chapman Catt</A>. Their goal was to encourage Wilson's efforts to mediate an end of the war by bringing the belligerents to the conference table.<SUP id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-50">[50]</A></SUP> Finally in 1917 Wilson convinced some of them that to be truly anti-war they needed to support what he promised would be "a war to end all wars".<SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[51]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Once war was declared, the more liberal denominations, which had endorsed the <A href="/wiki/Social_Gospel" title="Social Gospel">Social Gospel</A>, called for a war for righteousness that would help uplift all mankind. The theme—an aspect of <A href="/wiki/American_exceptionalism" title="American exceptionalism">American exceptionalism</A>—was that God had chosen America as his tool to bring redemption to the world.<SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[52]</A></SUP></P>
<P>American Catholic bishops maintained a general silence toward the issue of intervention. Millions of Catholics lived in both warring camps, and Catholic Americans tended to split on ethnic lines in their opinions toward American involvement in the war. At the time, heavily Catholic towns and cities in the East and Midwest often contained multiple parishes, each serving a single ethnic group, such as Irish, German, Italian, Polish, or English. American Catholics of Irish and German descent opposed intervention most strongly. Pope <A href="/wiki/Benedict_XV" class="mw-redirect" title="Benedict XV">Benedict XV</A> made several attempts to negotiate a peace. All of his efforts were rebuffed by both the Allies and the Germans, and throughout the war the Vatican maintained a policy of strict neutrality.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Jewish_Americans">Jewish Americans</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Jewish Americans">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/American_Jews" title="American Jews">Jewish American</A> sympathies likewise broke along ethnic lines, with recently arrived Yiddish speaking Jews inclined to <A href="/wiki/Zionism" title="Zionism">Zionism</A>, and the established German-American Jewish community largely opposed to it. In 1914–1916, there were few Jewish forces in favor of American entry into the war. Many regarded Britain as hostile to Jewish interests. New York City, with its well-organized element numbering 1.5 million Jews, was the center of antiwar activism.<SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[53]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-54">[54]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The different Jewish communities worked together during the war years to provide relief to Jewish communities in Eastern Europe.<SUP id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-55">[55]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-56">[56]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Of greatest concern to Jews was the tsarist regime in Russia because it was notorious for tolerating pogroms and following anti-Semitic policies. As historian Joseph Rappaport reported through his study of Yiddish press during the war, "The pro-Germanism of America's immigrant Jews was an inevitable consequence of their Russophobia".<SUP id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-57">[57]</A></SUP> The fall of the tsarist regime in March 1917 removed a major obstacle for many Jews who refused to support tsarism.<SUP id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-58">[58]</A></SUP> The draft went smoothly in New York City, and left-wing opposition to the war largely collapsed when Zionists saw the possibility of using the war to demand a state of Israel.<SUP id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-59">[59]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Irish-Americans">Irish-Americans</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Irish-Americans">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The most effective domestic opponents of the war were Irish-American Catholics. They had little interest in the continent, but were neutral about helping the <A href="/wiki/United_Kingdom" title="United Kingdom">United Kingdom</A> because it had recently enacted the <A href="/wiki/Government_of_Ireland_Act_1914" title="Government of Ireland Act 1914">Government of Ireland Act 1914</A>, allowing Irish Home Rule. However, the Act was suspended until the war ended. <A href="/wiki/John_Redmond" title="John Redmond">John Redmond</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Irish_Parliamentary_Party" title="Irish Parliamentary Party">Irish Parliamentary Party</A> (IPP) declared that Irish Volunteers should support America's pro-Allied war efforts first; his political opponents argued that it was not the time to support Britain in its attempt to "strengthen and expand her empire".<SUP id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-60">[60]</A></SUP> The attacks on the IPP and pro-Allied press showed a firm belief that a German victory would hasten the achievement of Irish independence. Yet rather than proposing intervention on behalf of the Germans, Irish American leaders and organizations focused on demanding American <A href="/wiki/Neutrality_(international_relations)" class="mw-redirect" title="Neutrality (international relations)">neutrality</A>. But the increased contact between militant Irish nationalists and German agents in the United States only fueled concerns of where the primary loyalties of Irish Americans lay.<SUP id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-61">[61]</A></SUP> Nevertheless, close to 1,000 Irish-born Americans died fighting with the U.S. armed forces in WWI.<SUP id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-62">[62]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Easter_Rising" title="Easter Rising">Easter Rising</A> in Dublin in April 1916 was crushed within a week and its leaders <A href="/wiki/Execution_by_firing_squad" title="Execution by firing squad">executed by firing squad</A>. The mainstream American press treated the uprising as foolish and misguided, and theorized it was largely inspired by the Germans. Overall public opinion remained faithfully pro-British.<SUP id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-63">[63]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Irish-Americans dominated the Democratic party in many large cities so Wilson had to take account of their views. They did not prevent him from being hostile to Germany, but they did force him to keep his distance from Britain. Indeed, Irish-American pressure influenced the United States into not accepting Britain's war aims as its own and define its own objectives, primarily <A href="/wiki/Self-determination" title="Self-determination">self-determination</A>. The Irish-American community thought they had Wilson's promise to promote Irish independence in exchange for their support of his war policies, but after the war they were bitterly disappointed by his refusal to support them in 1919.<SUP id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-64">[64]</A></SUP> Wilson saw the Irish situation purely as an internal UK matter and did not perceive the dispute and the unrest in Ireland as comparable to the plight of the various nationalities in Europe as a fall-out from World War I.<SUP id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-65">[65]</A></SUP> The progress of the <A href="/wiki/Irish_Race_Conventions" title="Irish Race Conventions">Irish Race Conventions</A> give a flavour of the differing and changing opinions during the war.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Pro-Allied_immigrants">Pro-Allied immigrants</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Pro-Allied immigrants">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Some British immigrants worked actively for intervention. London-born <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Insull" title="Samuel Insull">Samuel Insull</A>, Chicago's leading industrialist, for example, enthusiastically provided money, propaganda, and means for volunteers to enter the British or Canadian armies. After the United States' entry, Insull directed the Illinois State Council of Defense, with responsibility for organizing the state's mobilization.<SUP id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-66">[66]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Immigrants from eastern Europe usually cared more about politics in their homeland than politics in the United States. Spokesmen for Slavic immigrants hoped that an Allied victory would bring independence for their homelands.<SUP id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-67">[67]</A></SUP> Large numbers of Hungarian immigrants who were liberal and nationalist in sentiment, and sought an independent Hungary, separate from the Austro-Hungarian Empire lobbied in favor of the war and allied themselves with the Atlanticist or Anglophile portion of the population. This community was largely pro-British and anti-German in sentiment.<SUP id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-68">[68]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-69">[69]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-70">[70]</A></SUP> Albanian-Americans in communities such as Boston also campaigned for entry into the war and were overwhelmingly pro-British and anti-German, as well as hopeful the war would lead to an independent Albania which would be free from the Ottoman Empire.<SUP id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-71">[71]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Polish_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Polish people">Polish</A>, <A href="/wiki/Slovaks" title="Slovaks">Slovak</A>, and <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_Czech_Lands" class="mw-redirect" title="History of the Czech Lands">Czech</A> immigrants were enthusiastically pro-war and generally pro-British.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Popular_pacifism">Popular pacifism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Popular pacifism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:IDidntRaiseMyBoyToBeASoldierCoverMorton.jpeg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/IDidntRaiseMyBoyToBeASoldierCoverMorton.jpeg/220px-IDidntRaiseMyBoyToBeASoldierCoverMorton.jpeg" width="220" height="284" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/IDidntRaiseMyBoyToBeASoldierCoverMorton.jpeg/330px-IDidntRaiseMyBoyToBeASoldierCoverMorton.jpeg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/IDidntRaiseMyBoyToBeASoldierCoverMorton.jpeg/440px-IDidntRaiseMyBoyToBeASoldierCoverMorton.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="1587" data-file-height="2051" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:IDidntRaiseMyBoyToBeASoldierCoverMorton.jpeg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
The song "<A href="/wiki/I_Didn%27t_Raise_My_Boy_To_Be_A_Soldier" class="mw-redirect" title="I Didn't Raise My Boy To Be A Soldier">I Didn't Raise My Boy To Be A Soldier</A>" was a hit in 1915, selling 650,000 copies. Its expression of popular pacifist sentiment "helped make the pacifist movement a hard, quantifiable political reality to be reckoned with."<SUP id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-72">[72]</A></SUP></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P><A href="/wiki/Henry_Ford" title="Henry Ford">Henry Ford</A> supported the pacifist cause by sponsoring a large-scale private peace mission, with numerous activists and intellectuals aboard the "<A href="/wiki/Peace_Ship" title="Peace Ship">Peace Ship</A>' (the ocean liner Oscar II). Ford chartered the ship in 1915 and invited prominent peace activists to join him to meet with leaders on both sides in Europe. He hoped to create enough publicity to prompt the belligerent nations to convene a peace conference and mediate an end to the war. The mission was widely mocked by the press, which wrote about the "Ship of Fools." Infighting between the activists, mockery by the press contingent aboard, and an outbreak of influenza marred the voyage. Four days after the ship arrived in neutral Norway, a beleaguered and physically ill Ford abandoned the mission and returned to the United States; he had demonstrated that independent small efforts accomplished nothing.<SUP id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-73">[73]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="German_agents">German agents</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: German agents">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>On July 24, 1915, the German embassy's commercial attaché, <A href="/wiki/Heinrich_Albert" title="Heinrich Albert">Heinrich Albert</A>, left his briefcase on a train in New York City, where an alert Secret Service agent, Frank Burke, snatched it up.<SUP id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-74">[74]</A></SUP> Wilson let the newspapers publish the contents, which indicated a systematic effort by Berlin to subsidize friendly newspapers and block British purchases of war materials. Berlin's top espionage agent, debonnaire <A href="/wiki/Franz_von_Rintelen" title="Franz von Rintelen">Franz Rintelen von Kleist</A> was spending millions to finance sabotage in Canada, stir up trouble between the United States and Mexico and to incite labor strikes. The British were engaged in propaganda too, though not illegal espionage. But they did not get caught.<SUP id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-75">[75]</A></SUP> Germany took the blame as Americans grew ever more worried about the vulnerability of a free society to subversion. Indeed, one of the main fears Americans of all stations had in 1916–1919 was that spies and saboteurs were everywhere. This sentiment played a major role in arousing fear of Germany, and suspicions regarding everyone of German descent who could not "prove" 100% loyalty.<SUP id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-76">[76]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Preparedness_movement">Preparedness movement</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=American_entry_into_World_War_I&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: Preparedness movement">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<TABLE class="plainlinks metadata ambox ambox-content ambox-Refimprove" role="presentation">
<TBODY><TR>
<TD class="mbox-image">
<DIV style="width:52px"><A href="/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/50px-Question_book-new.svg.png" width="50" height="39" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/75px-Question_book-new.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/100px-Question_book-new.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="512" data-file-height="399" /></A></DIV>
</TD>
